11 Now begins the fourth section, the Yajñavaibhava-khaṇḍa, of the Sūta-saṃhitā.
Therein begins the first chapter:
[I bow] with reverence to the Lord, who is free from beginning and end and is most beautiful.
I bow to the form of Śiva accompanied by Umā, the medicine for the poison of saṃsāra. || 1 ||
Although the nature of knowledge and its status as a means to liberation were stated in the previous chapter, nevertheless:
"Those who eat the nectar of the remnants of sacrifice go to the eternal Brahman."

Based on such words of the Blessed One as, "This world does not exist for one who does not sacrifice; how then could another [world] exist, O best of the Kurus?", and because we observe that the word "sacrifice" (yajña) is established solely in the sense of various ritual actions, one might disregard its application to knowledge out of opposition to that usage.
Therefore, it must be stated that knowledge possesses the nature of a sacrifice and that it is superior in form to the sacrifices of ritual action.
And it has been stated by the Blessed One in brief: "O scorcher of the foe, a sacrifice of knowledge is superior to a sacrifice involving material substances.
Since that [sacrifice of knowledge] must also be examined, the Blessed Lord Bādarāyaṇa, beginning the fourth section on the majesty of sacrifice (Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa), says:
The author first sets forth his devotion (*praṇidhāna*) to Parāparaśiva with the words "I bow to the Lord" (*aiśam*).

Here, in the first sense, there is devotion to the partless (*niṣkala*) aspect as being of the nature of eternal and unsurpassed bliss; in the second, there is devotion to the manifest (*sakala*) aspect as the bestower of the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*); and [the phrase] "I bow" (*namāmi*) signifies the dedication of the activity of the three organs [of mind, speech, and body] unto Him.

It is thus bound [together]: "I bow to that very Satsāmba—the partless body which is the true nature [of the Lord], who has assumed a playful incarnation for the sake of favoring the worlds"—this is the connection. || 1 ||
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, they were fully prepared for the comprehension of the meaning of all the Vedas.
They are dedicated to the welfare of the entire world and are capable of distinguishing between the essential and the non-essential.

Regarding the phrase "the meaning of all the Vedas": even though the meaning of the lower Vedas (*aparavedārtha*) is understood through the same process as the meaning of the higher Vedas (*paravedārtha*)—namely, by the sages who have already attained their life's purpose (*kṛtakṛtya*) by knowing the meaning of the higher Vedas according to the sequence taught from the mouth of the Sūtra—their subsequent inquiry into the meaning of the lower Vedas serves the purpose of showing grace to the world; for it ensures that those not yet qualified for the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*) may attain qualification for it by means of ritual sacrifice (*karmayajña*).
He states the purpose: "for the welfare of the whole world. The remainder of the chapter is explained by its own words. || 2 ||
They are devoted to the study of their own sacred texts, composed in mind, and perfectly steady.
They are liberated from all calamities and are entirely freed from all enemies. || 3 ||

[Page 5] 232 Accompanied by the *Tātparyadīpikā*—
[In the Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa:
"The meaning of the Vedas is traditionally held to be twofold, according to the division into the higher (para) and the lower (apara)."
The meaning of the Vedas is supreme; it is directly the highest, higher than the highest.

Regarding the phrase "by way of the distinction between the higher and the lower": the meaning of the *Upaniṣads* is the higher; the other, however, is the lower. For it is heard in the *Muṇḍakopaniṣad*: "Two kinds of knowledge are to be known," so indeed say those who know [the truth]: "the higher and the lower. Therein, the lower consists of the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, Atharvaveda, phonetics (*śikṣā*), ritual manuals (*kalpa*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), and so forth.

"Nirukta, Chandas, and Jyotiṣa; then the higher [knowledge] by which that Imperishable (akṣara) is attained," and so forth. He states that very point: "The supreme meaning of the Veda. The meaning is that among all things mentioned, that which is superior to everything else—the partless (niṣkala) and supreme—is the supreme meaning of the Veda as described in the middle of the two aforementioned [categories]. || 2 ||
Another may have the notion that it is dharma, which is the means for attaining that supreme state.
Non-dharma is sometimes praised as the meaning of the Veda out of devotion for the sake of its avoidance by the tigers among sages, but never in its primary sense. || 3 ||
The other [dharma] is also of two kinds: enjoined dharma such as sacrifice and the like, and prohibited adharma such as violence and the like.

Regarding the first of these, he states its purpose with the words "the other" (apara). With the words "devoted to that" (tatparā), he means the Vedic scripture beginning with "Him, by the recitation of the Vedas," and so forth. To the question, "What is the use of teaching adharma, which is not to be practiced? he replies: "for the sake of avoidance" (parihārārtham).
Yet it has been stated in the *Śābarabhāṣya*: "Adharma, too, is to be investigated for the sake of its avoidance. However, this is not in the primary sense.

Dharma is "primary" because, like a face (*mukha*), it is the foremost thing to be practiced as a means to the highest good (*śreyas*). Adharma, on the other hand, being its opposite, is "secondary" (*jaghanya*) since it is to be investigated for the purpose of its abandonment. || 3 ||
But by the avoidance of unrighteousness, dharma shall remain undisturbed. || 4 ||
But by means of the Dharma practiced without confusion and with faith, [one attains the goal].
The supreme meaning of the Vedas is directly accomplished; of this there is no doubt.
Regarding the phrase "by avoiding unrighteousness" (*adharmaparihāreṇa*): if that [unrighteousness] is not avoided, the corruption of Dharma was explained by Arjuna to Kṛṣṇa in the *Gītā*:
"O Kṛṣṇa, from the predominance of unrighteousness, the women of the family fall," and so forth. || 4 || 5 ||
Thus, by its own supreme power, it appears as if bound.
Māyā alone is the supreme power, the performer of the impossible.

How can there be a lack of proof for that supreme reality of the Veda which is self-luminous, such that it is said that its realization is achieved through the performance of dharma? To this, he says: "This very [Self], though free from both itself and others... Even the eternally liberated Self appears as if bound by the power of Māyā resting upon Itself; and because it takes on the form of those who are bound—the transmigrating beings—Māyā also becomes the cause of bondage.

The *Sūtasamhitā* [verse 333] refutes the view that [the creation] is numbered by stating "only one. By means of this single [power], the manifestation of infinite individual souls occurs like a magical illusion (*indrajāla*).
It should not be assumed that there is more than one [birth] in a single birth. || 6 ||
That [bond] of Śiva, which consists of infinite forms, is destroyed by his Vidyā.
That which perishes is illusion, imagined within pure consciousness alone.

He supports its status as *māyā* by demonstrating that it is to be destroyed by knowledge—thus [he says] "of Śiva. Here, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) denotes either the relationship of locus and located (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*) or the relationship of object and subject (*viṣayaviṣayibhāva*). Thus, *māyā* has Śiva as its locus and Śiva as its object; it is the world...

It has two substrates (*dupādānam*). Its status as the individual soul (*jīvatva*) is conditioned by its being the locus (*āśrayatvopādhinā*), and its status as the "Other" (*paratva*) is conditioned by its being the object (*viṣayatvopādhinā*);

such is the established position. Now, it might be objected: ignorance is not possible in Śiva, who is omniscient and faultless; nor can there be a division of souls based on speech or *māyā* residing in the soul as its substrate, because that would lead to fallacies such as mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). To this, [the author] says:

He said: "It is consciousness alone. For in the case of the statement "there is a jar on this ground," since the ground is initially devoid of a jar, its connection with the jar would have to occur through the operation of that very connection itself.

If it were to become possessed of a jar by its own self, there would be the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). If it were already possessed of a jar [at the time of the relation], there would be mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) because both would require each other. If one were to accept a third moment and so forth, there would result an infinite regress (*cakraka*) and other such fallacies. Therefore, the jar must reside in the bare ground alone, which is common to both the presence and absence of the jar.
The connection [is as follows]: thus, [the notion] "it resides in consciousness" refers to pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) which is common to both appearance and its absence. || 7 ||
For the destruction of an imagined entity is indeed a destruction with a remainder consisting of its substratum.
For it is the very state of being that constitutes non-existence; destruction is the becoming of non-existence.
For that which is imagined is indeed other than both existence and non-existence as intrinsic natures. || 8 ||

Now, one might object: "If māyā is destroyed by knowledge (vidyā), then just as the ignorant person was possessed of māyā, so too the liberated knower would appear to possess a second entity upon that destruction. To this he says: "The substratum... The meaning is that since māyā is a mental construction (kalpita), its destruction is not distinct from its substratum (adhiṣṭhāna). One might further object: "But what is the so-called destruction of a jar that did not previously exist?"
That which is born is indeed a jar; and the destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) of an existing jar, by virtue of being a destruction, is indeed non-jar.

For it is precisely in that [non-jar] that the world’s cognition and linguistic usage regarding it are observed, not in the mere substratum alone. Therefore, how can it be said that destruction has the substratum as its remainder?
To this he says: "of the entity itself" (*bhāvasyaiva*). For existence and non-existence are mutually exclusive.

The destruction of that [illusory object] consists in its mutual non-existence with its locus. However, because Māyā is distinct from both being and non-being, the destruction of that [object] does not exceed its locus. For those who directly perceive mother-of-pearl do not recognize or deal with the destruction of the imagined silver therein as something distinct from the nature of that [locus]. [This means that] the destruction of the imagined [object] is not separate from the locus.
Whom do poets mock in common parlance?—that fool who, hearing from his own mouth that "these are pearls," mistook the drops of water on a lotus leaf for gems. Even more than him... [they mock him].
In all manuscripts, the word "yathā" occurs, though it is not required [by the sense].

For the apparent reality of such things as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is sublated only while the cognizer exists.

The reality of objects such as a jar, which are not sublated while a cognizer exists, is conventional (*vyāvahārika*); however, intending that the ultimate (*pāramārthika*) reality belongs to Brahman alone, who is here intended as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), the word "always" (*sarvadā*) was used. Since the Lord alone is the substratum for the entire collection of imagined entities other than Himself, therefore, through the knowledge of Him—

He states the instrument and the qualified seeker for the aforementioned knowledge of the supreme human goal with the words "having the Lord as its object. (9) (10) (11)
One who dwells in the forest, even one who is a lifelong ascetic, attains the world of Brahmā.
The householder [attains] the world of the ancestors, while the mendicant [attains] the knowledge of Śiva.

Having stated "in succession," he explains that very succession with the words "to the world of Brahmā. Although one who has not entered the stages [of life] in order is also included, the mention of the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*) is placed here because it is the fruit of the householder stage (*gārhasthya*), which occurs immediately after residing there. As for the knowledge of Śiva, however, it belongs to the mendicant (*bhikṣuka*) both directly and through the lineage. || 12 ||
In that regard, even there, the first monk is one who possesses the arising of the desire for knowledge and the removal of obstacles.
O best of sages, one is liberated from great sins without effort.

Indeed, there are four types of mendicants: the *kuṭīcaka*, the *baṭu-daka*, the *haṃsa*, and the *paramahaṃsa*. Regarding these, he states the manner of succession for the first: "Among them, the first is the mendicant. The fruit of performing the duties of the *kuṭīcaka* stage of life is the cessation of sins through the desire to know and the destruction of ignorance. || 13 ||

Having recognized the defect in the fruit of actions performed for desire, one should regard them as forbidden.

Regarding the fault in the fruit of performed actions: for by the enjoyment of the fruit, there arises passion (*rāga*) for that which is of the same nature; through that, there is the renewed commencement of such action, from which comes the fruit, and from that, passion—thus the fault characterized by non-liberation from *saṃsāra*.

By means of that very [knowledge], through the removal of obstacles by means of pervasion, and through the attainment of the instruments of knowledge—such as the desire to know, hearing, and reflection—fueled by truth and faith, they became equal to mendicants; this is the meaning. || 26 ||

Now begins the seventh chapter.
I shall proclaim the mantra of the Self in brief, and not at length.
The seer is Brahmā; the meter is Gāyatrī; the deity is the Self alone.
Its power (śakti) is said to end with the letter Śa; that which ends with it is called the seed-syllable (bīja). || 1 ||

Thus, regarding the worship of Sāvitrī, he states the mantra for achieving the arising of the knowledge whose object is the true nature of Paraśiva for one who has not yet produced the desire to know (*vividiṣā*):

"the *ātma-mantra*. It is called the *ajapā* because it establishes that the individual self (*jīvātman*), which is the witness of the states such as waking and so forth, is of the nature of the Supreme Self. This [will be explained] by himself further below.
He will explain [this]. He states the seer (*ṛṣi*) and other [constituents] of this mantra with the passage beginning "The seer is Brahmā" and ending with "is said.

Regarding the phrase "the end of *śānta*": the end of *śa* is *pa*; the end of that is *sa*, which means *śakti*. In the phrase "the end of that," the word "that" refers to the letter *sa*; its end is the letter *ha*.
The meaning is that "ham" is the seed-syllable (bīja) of this mantra. || 1 ||
Vidyā is the power (śakti) and Śiva alone is the seed (bīja), and not otherwise.
Therefore, this supreme mantra is remembered as consisting of the essence of Śiva and Śakti.

Thus, in order to demonstrate that the mantra—which is differentiated by way of the power of its seed-syllables (bīja)—is identical with Śiva and Śakti because it denotes them, he speaks of the meaning-aspect of the seed and the power: "Vidyā is the power. That which is the consciousness of the nature of Paraśiva is itself the Power; and the object denoted by her, the stainless nature of Paraśiva, is the meaning of the seed-syllable.
Both of these are expressed by means of the two parts consisting of sound, namely the *śakti* and *bīja* forms. To explain:

consciousness (*caitanya*), which is characterized by existence, knowledge, and so forth; which is devoid of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); which is self-established; and which is the innermost self of all—this is indeed the nature of Supreme Śiva.
That very [consciousness] can be expressed by the word "I" (*ahaṃ*), which denotes the inner referent (*pratyagartha*). That same [consciousness], being the nature of Śiva...

Form (*rūpa*), when defined as the capacity for opposition (*pratiyogitva*) by virtue of its own inherent power (*svamāpāvaśāt*), is that which is "other" (*parāgbhūta*); this is *śakti*. That too is expressed by the word "this" (*sa*), which denotes an object that is "other. Thus, it has been stated that the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and the power (*śakti*) possess the nature of manifesting Śiva and Śakti. Therefore, this mantra, consisting of the aggregate of the seed-syllable and the power, is of the nature of Śiva and Śakti.
This is the meaning. As it has been stated by Ācārya: "The letter *ka* is declared to be the Puruṣa, and *sa* is considered to be Prakṛti;
the Haṃsa consists of both Puruṣa and Prakṛti, and this entire world consists of that. || 2 ||

Having thus described the procedure for recitation (*japa*)— which is accomplished through the activity of the palate, lips, and other organs— for the person of dull intellect who is unable to contemplate in the manner that will be explained, [the author] now intends to state the secondary procedure for the person of middling capacity whose mind has been refined,
and which is independent of the activity of the palate and lips; [he does so] by means of the two previously mentioned portions of the mantra, which consist of the *veji* power.
Regarding the conjunction, he states another interpretation beginning with "or else" (*athavā*). When [the breath] is being restrained, the downward-turned function is the *apāna*;

such being the case, the word *sa* (he) denotes an external object (*parāg-artha*). Because of its connection with that external nature of the *prāṇa*-function, this portion of the mantra, *sa*, consists of the *prāṇa*-function itself. Furthermore, since the word *haṃ* signifies the internal self (*pratyag-artha*), and because of the [downward] function of the *apāna*...

The mantra portion "haṃ" consists of the nature of the non-return of the vital breath (apāna), due to its similarity with the state of being turned toward oneself (pratyagmukhatva) and its quality of being abandoned (pratyaktva). The meaning is that one should contemplate how these two mantra portions always persist within one's own body in the form of the nature of prāṇa and apāna. || 5 ||
Thus, he who understands the mantra preceded by the teacher [attains success].
Even though he does not recite it verbally, he indeed recites that which is called the *haṃsa*; of this there is no doubt.
Let it be so that the two parts of the mantra consist of *prāṇa* and *apāna*; but what is the excellence (*atiśaya*) of contemplating them?

To this he says: "In this way, he protects the breaths. Having thus described the distinction for qualified practitioners regarding the contemplation of the *mantra* "I" (*ahaṃ*), he now begins to state the distinction for the contemplation of the *haṃsa-mantra* by one of superior qualification—whose mind has been refined through hearing, reflection, and so forth—who is even more exalted than that:

It is not denotative [of the Self], because in common worldly usage the word "I" (aham) is employed conventionally in such expressions as "I am the principal" or "I am suffering. Furthermore, in the Veda it is said:

"In the beginning he uttered 'I am he' (so'hamasmi); therefore he became known by the name 'I' (aham). Therefore even now, when addressed, having first said 'Yes, I am here,' he then utters another name. Thus, the first part of the mantra establishes the individual soul (jīvātman).

The meaning is "water" (daka). Thus is the meaning. ||9||
Because he is well-known in the context of the subject at hand, the Supreme Lord is "well-known" (prasiddha). || 10 ||
The entire universe, from the Great Principle (Mahat) down to the subtle atom, including all that is moving and unmoving.
It is born, it exists, and it dissolves within the Supreme Lord. || 11 ||

Why is this so? To this he says: "The subject matter at hand. The referent of the word *tat* (that) is something well-known, previously introduced, and experienced. And since the Supreme Lord is well-known, He is the subject matter at hand here. Furthermore, that well-known status is to be understood through His being the substratum for the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the entire universe—consisting of moving and non-moving things, from the ether down to the atoms. That state of being the substratum...

And thus it is said: "That from which these beings are born; that by which, once born, they live; that into which they enter at death; and that into which they arise again. Therefore, the Supreme Lord, who is well-known as the cause of the manifold world of effects, is denoted by that word "He" in the mantra.
The meaning is that it is designated by means of a portion. || 10 || 11 ||
I, who appear as a transmigrating being, am indeed that Supreme Lord himself.
Therefore, I am indeed that, without a doubt, according to the authority of my own direct experience.
Having abandoned the variegated [lotus] for the sake of the two swans, who were the excellent companions at his feet.
I am full; thus one should know it by virtue of its nature as pure consciousness alone. || 13 ||

Having thus explained the meanings of the individual words (*padārtha*), he states the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) with the words "as being a transmigrating being" (*saṃsāritvena*). According to the proponents of the theory of the connection of the expressed (*abhihitānvayavādinaḥ*), the meaning of a sentence is that very relation (*saṃsarga*) which arises subsequently from the word-meanings denoted by words whose conventional relations have been grasped, by virtue of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*saṃnidhi*), and semantic competency (*yogyatā*). [They hold that] words denote their own meanings as connected with other word-meanings that are semantically compatible.

For those who maintain the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna-vāda*), the meaning of a sentence is a qualified whole (*viśiṣṭa*). Neither of these two [theories] is possible here, because there exists no other entity distinct from the nature of the Lord (*īśvara*). Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is precisely that ultimate identity with Supreme Śiva which belongs to the individual soul (*jīva*)—who is perceived as distinct through delusion—in reality. Now, [one might object]: "Darkness..."

How can the identity of these two, which possess mutually contradictory natures like light and darkness, be possible? To explain: the denoted meaning of the word "I" (aham) is the limited, individual consciousness (pratyak-caitanya), characterized by agency, enjoyership, and so forth, which is conditioned by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)—an effect of Māyā in which impure *sattva* predominates. And the denoted meaning of the word "That" (saḥ) is [the consciousness] conditioned by Māyā in which pure *sattva* predominates.

The referent of the word [Tat] is Consciousness (caitanya), which transcends all worldly transactions such as being an agent or an enjoyer, is omniscient, and is the cause of the origin and so forth of the universe; it is indicated indirectly by such scriptural passages as, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone.
[Objection: How can there be identity between two such things? [Reply: True. For this very reason, there is *lakṣaṇā* (indication).

It proceeds as follows: this is a *bhāgatyāga-lakṣaṇā* (indication by abandoning a part), consisting in the rejection of the contradictory portions and the acceptance of the non-contradictory portion of the two meanings expressed. For instance, the nature of Brahman as being of the single essence of existence (*sat*), consciousness (*cit*), and bliss (*ānanda*) is established by scripture. And because the individual soul (*jīva*) persists in the form of identity even while the states of waking and so forth fluctuate, it is [of the nature of] existence (*sad-rūpa*).

The fact that the Self is of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpatva*) as its witness, and that it is of the nature of bliss (*ānanda-rūpatva*) as the object of supreme love, is established by one's own experience. Thus, having abandoned the contradictory attributes found in both— such as limited knowledge and omniscience, or manifestness and non-manifestness, or mediacy and immediacy— one should contemplate the mutual identity between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), whose characteristics are the non-contradictory *sat*, *cit*, and *ānanda*.
The *haṃsa* mantra conveys non-duality (*advaita*) through the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) known as "abandonment of the parts" (*bhāgatyāga*). For it has been said:

"When there is a contradiction with other means of knowledge, yet the primary meaning is to be accepted, the cognition of that which is invariably connected with the primary meaning is called figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*)."
Intending all this, it has been said: "This one who appears as a transmigrating being is indeed the Supreme Lord himself."

In the *Tātparyadīpikā* (along with its commentary),
within the fourth section on the Glory of Sacrifice (*Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa*),
when the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) with the indivisible Brahman has been established through the power of the words "I am He" (*ahaṃ sa eva*), it follows by implication—

He points out, through the exchange of terms, the identity between the purified Brahman and the meaning of the word "I" in the statement, "I am indeed He. This very fact—that the meaning of the sentence here consists precisely in this identity—is the indicator [of the nature of the sentence]. Thus it has been said:
"Neither a relation nor a qualified entity is accepted here as the meaning of the sentence."
"The meaning of the sentence is held by the wise to be an indivisible single essence.

Thus, when the indivisible single essence of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is established through their mutual identity, the misconception that the *jīva* is not Brahman or that it is dualistic is removed; and for the Lord as well, such notions as being remote or not being the Self (*anātman*) cease.
That too has been said:
"The inward consciousness that shines forth is characterized by non-dual bliss;
and that which is of the nature of non-dual bliss is characterized solely by inward consciousness."
When there occurs such a realization of mutual identity,
the non-Brahmanhood of the referent of "thou" (tvamartha) is indeed eliminated at that very moment.
"And there is the mediacy (pārokṣya) of its meaning.

Having raised the objection that the meaning of the *haṃsa* mantra, as defined above, lacks coherence due to the absence of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*), he establishes the experience of the learned as the authority therein: "One's own experience," etc. (12–13).
The Śruti as well, which illuminates the ultimate truth, speaks in this very same way.
Maheśvara is the embodiment of bliss and consciousness, perfected in truth. || 14 ||

Fearing that this experience might not be determinative of the object—like the direct perception of a beloved woman when one is tormented by separation—he cites scriptural corroboration with the words, "The scripture also. He qualifies it by saying, "in the ultimate sense," because that [scripture] establishes the very same point as stated, in passages such as "Two birds... (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1), where the ultimate identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is taught.

The distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), which is imagined through ignorance, is set forth by the subsequent mantra, "On the same tree... (*samāne vṛkṣe*), in order to demonstrate non-duality (*advaita*). Therefore, passages such as "Two birds... (*vā suparṇā*) reveal what is not ultimately real. Consequently, only such scriptural texts as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) and "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*) reveal the ultimate reality.
The meaning is that even these [latter texts] establish the very point already stated.

Having stated the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), he describes the unconditioned form of the Lord in order to establish that identity, saying: "Existence, Bliss, Fullness. Now, [one might object]: "It is not gross, not subtle, not short, not long, without sound, without touch, without form, undecaying," and so forth.

And since [the nature of Śiva] is beyond hearing, how can the supreme nature of Śiva—which is devoid of all attributes such as grossness and possesses [attributes] such as reality—be made known by words like "real" (*satya*), which have as their basis the occurrence of those very attributes? It is said in reply: Just as when there is only one moon, due to the multiplicity of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as ripples and waves, many moons are imagined, and among them [one says], "this is the moon, this is the moon."

Just as "moon-ness" (*candratva*) is postulated as a universal (*sāmānya*) because of the persistence of the recurring cognition [of "moon"], so too is the nature of existence (*sad-rūpa*) [postulated] by the opponent.

"Even though it is one, by the power of its own māyā, it is joined with the manifest entities such as Mahat and the rest, which are imagined within itself."

Based on the force of the continuous usage [of terms] such as "the real cloth" (*san-paṭa*), universals that are both higher and lower—such as reality (*satyatva*), knowledge (*jñānatva*), and bliss (*ānandatva*)—are postulated. For this very reason, the Teacher [Maṇḍana Miśra] stated: "Bliss, the experience of objects, and eternity are the attributes (*dharmāḥ*).
And thus, words such as "real" (*satya*) denote these higher and lower universals.

They indicate, by means of secondary implication (*lakṣaṇā*), the undivided nature of Supreme Śiva as their substratum. For this very reason, it has been said that even the worldly terms "Real" (*satya*) and so forth indicate the undivided [Reality]. By the word "complete" (*saṃpūrṇa*), infinity (*ānantya*)—which consists in being devoid of the three kinds of limitation caused by space, time, and substance—is expressed. And by this, even the distinction between the universal and the individual [is negated].

The [opposite] object is thereby negated. Furthermore, it should not be suspected that the other words are redundant because the nature of Paraśiva is indicated by even a single word such as "Real" (satya) and so forth, given the absence of any object of knowledge (*prameya*) beyond that. For however many attributes—such as unreality, insentience, and the nature of suffering—are superimposed upon the nature of Paraśiva through delusion, the [other words] serve to exclude them.
Regarding the employment of numerous terms such as "vātsatya" and so forth, it has been said: "That which...
"The sublation of that which is superimposed upon Brahman, such as falsity and so forth, cannot occur without various words;
therefore, Brahman is indicated by them.
Scripture also reveals the nature of Supreme Śiva as truth, knowledge, and so on: "Truth, knowledge, infinite..."
"Consciousness, bliss, Brahman"—thus [it is said]. || 14 ||
And I, because of my non-deviation, am by nature existent; of this there is no doubt.
I alone am non-deviating, because I am the witness of those things that are deviating. (15)

Having thus described the innate form of Paraśiva, he states that the individual soul (*jīva*) also possesses such a form by declaring its nature to be "Being" (*sat*), beginning with the words "I am" (*ahaṃ ca*). The meaning is that while the states of waking and so forth fluctuate, the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*), which is consciousness (*caitanya*), persists in a single uniform manner; because it does not deviate [from its own nature], it is of the nature of Being (*sad-rūpatā*). To the objection that this reason is unproven (*asiddha*), he says:

"I am indeed non-deviating. Because the "I"-principle is the witness (*sākṣin*) of those deviating factors—the states of waking and so forth—which recede [from it], and because it directly perceives them without entering into their own nature, the "I"-principle is non-deviating. This is just as a single lamp, while illuminating many objects such as jars and cloths that are mutually deviating, remains the illuminator [of them all].

The meaning is that because it lacks differentiation (*bhedābhāva*), it is non-deviant (*avyabhicāritva*); it is like that [the Self]. This non-deviance is taught in the *Tāpanīya Upaniṣad* as follows: "That very Self is, in the waking state, without dreaming, without deep sleep; in the dream state, without waking, without deep sleep; in the deep sleep state, without waking, without dreaming; and in the fourth (*turīya*) state, without waking, without dreaming, without deep sleep—non-deviant."
Thus [ends the section]. 15.
Whether an object is known or unknown, I alone always know it in its entirety.
That object does not know me; therefore, my consciousness remains uninterrupted.

[In the fourth section, the *Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa*—having thus determined that the referent "I" (*ahamartha*) is of the nature of existence (*sadrūpa*) by virtue of its invariable presence—he establishes its nature as consciousness (*cidrūpatā*), beginning with the word "known" (*jñātam*).

That which is known by this is "the known," namely, a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*); through that [modification], by the power of contact with the eyes and other senses, the external...]
When an object such as a jar is pervaded [by cognition], then the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*), having been made the object of that cognition, manifests the object as being known;
at that very same time, it manifests everything else, which is subsumed under ignorance, as being unknown.
As it has been stated by the Teachers: "Every object [is related] to the witness-consciousness either as known or as unknown."

"...is the object. This is what is being said: "I always know the object, whether it be known or unknown. For the eternity of knowledge is established by the Śruti text: "Indeed, there is no loss of the seer's vision. Now, one might argue: by the verbal suffix *tiṅ* in the word "knows" (*veda*), the agent who is the locus of the cognition is denoted; and that [agent] is of the nature of a substance (*dravya*). Knowledge, therefore, is its quality (*guṇa*). Consequently, how [can knowledge be eternal]?

Since the nature of the means [of knowledge] consists of cognition, he says: "exclusive" (*kevala*). Just as in the expression "the iron burns," it is the fire itself that possesses the quality of burning, so too here, by distinguishing between what is attained and what is not attained, it is cognition alone that possesses the quality of illumination. As for the perception of difference—such as "cognition of a jar" or "cognition of a cloth"—that is produced by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the respective modifications of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*). Therefore, with respect to its object... [the qualified...]

The Self, which exists as the witness of the internal organ and its modifications, is purely of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*) alone. He establishes this very point with the words "that object" (*so 'rthaḥ*). If the Self, being of the nature of knowledge and substantial in form, were to illuminate an object through the states of being known or unknown, then even an external object characterized by a jar or the like would [illuminate] the internal subject (*pratyag-artha*), which is the locus of its own cognition.
One would know [it], yet one does not know it; therefore, the referent of "I" (ahamartha) is exclusively of the nature of consciousness alone. || 16 ||
Since there is no state of being a remainder for consciousness apart from [itself], consciousness can certainly not have non-consciousness as its remainder.
Because it would follow that objects such as clay bowls and the like possess consciousness. || 17 ||

Now, one might ask: why is the substratum of consciousness (cidādhāra) of the nature of a substance (dravyarūpa)? To this he says: "Of consciousness" (citaḥ). The meaning is that it is impossible for the non-deviating witness-consciousness (sākṣicaitanya) to be subordinate to the deviating objects of witnessing. To explain: a proponent who asserts that consciousness is subordinate to the Self, which is of the nature of a substance, must be asked: is this Self non-conscious (acidātmaka) by nature?

Having raised the threefold alternative—whether it is of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), or whether it is non-conscious (*acetana*)—he refutes the first with the words "a fragment of consciousness" (*cito 'cic-chedaḥ*). For a thing is not established merely by a proposition; therefore, he says "like a bowl and so forth. If this [fragment] were a part of the Self which is conscious-cum-inert, then, because there would be no distinction in its inertness, even bowls and the like would possess the status of being fragments of consciousness.
It would follow that [the self] possesses consciousness; therefore, it is not tenable to say that consciousness is a quality (śeṣa) of an insentient self. || 17 ||
Nor indeed does the state of being a cutter exist, for consciousness is not divided from consciousness.
If the non-conscious were to become conscious through division, then the non-consciousness of the conscious would be contradicted. || 18 ||

Nor is the second [alternative] tenable; thus he says: “And [the soul would be] a remnant of consciousness. Under this view, it would be asserted that the conscious Self is a remnant of something else. But that is not logical, for the relationship between a remnant and that of which it is the remnant (śeṣa-śeṣibhāva) depends upon a distinction [between two entities].

Here, there is no difference between this consciousness and another consciousness; for, apart from differences based on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-bheda*), they are understood to be one in their nature as luminosity. Now, it may be objected that an ultimate difference between one consciousness and another is indeed perceived.

To this he says: "If it were divided. If consciousness (*cit*) were inherently divided even apart from contact with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), then, like a jar or other objects, it would follow that it is non-consciousness (*acittva*) because of its division from consciousness. He dispels the suspicion that this might be an acceptable consequence by stating: "The non-consciousness of consciousness is a contradiction. (18)
Likewise, even that which is insentient would not attain the status of being a subordinate element (śeṣatva).
When subsidiariness exists, there is the establishment of that [principal]; when that is established, there is subsidiariness for the consciousness.

Nor is the third [alternative] tenable, because it entails the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Thus he says: "Likewise, even for consciousness (*citi*). That which is a subordinate remainder (*śeṣa*) of consciousness is conscious; that which is conscious has consciousness as its subordinate remainder. Since their definitions are mutually dependent, neither one can be established. Thus, because consciousness cannot be defined as being subordinate to anything else, it exists by virtue of its own primacy.
The referent of "I" is consciousness alone. || 19 ||
Therefore, in the world, the subservience of consciousness to something else is perceived through delusion.
I am indeed of the nature of bliss, because I am always the object of love.

One might object: "In such cases as 'the jar is known' or 'I know,' how can there be a perception of consciousness (cit) as being subordinate to something else? Anticipating this doubt, he says, "Therefore, [the notion of] subordination to another is merely a delusion. Having thus established that the individual soul (jīva) has the nature of consciousness, he states its nature as bliss: "Its essential nature is happiness. This [nature] exists always, throughout the three periods of time characterized by the past, future, and present.

Because it is the object of supreme love, the referent of the "I" (ahamartha) is indeed of the nature of unsurpassed bliss. For it has been said: "One should ascertain that 'I' is he who perceives: 'May I never cease to be the object of supreme love; may I always exist. And this status as the object of supreme love is established by scripture: "Indeed, O Maitreyī, it is not for the sake of the husband that the husband is dear, but for the sake of the Self (ātman)."
[The text] begins with, "The husband becomes dear," and so forth, and concludes with, "Indeed, O Maitreyī, it is not for the sake of all that everything becomes dear;

rather, it is for the sake of the Self that everything becomes dear. For in the world, whatever is dear as being subordinate to something else is seen to be even more dear than that [subordinate object]. For example, a wife and other such things are dear to a son because they are subordinate to the son.

Just as a father’s dear ones are dear to him, yet his son is even more dear to the father than they are, so too it is understood that for one whose own self is dear because it is the remainder [of all things], that self is dearer than everything else. And thus it has been said:
"Understand this: he for whom objects such as son, wealth, and the like are dear because of their being his own, is like one who sees a snake; such a person am I."
The meaning is that, because the referent of "I" (ahamartha) is the object of our supreme love, its nature as supreme bliss is established. ||20||
In the *Tātparyadīpikā* (included in the fourth section, the *Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa*):
"Indeed, that which is not happiness is never observed to be an object of love."
For I am not a remnant of another; rather, I am always the sovereign remainder of all.

Anticipating the objection that "let there be a reason [for desirability], but let there be no probandum [in the form of bliss]," he states—namely, that the very consequence of the cessation of the reason (*hetūcchitti*) is the subverting argument (*bādhaka*)—saying: "For one who is not happy... Now, an objection may be raised: "Indeed, we observe that things which are not themselves of the nature of pleasure, yet serve as means to pleasure, as well as the absence of pain, are objects of affection (*premāspadatva*). How, then, can the proof of its being of the nature of bliss (*ānandarūpatā*) be established by this? To this, he says:

The phrase "not for another" means this: while the body and so forth are objects of love because they are subordinate to oneself as the means to pleasure and the avoidance of pain, why should the referent of "I" (the *ahamartha*) not be of the nature of supreme bliss?
For it is the object of love by virtue of being non-subordinate and being self-sufficient (*svapradhānatayā*). This is the meaning. || 21 ||
I am eternally full from the ultimate standpoint, because I am the witness of all.
No one who is incomplete can simultaneously know everything.

It joins even the state of fullness (*pūrṇatva*) with the sense of "I," which is the nature of the Lord, as expressed in "I am full. This is because, in reality, every object—such as a jar or a cloth—existing at all times (past, future, and present), in all states (waking and so forth), and in all places, is devoid of the distinction between internal and external; for it is directly [perceived] as being merely imagined by one's own ignorance (*svāvidyā*).

Because it is the initiator (*dīkṣitṛ*), the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*) is complete; the meaning is that it is devoid of limitations (*avaccheda*) created by space, time, or objects. He states that the aforementioned nature of witnesshood (*sākṣitva*) is not possible for that which is limited—hence the word "incomplete" (*apūrṇa*). Since the witness-consciousness simultaneously and at one and the same time makes all things its object, both in their state of being known and unknown, it is therefore all-pervading (*sarvagata*).
The meaning is that, if it were of such a nature, one would not be able to know everything simultaneously. || 22 ||
He is directly the Supreme Lord, eternally free from saṃsāra.
Because I am the witness of saṃsāra, I am likewise free from saṃsāra.
Thus, having superimposed upon the referent "I" (*ahamartha*) that previously mentioned supreme form of the Lord characterized by truth, knowledge, and so forth,
he also dispels the delusion of duality consisting in the nature of transmigratoriness and being subject to transmigration with the words "devoid of transmigration.

Because He has as His limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) Māyā, whose primary constituent is pure *sattva*, the Supreme Lord is the creator of the world, endowed with unimpeded knowledge, dispassion, and other such qualities.

He is free from *saṃsāra* because he has realized the falsity of the *saṃsāra* manifested by his own *māyā*, and because of such scriptural passages as, "Being unattached, he does not cling. But one might object: while it is appropriate that the Supreme Lord is free from *saṃsāra* due to having *māyā*—predominantly pure *sattva*—as His limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), how can this be said of the individual soul (*jīva*), who is overcome by *māyā* predominantly consisting of impure *sattva*?

To show that it is devoid of that [transmigration], he says: "I am transmigration. That which is the witness is seen as free from transmigration. Just as the witness is distinct from a pot, so too is transmigration—like any other object—subject to the witness; therefore, the witness is indeed distinct from transmigration, and thus, even in its essential nature, it is free from transmigration. As in the world...

Victory and defeat belong only to those who are disputing; the witnesses, however, possess only neutrality. As for the state of being a false witness—[the text here contains various manuscript variants regarding the specific qualities or conditions]. Among those two, the witness (sākṣī) takes a particular person as his own self and thus becomes a partisan; he consequently shares in that person's victory or defeat. In exactly the same way, for consciousness (caitanya) which identifies with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) as its own self, [the qualities of that organ belong to it].
The meaning is that transmigratory existence belongs to that [conditioned self], but not to the changeless witness-consciousness (sākṣicaitanya) which is unconditioned by it.
Thus, by means of reasoning following the scriptural statements, with the Teacher at the forefront—
The wise one should realize: "I am he; I am indeed that very same person."

Having thus established the similarity between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) through the application of the meaning of the mantra words, he concludes the previously mentioned realization of oneness with the word "evam" (thus). The statement previously cited as authoritative, such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), is the removal of any alternative interpretation of the meaning conveyed by the *haṃsa* mantra; this is what is meant by "following the reasoning. For it has been said:
"Reasoning (tarka) serves as an auxiliary to direct perception and other means of valid knowledge;
its assistance consists in the cessation of the desire to know [the truth] regarding the opposing side.
Thus, preceded by such reasoning, you should learn from the mouth of the Teacher the meaning of the *haṃsa* mantra, which is characterized by the oneness of Brahman and the Self.
This is the meaning. || 24 ||
Whoever, by means of this self-mantra, [unites] the individual self and the supreme self...
One perceives with firm certainty the ultimate oneness.
He alone is the foremost knower of Brahman, and not another who is deluded by ignorance.

Having thus ascertained the meaning through hearing and reflection, and having performed meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*), he who realizes the actual identity of the individual self and the Supreme Self through this mantra— doing so in such a way that he is free from friendship, doubt, and contrary conceptions— he alone is the best among the knowers of Brahman. But he who is otherwise, being of a different character than that, is not so.

"Knowledge is shrouded by ignorance; by that, living beings are deluded.
And the Śruti says: "Now, he who worships another deity, thinking 'He is one and I am another,' does not know, like a beast. || 25 ||
When such thorough knowledge as this has arisen in someone on earth, [then he is a knower].
At that very moment, there is no doubt that his cycle of worldly existence is destroyed. || 26 ||

Now he states the fruit of this direct realization (*sākṣātkāra-jñāna*) with the words "Thus" (*evam*). As soon as the direct realization whose object is the unity of Brahman and the Self arises, at that very moment, ignorance—the root of all misfortune—is removed; consequently, for the knower, transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), which is its effect, also ceases. It does not, however, [require] another place or time, like the fruit of heaven and so forth.

Liberation is not to be attained elsewhere or at another time; for the identity of the inner self with Brahman, which is its own inherent nature, remained as if unattained until the direct realization of its true form due to its concealment by ignorance. And upon that direct realization—
When that ignorance is eradicated along with its root by the consciousness delimited by the mental modification in the form of Brahman,
the innate state of being Brahman itself is attained by the knower at that very moment and in that very place through the removal of the veil.
For it is heard in scripture:

"The knot of the heart is rent asunder, all doubts are cut away, and his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen. And also: "His vital breaths do not depart; right here they are completely absorbed. (26)
He who exerts effort toward liberation without knowing the Haṃsa-vidyā.
He will bring about the cessation of hunger by consuming the sky alone. || 27 ||
He shows that only one who knows the *īśī* mantra-vidyā has the qualification for liberation, and no other—thus he says: "the *haṃsa*-vidyā. (27)
This is the supreme Haṃsa-vidyā, which pierces through the most secret mantras.
She bestows all sovereignty, she is the deity of all, and she brings satisfaction to all the gods. || 28 ||
And by the mere recitation of this, one shall attain long life.
One obtains health, victory, and knowledge; of this there is no doubt. || 29 ||
What is the use of much speaking? This knowledge called Haṃsa grants all desires.
He who always says "Haṃsa, Haṃsa" is indeed Śiva himself.

Having thus declared that the mantra of the mind-self (*mātyātmamantra*) is a means to liberation for those seeking release, he now demonstrates that it is also a means to achieve results pertaining to this world, with the passage beginning "savidyā parā" and ending with "sarvakāmadā. It pierces through the supreme mantras; even those mantras of death employed by enemies for the purpose of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), this *haṃsa*-mantra completely shatters.

Knowledge: Because this mantra consists of the nature of *prāṇa* and *apāna*, it is the cause for the increase of longevity. "Haṃsa, haṃsa"—the meaning is that even one who is unable to contemplate the intended meaning [of the mantra] but constantly utters "haṃsa, haṃsa," shall in the course of time become Śiva himself. || 28 || 29 || 30 ||
By Śiva, by Viṣṇu, by Brahmā, and by all the deities.
Once born, she bestows accomplishment upon those who are submissive to her in no time at all.

Now, he states that this mantra is a means for the swift attainment of results with the words "by Śiva": "Thus indeed is this Haṃsa-vidyā."
Even all the gods, such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others of great power, hold her in high esteem; therefore, the meaning is that this mantra bestows the desired fruit swiftly. || 31 ||
Having released the recaka and the narakas, the wise man remains well-established in kumbhaka.
Having made the prāṇa and apāna breaths equal within the bulb of the navel, he remains concentrated.
Having respectfully drunk the taste of nectar situated in the head through meditation,
One should meditate upon Mahādeva in the form of a lamp, blazing in the center of the navel.
Having been consecrated with nectar itself, he who should mutter "haṃsa, haṃsa," [attains success].
For him, old age, death, disease, and the like do not exist upon this earth.
Now he shows the yoga for the constant practice, beginning with "recaka" and so forth. Regarding "nābhikanda":

the *kanda* (bulb) situated at the root of the navel is the *nābhikanda*; that is to say, the navel-wheel (*nābhicakra*). On its left and right sides are two channels called *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*. Between them, [the channel] has arisen from the center of the *nābhikanda*.

The channel named Suṣumnā extends as far as the *brahmarandhra* (the aperture of Brahmā) with its opening directed downwards. From there, below it, the vital air (*pavana*) rising from the *mūlādhāra* exits through the two side channels in the form of the *prāṇa*, because the mouth of the Suṣumnā has been closed. Regarding this, the teachers say:
"The nāḍī consisting of both [energies], extending downwards, should be long and straight;
it is downward-facing, and there should be a pair on each of its two sides."
Among those, the first channel is called *suṣupti*;
that which is on the left is declared to be *iḍā*, and the one on the right is considered to be *piṅgalā*.
"Even within the body, when the vital breath (samīraṇa) rises from this mūlādhāra,
it sets through the two channels at a distance of twelve finger-breadths from the nose.

Thus, in the prāṇāyāmas consisting of exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kumbhaka), these three— Piṅgalā, Iḍā, and Suṣumnā— are of the nature of female, male, and neuter respectively.
The channels are employed in sequence. For it has been said:
"One should exhale the wind through the right [channel], fill the right [side] with the left [channel], and again [fill] the middle channel."
"One should retain what has been described; there are three [stages] beginning with exhalation (*recaka*), known as the *Kailāda* and *Antavidyā*, consisting of measures (*mātrā*).

Likewise, having set aside the two types of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) consisting of exhalation and inhalation (*pūraka*), and by means of proficiency in the practice of the vital air (*pavana*), having opened the obstruction of the *suṣumnā*—which is naturally closed—one causes the vital air rising from the *mūlādhāra* to enter into it, [performing] the *kumbhaka* breath control.

Established in the mouth, the prāṇa and apāna move through the iḍā and piṅgalā with their openings facing upward and downward respectively; sixteen [kalās] at the navel, thirty-two teeth, and likewise two vidyās—thus the field consists of sixty-four.

Having made the two nostrils equal so that there is no inequality in the entry and exit [of the breath], and having restrained [the breath] right there,

being composed with a one-pointed mind, wise, and possessing beautiful knowledge that transcends the sphere of the senses, [he should practice] with a well-filled [breath] extending as far as the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).

Having personally and respectfully drunk, through meditation characterized by such qualities, the stream of nectar flowing from the lunar orb situated at the *dvādaśānta*— which has been liquefied by the impulse of the *tapas* forest and entered within the *suṣumnā*— one becomes bodiless (*amṛtadeha*).
Then, one perceives the blazing, illuminating [Self] residing in the heart-lotus, which has arisen from the center of the *nābhikanda* in the middle of the navel.

It has the form of a lamp, being self-luminous like a lamp. Alternatively, the gastric flame situated in the center of the navel-wheel stands like the wick of a lamp within the cavity that exists at the front of the heart-lotus; because it is delimited by that [flame], Paraśiva also has the form of a lamp. For it is heard in scripture:
At its end is a subtle aperture; in it, everything is established.
In its center is the Great One, beyond the universe, manifest, and facing in all directions.
Eating the first portion, distributing [the food], standing, free from decay, the wise one [pervades] horizontally, upwards, and downwards. (*N: lying down)
His [the enemy's] power is continuously severed.
It heats its own body from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head;
in the middle of that, a flame of fire, extremely subtle, is situated pointing upwards.
Resplendent like a streak of lightning situated in the midst of dark clouds,
she is slender like the awn of wild rice, golden-hued, radiant, and subtle as an atom.
"In the center of that crest, however, the Supreme Self is established."

Having thus flooded with nectar the Paraśiva, who is the object of the Haṃsa-mantra and is situated within the heart-lotus according to the aforementioned method, one should mutter the Haṃsa-mantra; by that, one attains immortality. This yoga has also been stated by the Teachers:
"One should contemplate this [Self] in the form of a swan's egg, consisting of the excellent supreme nectar, dripping from the moon at the crown of the head."

Having led [the patient] along the Sopunna path, the practitioner of mantra, with sharpened intellect, having remembered and recited the mantra over his entire body and limbs, removes gray hair, poison, headaches, fever, insanity, spirits, epilepsy, and so forth, as well as sins, misfortune, poverty, and the faults of intoxication.
Thus [ends verses 32, 33, and 34].
In this manner, one should perform [this practice] day by day for the sake of attaining the supernatural powers (vibhūti) such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest.
A person who is constantly devoted to practice attains the state of lordship.

He states that for one who practices this yoga daily in the manner described, even the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā* are not obstacles—thus he says, "In this way. He speaks of the attainment of lordship by one who is always absorbed [in meditation]—thus he says, "Lordly," etc. (35).

Meditation (*dhyāna*) is a continuous flow of mental modifications (*manovṛtti*) of the same genus as the object of meditation, uninterrupted by mental modifications of a different genus.

It must be accepted that the object of meditation is pervaded by a modification (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); and since this [pervasion] is for the purpose of removing the veil from the specific [nature] obscured by ignorance, how could such a thing— the unconditioned nature of Supreme Śiva, which is unveiled, non-dual, self-established, and the witness (*sākṣin*) because it illuminates all things including the internal organ and its modifications through the light of its own essential nature— be [the object of the internal organ]?

If the function of the internal organ were to pervade [the Self], or if that very function, upon such pervasion, were itself the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), then it would follow that the Self possesses a limiting adjunct (*sopādhika*).

Therefore, because the Self, as the witness of all, is not an object of the functions of the internal organ, the nature of the Self—which is devoid of limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*)—cannot be an object of meditation.

"By those who possess the habit of measuring" (*mānamānibhiḥ*) means by those whose nature it is to measure—that is, to determine through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). [They are] knowers of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-vedin*).

Whatever appears as existing, and whatever also appears as non-existing;

Having thus stated that the entire world, consisting of the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*), is to be meditated upon as having Brahman as its self, he says "by way of existence" (*astitayā*) to include what has not been mentioned. The meaning is that whatever appears as an object of the cognition of existence and as an object of the cognition of non-existence—all that is to be contemplated as having Brahman as its self. For there is nothing whatsoever that is not of the nature of existence or non-existence.
Because no entity exists apart from what has been stated, there is a comprehensive inclusion of everything consisting of both existence and non-existence. || 44 ||

Thus, for the seeker of liberation whose impurities have been destroyed by actions of body, speech, and mind, he praises the means of knowledge (*jñānopāya*) for the realization of the true nature of Supreme Śiva—beginning with the word "atha" (*now*). He states its distinction from other sacrifices as follows:

Regarding the phrase "by means of knowledge": in the Śruti, it is stated that "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," "Having known Him thus, one transcends death," and "Having known His very Self as the path, one is not smeared by evil action. Thus, knowledge alone, without dependence on anything else, is the direct means to liberation.
This has been declared in the sacred tradition (*āmnāta*). It is also stated in the *Smṛti*:
"O scorcher of foes, the sacrifice of knowledge is superior to the sacrifice consisting of material objects;
O Pārtha, all action in its entirety culminates in knowledge."
"In the Manusmṛti it is said: 'The supreme purification of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is considered to arise from the knowledge of the Self. || 1 ||
Knowledge has been declared to be of many kinds by those who have reached the further shore of the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas.
The essential nature of Śiva, the Supreme Self, is a single consciousness.
That very [reality] becomes manifold through the distinction between illusion (māyā) and its effects. || 3 ||
He states that prior to creation, there was the self-luminous knowledge, which is non-dual and established in itself as the very nature of Paraśiva;

that same [knowledge], subsequent to creation, undergoes differentiation into the categories of individual souls (jīva), the Lord (īśvara), and so forth, due to the influence of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) consisting of Māyā and its effects—this he expresses with the words beginning "Knowledge is of many kinds," etc. (verses 2 and 3).
But for Śiva, who possesses the power of consciousness, it is augmented by Māyā.
And knowledge, known as the Lord, shall be the controller of the world.

In this context, he states the essential nature of the Lord (Īśvara), the ruler of the world, with the words "in the form of Māyā. He distinguishes Him from the Supreme Śiva-nature—which is the object of the highest yoga and is said to be the Supreme Power (Paraśakti) whose essence is consciousness—by saying "of the inert power" (jadaśakteḥ). That which is called *māyā* by the Vedāntins and *avyakta-prakṛti* (the unmanifest primordial nature) by the Sāṃkhyas is here [referred to as] the Supreme...

This is the power of Śiva. And when that power, having abandoned the equilibrium of the *guṇas*, transforms into the form of *māyā*—which is predominantly pure *sattva* through the complete suppression of *rajas* and *tamas*—then consciousness conditioned by that [power] becomes the omniscient Lord, the creator of the world; such is the meaning. || 4 ||
The power (śakti), when connected with the form of ignorance, is designated as the individual soul (jīva).
Consciousness, which is designated as the "living soul," is established in two ways in the world.
In reality, however, knowledge is essentially one; the other is merely so from the perspective of conventional cognition.

Māyā, in which the principle of impurity (mala) predominates, is called avidyā because it causes delusion in its own substratum. Knowledge conditioned by that [avidyā] receives the designation "jīva"; thus he says: "of the power (śakti), [it is] avidyā. Of that very [power] designated as jīva, there are two kinds...

[In the fourth section, the *Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa*, he says:
"That which is designated as the *jīva*. Among these, one is primary in terms of its actual meaning (*arthataḥ*), while the other is primary in terms of conventional perception (*pratītitaḥ*).]
Consciousness bound by ignorance is said to be primary in its actual sense.
It is perceived as being delimited by the gross and subtle bodies.

This [text] demonstrates both of these by the phrase "possessing ignorance" (*avidyāvad-dha*). That *māyā*—which is synonymous with *vidyā*—and which consists primarily of impure *sattva*, serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*); because it is the cause of the two bodies (the gross and the subtle), it is called the "causal body" (*kāraṇa-śarīra*) of the *jīva*. The consciousness of one's own nature (*svarūpa-caitanya*), when connected with and conditioned by that [causal body], is in reality [the basis for] the distinction between self and other.

The cause of the *hāra* (the means of liberation) is that which, by virtue of being of the nature of luminous consciousness (*prakāśacidātmakatva*), is in reality the primary [cause]; it is that which, delimited by the two bodies—gross and subtle—which constitute the effects of ignorance (*avidyā*), and which, as their underlying cause, pervades them as a constituent part of *māyā*; and which, through the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of self-luminous consciousness, becomes identical with that [consciousness]—namely, the *sattva* (pure being) that serves as the material cause (*upādāna*) for the modifications (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) of such a kind. That [is the cause].

Because it possesses the nature of the light of consciousness (citprakāśa) during experience, it appears as such; however, from the perspective of ultimate reality, that existence is indeed insentient (jaḍatva).
Its designation as "knowledge" occurs because it has become unified with the consciousness of its own nature, like an iron ball heated by fire. || 6 ||
The mind, which is the locus of its own activity, manifests in the form of the individual soul (jīva).
The state of being a knower is the cause of the individual soul's existence, as well as the cause of its suffering and so forth. || 7 ||

He states that the connection with all empirical functions—such as being a knower, an agent, and an enjoyer—belongs to the consciousness of the *jīva* (the individual soul) as conditioned by ignorance (*avidyā*) solely through its relation to the activity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which consists of such transformations of being; thus he says: "having its own movements as its locus.
By the word "its own" (*sva*), the mind (*citta*) is referred to. Its "movements" (*pracārāḥ*) are the mental modifications (*vṛttayaḥ*) in the form of objects. Their...

The meaning is that it is of the nature of destruction (*ghātātmaka*). Through the habitual identification (*tādātmyābhyāsa*) with such an internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the agency, enjoyership, and so forth belonging to that organ are superimposed (*adhyāsa*) upon consciousness (*caitanya*); thus, this [consciousness] possesses the character of illuminating the individual soul (*jīva*). It is heard in scripture that the entire cycle of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) belongs to the internal organ alone and is not ultimately real for the Self (*ātman*): "Desire, resolve, doubt, faith, lack of faith... [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.3].
"Steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, desire, and anger—these are indeed the mind. || 7 ||
O Lords of Sages, [they appear] in the form of valid cognition, error, doubt, and so forth.
The mind becomes manifold in form due to the ripening of time and karma. || 8 ||

Having raised the doubt as to how the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) can possess causality with respect to agency, enjoyership, and so forth, he states its manifold nature—consisting of the functions of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the rest—in order to establish that point, beginning with the word "pramāṇa. Regarding the phrase "due to time, action, and maturation": for time is indeed the cause of the ripening of karma. By the power of time, [the fruits of] merit and demerit, which are the causes of pleasure and pain, [ripen].
The meaning is: from the ripening—that is, the state of being ready to yield its fruit—of the karmas of living beings whose natures are evil. || 8 ||
O bulls among sages, consciousness is permeated by the respective forms [of its objects].
O sinless ones, it is called the knowledge of valid cognition, tranquility, and doubt.

The Sūtasamhitā [states]: "The designation of distinctions such as the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and so forth arises precisely from the diversity of the forms of their respective objects. Thus he says: "tattad... (that-that...).

Regarding the term "consciousness" (vijñāna): it refers to the cognition that is a modification of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇavṛttijñāna), which has become one with the consciousness of one's own nature through the superimposition of identity (tādātmyādhyāsa). || 9 ||
O bulls among sages, consciousness arises from unimpaired sense-faculties.
The sages who perceive the subtle have declared this to be valid cognition (pramāṇajñāna). || 10 ||

In this context, he states the nature of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with the words "not defective" (*aduṣṭa*). The sense organs, such as the eye, when corrupted by defects like cataracts or jaundice, are the producers of doubt (*saṃśaya*), which consists of non-determination regarding the true nature of objects such as color and form.
Then he turns [the objection] aside with the words "not defective" (aduṣṭā). || 10 ||
Cognition produced by defective causes is declared to be erroneous cognition.
O believers, knowledge characterized by doubt would be that which clings to both sides.
O wise ones, that manifestation which takes the form "this is exactly thus" is indeed this very [reality].
That alone is declared to be certainty by those intent upon right vision.

He states the definition of error (*bhrānti*) as "due to a defective cause" (*duṣṭa*). The meaning is that error is the cognition of something as being what it is not, arising through the influence of a defective cause.

He defines doubt (*saṃśaya*) as "having two alternatives" (*koṭidvaya*). The meaning is that doubt is a cognition that clings to two or more contradictory alternatives, such as "Is it a post or a person? (vv. 11–12).
Therefore, I have stated that the validity [of cognition] consists in its connection with knowledge.
O wise ones, the causal complexes for valid cognition have been described by me.

He states that only that specific modification of the intellect (*buddhivṛtti*) in which there is the manifestation (*sphuraṇa*) [of the object] possesses validity—namely, "of knowledge" (*jñānasya*).

Thus, in cognitions such as "this is a jar," because there exists the manifestation of objects like jars which provide their own forms to the cognition, those cognitions possess validity. However, in erroneous cognitions such as "this is silver," the mind [is directed] toward the form of "this."

There are two types of mental modifications (*vṛtti*): one is a modification of *māyā* residing in the consciousness limited by that [silver-illusory] modification; the other is a further modification of *māyā* residing in the consciousness that is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the conch-shell, having as its object the silver which is an illusory appearance (*vivarta*). Both of these manifest this single consciousness, which is common to both through its being the substratum of the conch-shell and through its being delimited by the two modifications. And that—

Because it is characterized by two modes of functioning (*vṛtti*), it manifests the two objects—consisting of the superimposed and the substrate—in their state of being conjoined. Thus, since there is no connection between the manifestation of the qualified [object] and the mental mode (*manovṛtti*) whose object is the form "this" (*idamākāra*), there is no validity (*prāmāṇya*) with respect to that [qualified part]. However, because there is a connection with the manifestation of the mere form "this," there is validity with respect to that portion. For it has been said:

From the *Tātparya-dīpikā*:
"All knowledge of an object is non-erroneous regarding its substratum (*dharmin*), but there may be error regarding its mode (*prakāra*). And that means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is sixfold—
He says "dham" — namely, "pramāṇajñāna" (valid cognition). || 13 ||
In that regard, O twice-born ones, one set of causal conditions for the cognition of non-existence has been described.
But another collection of conditions for the cognition of existence has been proclaimed. (14)
He states the twofold nature of those means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) based on the duality of their objects, characterized as either existent or non-existent: "Among these, one... (verse 14).
O believers, it is by the very non-perception of what is suitable [to exist] that produced consciousness is established.
That would be the cognition of non-existence, according to the righteous who are most learned in the Vedas. (15)

Regarding this, he states the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends non-existence: "If [an object] is suitable... He qualifies [the definition] with "suitable" because it would be an over-extension (*atiprasakta*) to claim that mere non-apprehension (*anupalambha-mātra*) generates the knowledge of non-existence. The suitability (*yogyatva*) of non-apprehension consists in the presence of the totality of conditions for the apprehension of the counter-positive (*pratiyogi*), excluding the counter-positive itself. By such a non-apprehension, that which is the non-existence of the object of knowledge (*prameya-abhāva*)...

The meaning is that when the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) do not arise with respect to the nature of a thing, a cognition arises that apprehends its absence; this is the means of valid cognition for the purpose of understanding the non-existence of the thing. As it has been said:

"When the five means of valid cognition do not arise with respect to the form of a thing, then 'existence' (*bhāva*) serves as the means of valid cognition for the sake of awakening to the existence of the thing. (15)
Cognition produced by the sense faculties is defined as direct perception (pratyakṣa).
Inference is held to be the thorough knowledge produced by pervasion. || 16 ||
Among those who apprehend existence, he defines perception as "that which arises from the sense organs. For it has been stated:

"Perception is knowledge arising from the contact of a sense organ with its object, which is non-erroneous and of a determinate nature. He states the nature of inference as "pervasion" (*vyāpti*). [This refers to] between two things of fixed relation, the pervaded and the pervader, such as smoke and fire.

Inference is the knowledge of the pervader (vyāpaka) arising from the force of perceiving the pervaded (vyāpya); thus, the knowers of reality define inference as "the cognition of the pervader resulting from the perception of the pervaded. (16)
Knowledge produced by the cause of similarity is declared to be analogy (upamāna).
O Brahmins, presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) is said to be that which arises from the impossibility [of an observed fact otherwise].

He defines analogy (*upamāna*) with the words "similarity" (*sādṛśya*). The meaning is this: for an urban dweller who has previously experienced a cow in the city and later goes to the forest, where he perceives a *gavaya* directly, the knowledge that arises—caused by the similarity residing in the *gavaya*—to the effect that "my cow is similar to this," which has as its object the similarity residing in the cow (which is not present there), is analogy.

He states the nature of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) with the words "presumptive testimony" (*arthāpatti*). It is the cognition of that which makes something possible, arising from the observation of something that is otherwise inexplicable.

Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is as follows: for example, the absence of the living Devadatta from his house is not intelligible without his existence outside;
thus, it leads one to postulate his existence elsewhere. The meaning is that presumption is the cognition whose object is his existence outside. || 17 ||
Knowledge arising from words endowed with their intended meaning is declared to be verbal (śābda).
But sound, O best among the knowers of Brahman, is proclaimed to be of three kinds. || 18 ||
Likewise, O brahmins, there are syllables and similarly words as well.
And there, O best of the twice-born, some [uttered] these words as well. (19)
Next, he defines scripture (*āgama*)— as that which possesses *tātparya* (intentional meaning)—
with the verse:
"The beginning and the conclusion, repetition, uniqueness, purpose, and the fruit..."
"And the justification for the partial statement (ardhavāda) is a mark for determining the intended meaning (*tātparya*).

Thus, the meaning is that verbal testimony (*śabda*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that knowledge whose object is the denotation [of the word], which is endowed with such marks of intended meaning.

He states its threefold division according to the distinctions of syllables (*akṣara*), words (*pada*), and sentences (*vākya*)—beginning with "But the word..."—and so on. According to some teachers...

He states that, according to the opinion of some, it is the phonemes (*varṇa*) themselves that denote meaning—referring to those who say: "The venerable Upavarṣa maintains that the phonemes alone are the word (*śabda*). It is the phonemes themselves, as apprehended under the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of conveying a single meaning, that possess the capacity to denote meaning; there is no entity distinct from them known by the synonym *sphoṭa*.

The meaning is that the oneness of the conscious self (cidātman)—which is devoid of internal distinctions, as well as of similar and dissimilar entities—is established with intentional emphasis by such scriptural passages as: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," "Brahman is one only, without a second," and "There is no diversity whatsoever here.
