Is the plurality [of the Self] due to its nature as self-luminous consciousness (*svaprakāśacidrūpa*), or rather due to its form as the object of the "I-notion" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) qualified by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)? It is not the first; thus he says: "There is no difference from the nature of consciousness. While specific subjects such as Devadatta and others—being the objects of the "I-notion"—and the various cognitions (*caitanya*) are excluded, the pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) remains uniform in all cases.
The meaning is that because of the continued persistence [of the same cognition], there is no room for the postulation of a distinction between them. || 43 || 44 ||
The distinction exists in the form of the *caitya*, but there is indeed no distinction in the *caitya* itself, which is consciousness (*cit*).

For Śiva is indeed the self, manifest as the light of pure consciousness alone. [45] — Now, suppose it is argued that there is a distinction by way of the nature of the object of cognition (*caitya*) characterized as the subject (*pramātṛ*); this is the second alternative. To this, he says: "by way of the nature of the object of cognition. Since the objects of cognition in the form of subjects are excluded while consciousness persists everywhere, [consciousness is not distinct from them].

[The distinction] is divided. Since it is observed in the case of universals (jāti) and individuals (vyakti) that the inclusive (anuvṛtta) is other than the exclusive (vyāvṛtta), therefore, when difference is manifested in the form of consciousness (caitanya), it belongs to consciousness alone, not to the conscious self (cit). The meaning is that the difference between a jar and a cloth does not bring about a multiplicity in space. Then, suspecting that the Self might be of the very nature of such consciousness, he says: "being the Self" (ātmabhūta).

Regarding the phrase "the light of pure consciousness" (*cinmātrajyoti*): by the word *mātra*, the ego (*ahaṃkāra*)—which is a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) consisting of various forms conjoined with consciousness within all subjects—is excluded. Therefore, the meaning is that even though that [ego] is manifold, one should not suspect any difference in the Self, whose sole body is the pervasive consciousness. || 45 ||
But because one perceives that sacred trees such as the *vaṭa* lack selfhood (*anātmatva*).
Some lords of sages have stated that even the Self has a difference from itself. ||46||

Sūta-saṃhitā:
Intending to show that "the disputed ego is not the Self because it is perceivable by consciousness, like a jar," he says—regarding the jar and so forth—

"Not so," he says. Having thus established the unity of the Self (*ātman*), whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*), according to his own view, he introduces the refutation of the opposing view with the words:
"Of the Self also... By the term "by itself" (*svataḥ*), he means "by its very nature alone, and not due to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
Accordingly, there is the *Kaṇāda-sūtra*: "The selves are manifold because of their distinct dispositions. And the Sāṃkhyas say:

"The plurality of Puruṣas is established from the specific determination of births, deaths, and instruments, from their non-simultaneous activity, and indeed from the variation of the three guṇas. If the Self were one, the distribution of pleasure and pain among the bodies of Caitra, Maitra, and others would be untenable, and the specific determination of birth, death, and so forth would likewise be impossible; therefore, there is a distinct Self for each body.
This is the intention of Vepā. || 46 ||
Therefore, it would not be consistent at all that the self is the establisher of difference.
O twice-born ones, since the Self is indeed Śiva, the witness of all differentiation, how could it be divided? ||47||

Intending to show that all this is consistent even by accepting a difference based on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-bheda*) despite the unity of the Self (*ātman*), he refutes [the opponent's view] with the word "that" (*tad*). The meaning is that the claim that the difference of the Self is intrinsic (*svābhāvika*) is not tenable. Why?
To this he says: "The Self... The phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of the elements and elemental products, beginning with suffering, is indeed distinct from the Self.

It is established by such scriptural passages as, "From the Self, space was produced. Furthermore, since difference is included within the phenomenal world (prapañca), it must be stated that it arises from that very same source. Therefore, difference exists subsequent to its production from that [Self].

How could there be a quality (*dharma*) belonging to the beginningless Self (*ātman*) which has existed from before, by whose conjunction the Self would become divided? Therefore, the meaning is that multiplicity of the Self is not tenable, because [if it were so] it would entail the division of the Self. Intending to show that difference is not an inherent quality of the Self—since it is a mark [of something else] like a water-pot and other such objects—he says: "the witness of difference" (*bhedasākṣī*). (47)
Therefore, the distinction within the self is established by delusion and not in reality.
Just as the division of the single sky is perceived through delusion. || 48 ||

Intending that, in the contrary case, the state of being perceived by the witness (sākṣin) for that which possesses the nature of consciousness would be lost, he concludes his own position—that the difference residing in the self is merely adventitious (aupādhika)—by means of an illustration, with the words "Therefore" (ataḥ). || 48 ||
O you of excellent vows, whatever belongs to someone by its very nature, that is other than him.
It is established in the world that [an action] would be performed by means of some other accessory condition.
Therefore, the distinction of the supreme Self, which is by its very nature non-dual, is an illusion.
He establishes that the aforementioned distinctions are merely conditional (*upādhika*) by demonstrating a worldly maxim: "Of whatever... and so forth.
For indeed, whatever is the natural form of a thing such as a crystal—such as its whiteness—that [form] is opposed by another form, such as redness.
(Note on variants: *gha* reads *kṣilaṃ bhā*; *ca* reads *kṣiṇā bhā*; *dha* and *ca* read *kaṃru*.)
[From] the *Tātparyadīpikā*:
"It is indeed caused by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the *japā* flower; since the worldly convention is thus established, for that reason—"

Even the difference that contradicts the self's natural non-duality must necessarily be admitted to be caused solely by another limiting adjunct (upādhi). Now, one might object: "In the case of a 'red crystal,' the redness of the crystal can be understood as adventitious because it appears when a hibiscus flower (*japākusuma*) is near and disappears when it is not; however, such is not the case for the difference of the self."

Regarding this, he says: "It is an error. This is the meaning: since the connection of the consciousness of the Self with limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as ignorance (avidyā), its effects, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), and so forth, has been established from time immemorial, there is no separation from these adjuncts; thus, the fact that their difference constitutes the nature of the adjunct is not recognized. Therefore, just as in the case of "the conch is yellow," because the attribute of one thing is superimposed upon another, [the attributes] residing in the Self...
The meaning is that difference is established solely through delusion. || 49 ||
Having accepted the difference between jars and other such objects, those who have reached the further shore of the meaning of the Vedas [say this]. (50)
The distinction between selves has been refuted, as has the distinction between jars and other such objects.
Established through delusion, it is not said to be real either by means of reasoning or by means of valid cognition. //51//

Now, one might object: "If you say that the difference of the Self is merely conditional (*aupādhika*), then you must be admitting that the difference of the non-Self, which serves as the condition, is ultimately real (*pāramārthika*). If that is so, how can it be established that the non-duality of the Self is its inherent nature?
To this, he says: "Having granted... [referring to the phrase] "the difference residing in the non-Self, such as 'the cloth is different from the jar.'"

The meaning is that even that appearance is merely illusory and not ultimately real, because it cannot be established by means of either valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or reasoning (*tarka*). Both valid cognition and reasoning will be demonstrated later. || 50 || 51 ||

O Lords of Sages, the distinction between jars and other such things is certainly not merely an illusion according to perception; rather, through perception, it possesses a real nature within the sphere of worldly convention. (52)

But if the difference existing in jars, cloths, and so forth were established through delusion, then there would be a failure of correspondence (*visaṃvāda*) in the worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) of a person acting toward them. For there is no such thing as successful activity toward things established through delusion, such as nacre-silver and the like.

Because it is consistent in empirical usage (*vyavahāra*), he says: "of jars and so forth. The mutual difference between jars and so forth is not erroneous in the state of empirical usage—unlike the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and the like—because it is established by experience as being unsublated so long as the knower exists. However, since the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and such things are sublated even while the knower exists, it is logical that there be a discrepancy (*visaṃvāda*) in that case.

The meaning is "the doctrine" (*vāda*). Indeed, existence (*sattva*) is threefold: empirical existence (*māyītika-sattva*), as in the case of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell; conventional existence (*vyāvahārika-sattva*), as in the case of jars, cloths, and so forth; and ultimate existence (*pāramārthika-sattva*), characterized by the absence of sublation at all times, which belongs to Brahman. In this context, with the intention of referring to the absence of ultimate existence, it was stated that the distinction of the non-self manifold is established through delusion (*bhrānti*). [Conventional...]

[page 98]
O Brahmins, whether as its own essential nature or as its very attribute, there is indeed a distinction.
Even in a hundred years, it cannot be determined in reality. || 53 ||

And since that conventional difference is accepted by the proponents [of various schools] both as having the nature of a real entity (*vasturūpa*) and as a property distinct from it, he says: "as its own-nature" (*svarūpatvena*). In this regard, first of all, the Prābhākaras [hold that] in the case of the statement "the cloth is different from the jar," [the difference is the very nature of the cloth].

They maintain that difference (*bheda*) is merely the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the cloth as constituted by its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), and not something distinct from it. Consequently, if difference were nothing other than the nature itself, then just like the apprehension of that nature, the apprehension of difference would also entail the consequence of being independent of a counter-correlate.

[This is because] in indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*), difference is perceived as the very essence of the object's nature, and [this same difference is then manifested] in determinate perception (*savikalpaka*) for practical usage (*vyavahāra*) in relation to a counter-correlate.

The Vaiśeṣikas and others maintain that difference is indeed a property (*dharma*) distinct from the essential nature of things, because it is established through dependence [on other factors] and is apprehended as "this is the difference between these two. Now, if difference is real because there is no contradiction in worldly practice, what is the point of talking about non-duality? To this he says: "Even for years... The reality of difference is not like that of Brahman.

That is the ultimate reality, because it is impossible to define it in terms of a real entity (*vastu*). To explain: first, the position that difference is an essential property of the thing itself (*svarūpa-bheda*) is untenable. For, just as in non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even in conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) it would not depend upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). Indeed, the apprehension of a thing's own nature does not depend upon the apprehension of a counter-correlate. Furthermore, [if difference were essential,] it would be constituted by a counter-correlate—

If difference were the very nature of a thing, then because the counter-correlate (pratiyogin) would also be included within that nature as a qualifier of the difference, it would follow that in such statements as "the self is different from the world," there would be a collapse into monism (advaita) of the self. Furthermore, if difference, which consists of a tearing apart,

were the nature of an object, then because unity— which inheres in the same substrate as non-difference— would be destroyed, nothing at all would remain as a single entity for the proponent of the theory that difference is the nature of things.
The entity would not be established. As it has been stated by Citsukhācārya:
"Because it is dependent, because it has a limit, and because duality would result in reality;
and because there is neither unity nor absence of doubt, difference is not the nature of the entity. (53)
Indeed, difference always belongs to one thing relative to another, never to a single thing by itself.
The logical proof of the distinctness of an entity is established only when its difference [from others] has been proven. ||54||

Nor is the position that difference is a distinct attribute (dharma-bheda) tenable; thus he says: "from another" (*anyataḥ*). For it is precisely through a qualified cognition—such as "this cloth is different from the jar," or "this is the difference between these two"—that difference, which is constituted by the locus (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), is apprehended. This is not correct, because it cannot withstand logical analysis (*vikalpāsahatvāt*). Does this [cognition] have difference alone as its object, or does it also have the entity itself? If it also has the entity...
Even then, does that [perception] arise preceded by difference, or preceded by the cognition of its objects, or else are both simultaneous?
Not the first; for it is impossible to cognize mere difference without the prior apprehension of the substratum (*dharmī*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).
For this very reason, the claim that the apprehension of an object is preceded by difference is also refuted. First, the characteristics of the substratum and the counter-correlate—

The third position—that one apprehends the object first and subsequently apprehends its difference—is also not tenable; for words, cognitions, and actions persist for only three moments, and thus there is no such thing as an operation that ceases after having already begun. Nor is the fourth position possible; for the cognition of difference would then have the substratum (dharmin) as its object.

For the cognition of the counter-correlative (*pratiyogijñāna*) is indeed the cause [of the cognition of difference]. And since that [cause] is restricted by the rule of existing in the immediately preceding moment, simultaneity is precluded. Furthermore, the qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) whose object is difference—such as "this is different from that"—[requires] the substratum (*dharmin*) which serves as the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).

It must indeed be accepted that [the cognition] is preceded by its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), because there is a rule that every qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*)—such as "Devadatta possesses a staff"—is necessarily preceded by the cognition of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), the qualified (*viśeṣya*), and their relation (*saṃbandha*). As it has been said:
"The qualifier, the qualified, the relation, and the worldly state [of things]..."
"Having grasped and synthesized this, one understands it as such and not otherwise."

Furthermore, the relationship of qualifier and qualified exists only between two distinct things; for a single entity cannot be both the qualifier and the qualified of itself. Now, regarding that difference by which those two, as qualifiers, are distinct from their counter-correlates—is this very same difference [that establishes their distinction], or is it another difference? If it is this very same one, there is the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). If it is another difference...

Since it is only between two distinct entities—the substratum (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*)—that difference exists, that [difference] too must be preceded by another difference. If that [second difference] is the very first one, then there is mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatā*). If, on the other hand, it is a third distinct difference, then a circularity (*cakraka*) results. If an infinite series of individual differences is accepted, then even for the final difference it would be the same; thus, because that [final difference] is unestablished, the root...
Because the limit of differentiation is unestablished, an infinite regress would result, which would destroy the very foundation [of cognition]. As it was stated by Citsukhācārya:

“Due to the impossibility of simultaneous apprehension, because of the consequence of an infinite regress, and because of mutual dependence, there is no sensory cognition even when there is a difference in properties.”

Intending all of this, he says: "of one from another. As for the literal meaning: indeed, the difference of one thing from another is defined by such expressions as "the cloth is different from the pot," and so forth. For it is not possible to define the difference of a single thing alone, because the apprehension of difference is necessarily preceded by the apprehension of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). Furthermore, otherness (*anyatva*) resides in difference.

When [difference] is established, it is established; yet, since difference between the locus (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is established only when their otherness is established, and difference is subsequently established, there arises the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*), mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), or circularity (*cakraka*). This is the meaning. || 54 ||
The Śruti declares with emphasis: "Being is one alone, without a second."
And the supreme Śruti declares: "This duality is mere illusion. (55)

Having thus dispelled difference through reasoning, he also states the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) supported by reasoning that reveals the absence of difference, beginning with the words "one alone," etc.: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1), and "One alone, without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1). Therein, by the word "one," internal difference (*svagatabheda*) is excluded; [the word] "one" refers to the partless (*akhaṇḍa*).

The meaning is "identical" (*karasa*). By the word "only" (*eva*), difference within the same class (*sajātīya-bheda*) is excluded. By the phrase "without a second" (*advitīyam*), even difference from other classes (*vijātīya-bheda*) is excluded. Regarding the non-duality of the supreme Śiva, whose nature is ultimately real and existent (*sad-rūpa*), there is no need for further evidence here;
the mention of "difference later on" is unnecessary.

Having thus presented [the argument], he states that even though the manifold expansion of non-self (*anātman*) is illusory, the Śruti is nonetheless the authoritative source:

"It is mere illusion" (*māyāmātram*). This refers to the verse in the *Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad*: "This duality is mere illusion; from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), there is non-duality. The meaning is this: all this visible world, which consists of the external and internal forms, is entirely nothing but mere illusion.

It is indeed composed of illusion (*māyāmayam*), because it is imagined through *māyā* within Brahman, which is established in its own nature. When *māyā* is sublated by the knowledge of the reality of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), its effect is also sublated; thus, in the ultimate sense, non-dual Brahman alone remains—this is the meaning. || 55 ||
For it has indeed been said: "For one who perceives oneness, what delusion is there? What sorrow?"
Indeed, there is fear from a second; it has also been said that there is no happiness in what is small. //56//
Thus, having ascertained the falsity of the phenomenal world (prapañca) superimposed upon Himself,

[the author] cites scripture as authority regarding the fruit that arises from the knowledge of the nature of the Supreme Śiva— who is the Self of all— as the innermost Self (pratyagātman): "Oneness..."

"Behold! Thus it is taught in the Vājasaneyaka Mantra-Upaniṣad: "When for the one who knows, all beings have become the Self alone, what delusion and what sorrow can there be for him who perceives that oneness?

Through the knowledge of the true nature of Brahman as the substrate, the phenomenal world—which consists of ignorance and its effects—dissolves, and [one attains] Brahman, which is unsurpassed bliss.

The meaning is that for the wise person who realizes non-duality (*advaita*), there is not even the possibility of attachment to grief and delusion. He states—by the words "from a second"—that if one does not accept the falsity of the world and instead accepts that the Self has a second entity, scripture itself demonstrates the contradiction: "From a second indeed comes fear," as stated in the Vājasaneyaka. From duality...
For if one accepts [the existence of] another, there must necessarily be fear of that other; therefore, the meaning is that duality alone brings about fear.

And in the Taittirīyaka, it is traditionally taught that the direct realization of Brahman as the Self is the means for attaining fearlessness, while the perception of difference is the cause of fear: "When, indeed, one finds refuge in this which is invisible, incorporeal, indefinable, and supportless, then one has no fear."

"He finds a firm foundation; then he becomes free from fear. But when he perceives even a slight difference in this [Self], then fear comes upon him. Having thus shown by the Scripture itself that undesirable consequences arise when there is the appearance of duality, [the author] cites the Scripture which demonstrates that even the desired goal is attained through the Scripture alone: "There is no bliss in the small..."

Thus it is said: In the seventh chapter of the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, Sanatkumāra instructs Nārada with these words: "The Infinite (*bhūman*) alone is to be sought after; that which is the Infinite is indeed bliss; in the finite there is no bliss.
That which is the unlimited, non-dual nature of Supreme Śiva is itself bliss, because it is unsurpassed.

The happiness existing from that of a universal monarch up to the end of the world of Brahmā is limited, established as increasing hundredfold at each successive stage; because it is subject to gradation and is perishable, it does not possess true happiness. Therefore, the meaning is that only *bhūman* (the Infinite), which consists of eternal and unsurpassed bliss, is to be known. || 56 ||

Therefore, through both reasoning and valid means of knowledge, the oneness of reality is firmly established.
And by the experience of the wise, the oneness of reality is firmly established.

Thus, because the scriptures establish with full intent the non-duality of the Self, and because the doubt regarding any contrary meaning has been dispelled by the force of the previously stated reasoning, he concludes that the nature of the supreme Śiva, which is without a second, is known solely through the Upaniṣads: "Therefore" (ataḥ). || 57 ||
Those people who understand the oneness of the Reality from the Great Saying (mahāvākya) alone—
For they are indeed liberated from saṃsāra, just as one is [liberated] upon awakening from one's own dream.

Regarding the phrase "the oneness of the reality": just as the dream-multiplicity ceases upon mere awakening and does not require any other action, in the very same way, the entire expansion of ignorance ceases without any effort simply through the knowledge of the direct realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self (*brahmātmaikya-sākṣātkāra*) produced by the great Vedānta statements (*mahāvākya*). This is the meaning. || 58 ||
Those men who, relying on the perception of duality, desire liberation;
They fall indeed into the most terrible cycle of existence; of this there is no doubt. || 59 ||

He states the sublation for one who, having abandoned the non-difference established by both valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*), accepts only difference: "Difference," etc. The meaning is that it is based on the scriptural text: "He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were multiplicity. (59)
And [he sees] the Self in all beings, and all beings in the Self.
Perceiving this, one becomes a sacrificer for the Self and attains self-sovereignty.

He states that the sacrifice of knowledge (*jñānayajña*) is none other than the very experience of the Self as the essence of all, which is universally recognized—not something distinct from that—by saying, "In all beings... For it is heard in scripture: "But he who perceives all beings in the Self alone, and the Self in all beings, therefore does not feel aversion. (BhG 6.29) [60]
Beholding all beings within oneself alone, O lords of sages.
He would undoubtedly have crossed over this ocean of saṃsāra. || 61 ||

By means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), [the Lord] declares through the verse beginning with "He who does not cause pain to any being" (*sarvabhūtānām*) that the aforementioned knowledge alone is the means to liberation, whereas ritual action (*karman*) is not a means to it. The remainder of the chapter is clear. || 61 ||
Many have been liberated from the bondage of worldly existence through the knowledge of non-duality.
There is nothing anywhere equal to this sacrifice of knowledge.

Those men who, having attained the knowledge of duality, desire liberation, [are bound] by the Sūta-saṃhitā. (427)
They have undoubtedly been bitten by the serpent of the great delusion of saṃsāra. || 63 ||
Excluding the sacrifice of the knowledge of the true nature of the Self, the lowest of men [perform other sacrifices].

Those who cross the ocean of saṃsāra by means of the sacrifice of karma.

The tenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Sacrifice of Knowledge."
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Sacrifice of Knowledge," in the fourth section, the Yajñavaibhava-khaṇḍa, of the *Śrī Sūta-saṃhitā-ṭīkā* known as the *Tātparya-dīpikā*.
Sūta said:
Now begins the eleventh chapter.
Once again, I shall explain the sacrifice of knowledge (jñānayajña) in brief.
O best of sages, listen with great joy to this source of bliss.

Thus, it has been established that the knowledge of the inner self as having the nature of Paraśiva alone is the means to liberation, and in this regard, the Vedāntic texts themselves are the authority, not any other means of knowledge. Now, this chapter is commenced to demonstrate how the identity of these two— which possess contradictory natures such as being subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*) and being free from it (*asaṃsāritva*)— can be logically consistent.
The king also [acted] thus. || 1 ||

The meaning is that the supreme Śiva-consciousness, characterized by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*), is the most excellent. Prior to that, the supreme Śiva-consciousness itself, characterized by the limiting adjunct of *māyā* dominated by pure *sattva*, is the omniscient one; for he [is superior] in comparison to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others.

The meaning is that the Supreme (para) is the most excellent, because it is the cause of all those previously mentioned beings beginning with Brahmā, by virtue of being the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for the Māyā that is about to evolve in the form of the world; it is self-established (*svapratiṣṭha*) and is the nature of Paraśiva. Even more excellent than that [Supreme], which is qualified by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of causality, is the Reality-Consciousness (*saccidānanda*) characterized by causality.
The meaning is that the nature of the Supreme Śiva, which consists of the singular essence of bliss, is superior even to everything that possesses limiting adjuncts (upādhi). || 19 ||
"Those who know through valid means of cognition that 'the soul exists' or 'it does not exist'..."

Thus, under the guise of establishing that [Brahman] is the most excellent of all, the unconditioned Supreme Brahman— which is understood through such scriptural passages as "neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long, intangible, formless, and imperishable," as being devoid of all attributes— is explained as that which is indicated by the word *tat* in the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*) "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*). Now, the true nature (svarūpa) indicated by the word *tvam* is likewise explained.

He demonstrates this with the words "There is a living self," and so forth. For the proponent of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*), who holds that "there is no living self," considers even the Self to be empty because of his adherence to the doctrine of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*). It is his view that the perception of the world as consisting of the diversity of selves is established merely through the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the Self. However, since an illusion without a substratum (*niradhiṣṭhāna-bhrānti*) and an absolute negation (*niravadhika-bādha*) are impossible, there must be a substratum for that [illusion].

Something must be accepted as the limit (*avadhi*) for the sublation [of the world]. That real entity which remains as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and as the limit for both the appearance of the world and its sublation is what we call the "Self" (*ātman*). Therefore, the meaning is that even by the proponent of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*), the existence of the Self must be admitted, because otherwise the occurrence of error and its subsequent sublation would be inexplicable. || 23 ||

He states that even intellect (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and so forth do not possess the nature of the Self precisely because they are instruments (*karaṇa*)—beginning with the words "momentarily perishing" (*kṣaṇapradhvaṃsī*). The word "na" (not) has no referent here. Egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) is a mental modification (*manovṛtti*) directed toward the Self that is distinct from it; because it is rooted in that [Self], it is the cause of the misfortune of saṃsāra.

[In the fourth section, the *Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa*—first, it describes the unconditioned form of Brahman, which serves as the substratum: "Brahman. According to the Śruti, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," and "Brahman is consciousness and bliss. Of this Brahman, which is of one undivided essence...]

It was previously established that words such as "truth" (*satya*) are indicative (*lakṣaka*) by means of the exclusion of falsity, insentience, suffering, and finitude. "By the state of being the imperishable Self" (*amaccyutātmabhāvena*) means by way of the non-obscured inner Self (*pratyagātman*).
By this, the non-selfhood of Brahman is excluded. "But always indeed" (*sarvadaiva tu*) means that it is not only after the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) that Brahman [is realized].
The meaning is that the personal existence (ātmabhāva) [exists] even prior to that. || 2 ||
Through the union with one's own power, it is without beginning or end and beyond the reach of logic.
O twice-born ones, although it is self-luminous, it appears as if unknown.
Though it exists, the wise man regards it as if non-existent; though it is one, he regards it as if divided.
Having assumed such a form, it appears as the phenomenal world (saṃsāra). || 4 ||

[Objection: Is it not observed that an object known in a general way through its white and luminous form, yet unknown in its specific forms such as being blue-backed or triangular, serves as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for the superimposition (*āropa*) of silver and so forth? But since Brahman is manifest in its entirety by virtue of its self-luminosity, how can it be the substratum? To this, he says: "The power of the Self" (*ātmaśakti*).

The meaning is that the power (*śakti*) of the Self resides within its own pure consciousness as *māyā*, and is not independent like the *prakṛti* postulated by the Sāṃkhyas. Regarding the phrase "without beginning or end": because such *māyā* and the Self are both beginningless, the relationship resting upon both of them is also beginningless. Furthermore, apart from the knowledge of that [Self], *māyā* is devoid of any finitude.

That connection would be infinite. How could such a connection with Māyā possibly exist in the self-luminous nature of Parameśvara? To this, he says: "from the inconceivable" (*atarkitāt*). This means "that which cannot withstand inquiry. By virtue of its connection with such Māyā, that Brahman, though self-luminous, appears as if it were not manifest. This is due to the power of concealment (*āvaraṇa-śakti*).

Because it is so enveloped; for this very reason, although its nature is Being (*sad-rūpa*), it becomes as if non-existent, and although it is non-dual, it appears to possess manifold forms due to its connection with various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Although by its own nature it is not subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsārin*), pure Consciousness (*cin-mātra*), having attained identification (*tādātmya*) with this or that internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) through superimposition (*adhyāsa*), becomes as if a transmigrating being. Therefore, it is said in the *Vārttika*:
The author says:
"What is this intolerance of yours regarding the postulation of [the self] as the prover?"
"Do you not see that saṃsāra is constructed right there by ignorance? || 3 || 4 ||
But within the non-differentiated form of Brahman, there exists that which consists of both the conscious and the unconscious.
O best of scholars, this division is imagined through its power, not by itself. ||5||

And thus, having established the possibility of that [Self] being the substratum— since even within its own self-luminous nature everything can be made to appear by the power of *māyā*— it is now possible to superimpose the two-fold world consisting of the sentient and the insentient.

He explains the twofold nature of that substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) through the power of Māyā, stating: "Of Brahman. In the non-dual, undivided form of Brahman itself, two parts consisting of the conscious and the unconscious are conceptually constructed by the power of Māyā—through the imposition of the quality of *sattva* and the imposition of the qualities of *rajas* and *tamas*—but not inherently. Since this occurs solely through Māyā, therefore... [it is not real].
The meaning is "intrinsic" (svābhāvika). || 5 ||
The distinction between consciousnesses is imagined within the conscious form of Brahman.
From omniscience down to a pillar, [all things] exist only through illusion.
Increase and decrease are merely imagined among them through illusion.
And the forms of being a controller, being controlled, and so forth, are merely conceptual constructs. ||7||
But by the power of Mahāmāyā, Brahmā was placed in an unconscious state.
The world, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) and ending with emptiness (śūnya), is merely imagined (parikalpita).
O lords of sages, there is both increase and decrease even in this world.
It is imagined as being superior in every respect, yet in worldly practice it is [merely] through illusion.

Now, he demonstrates by distinguishing between these two—the Supreme Brahman and the form—wherein and for whom each is postulated, beginning with the words "the conscious form of Brahman," and so forth. Because the quality of *sattva* consists of luminosity (*prakāśa*), the form conditioned by that is the conscious form; because *rajas* and *tamas* are the opposite of that, the form conditioned by them is the unconscious form. In the form of volition (*cetanākāra*), beginning with the omniscient Lord (*īśvara*)—who is characterized by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of *māyā* and is primarily composed of pure being (*viśuddhasattva*)—and extending down to a mere pillar, the entire manifold of enjoyers (*bhoktṛprapañca*) is imagined through *māyā*. Thus, having established the falsity of the phenomenal world—which consists of the objects of that [consciousness]—on the grounds that it is sublated by knowledge, the author now proceeds to demonstrate the falsity of even the Supreme Power (*paraśakti*), which is of the nature of pure consciousness (*saṃvidrūpā*), lest there arise the suspicion that she too is distinct from Supreme Śiva (*paraśiva*). He begins this with the words:
"Even the King... (verse 1).
O best of the twice-born, [this occurs] within the form of the power of Māyā, which has pure consciousness as its substratum.
That consciousness which has entered [into all things] is non-conceptual and self-luminous.

To dispel the delusion that Māyā alone is His supreme power, He reveals the true nature of that supreme power with the words beginning "cinmātra" (pure consciousness). Prior to the creation of the universe—which consists of the enjoyer and the enjoyed and is governed by a controller—during its state of dissolution, there is an utter absence of the causes of conceptual construction; thus, the nature of Supreme Śiva is entirely free from conceptualization (*nirvikalpaka*). While abiding in its own nature, even Māyā, though superimposed upon it, remains entirely free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). And that [Māyā], being slightly conceptualized through the ripening of the karma of living beings, at that time—since even the distinction between Śiva and Śakti does not exist—accepts as its substrate nothing other than pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), which is common to both. Even Paraśiva, whose form is pure consciousness, [remains thus].

By virtue of that connection, [the Supreme] abandons its own self-established state to some extent and becomes oriented toward that [individual soul]. Now, one might object: how can the Supreme Śiva—who is unattached, indifferent, whose nature is supreme bliss, and who is changeless—be the cause of the creation and so forth of the universe by resorting to *māyā*? If it is argued that this occurs "by virtue of the ripening of the fruits of the souls' karma," we say no; for that [Supreme Being], being independent, cannot possess dependence upon that [karma].

Because of [His] yoga. Nor is it logical that He acts for the sake of His own enjoyment, since He has attained all desires (*āptakāma*). Nor is it appropriate to say it is for the sake of sport (*līlā*); for if that were the case, there would be no justification for the specific regularity (*pratiniyama*) of the diversity of mountains, rivers, oceans, and so forth, nor for the specific regularity of the diversity of happiness and the like. This is not a fault; for the specific regularity [is determined] by the gradations of the fully ripened karma of sentient beings.
Because [merit and demerit] are the causes. Nor does this entail that Paraśiva falls under the subjection of karma; for [the Lord acts] by means of His own volition (*svasaṃkalpa*).

At the time of initiating the play (*līlā*) of creating the world and so forth, the arising of effects without an external cause would be highly improper; thus, merit, demerit, and the like serve as the causes of pleasure, pain, and so on, while the creation of the specifically determined phenomenal world (*prapañca*) serves as the cause for their experience.

And having so resolved, Paraśiva engaged in the sport (*līlā*) of manifesting His own power; and in order that His own resolve might remain true and unimpeded, He performs the same forms of creative play, such as creation and so forth, in all Brahma-kalpas.

*Tātparyadīpikā* commentary—[In the section on the manifestation of the universe]: There is no impairment of the independent nature (*svātantrya*) of Paraśiva when he engages in the play (*līlā*) of creation and so forth. For this very reason, the Blessed One—

Drahyāyaṇa established in his Sūtra, "But like the world, it is mere sport (līlā) alone," that for the Supreme Lord’s engagement in creation and so forth, the sole cause is sport, as in the case of a king and the like. And thus, that Māyā, which rests upon the pure consciousness (cinmātra) common to both Śiva and Śakti, further becomes twofold. [It is] the object of power (śakya), dependent on the cognition of the correlate...

[It is distinguished] by way of being the object of the act of naming (*paṇa*) and by way of having its determination dependent on that [naming]. Thus, due to the two-fold nature of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), even the pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) which is the substrate (*upadheya*) is divided into two. Therein, *māyā* is that power (*śakti*) whose determination is dependent on the capacity for cognition;
just as a seed in its state of swelling, under the influence of the conjunction of water, wind, and so forth, [produces a sprout], so too—just as a finger... [is perceived].

The state of *rāva* (sound) likewise means that, by the power of the ripening of the karma of living beings, it is the state of the sprout of *māyā*—accumulated through skillful means—which serves as the cause for the manifestation of the world. Śiva is consciousness (*caitanya*) as conditioned by that form of *māyā* whose definition does not depend on the cognition of a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*). It is that consciousness which is delimited by the power (*śakti*) that takes the form of the sprout of the world.

That which consists of the nature of consciousness is called the Supreme Power (*parā śakti*). Therefore, it is solely due to the limitation imposed by adjuncts (*upādhi*) that the single, pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) appears divided into the forms of Śiva and Śakti; in ultimate reality, however, there is only oneness as pure consciousness—this is the meaning.

The meaning is that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), there is no difference because [all things] consist of the previously mentioned nature of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). Thus, regarding the non-difference of Śiva and Śakti—

Having thus described the supreme power (*parā śakti*) in its general form, he explains—by means of the passage beginning with "the world" (*jagat*)—that when that very power is defined by the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) of specific objects of action (*śakya*), it becomes the nature of those respective particular powers. The term "cause of the world" (*jagatkāraṇa*) is a designation referring to the state of being [the cause]. Śiva, having attained the state of being the cause of the world, is the sprout-form of the world.

Because, subsequent to the state of *ṛ* (the letter *r*), that [state] is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of *māyā*, which is about to evolve in the form of the world, that aforementioned supreme power (*parā śakti*) of Śiva himself becomes the power of the creation of the world. Thus, the meaning is that Śiva, devoid of power, would be incapable of creating the world due to his lack of power. This should be applied in the same way everywhere hereafter. || 4 ||

In the state of Śiva’s being the cause of the universe, Māyā serves as his limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). When that Māyā possesses an equilibrium of the powers of knowledge and action (*jñāna-śakti* and *kriyā-śakti*), if it is dominated by pure *sattva* and the power of knowledge is predominant, then Śiva, having that as his adjunct, becomes omniscient. However, when the power of action is predominant, then Śiva, having that as his adjunct, is [the Lord] directly manifest.
Thus, he becomes the agent of that act of vision (*īkṣaṇa*) which consists of the contemplation of what is to be created. This is what is meant:

the one supreme Śiva himself, directly, becomes fivefold through the influence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). That Śiva who is conditioned by Māyā, whose powers of knowledge and action have not yet emerged, is called [Śiva]. His definition is dependent upon the counter-correlate of that power.

Śiva is Śakti, whose form is conditioned by that [power]. When she possesses the powers of knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*), which have arisen from *māyā* and are equally predominant, the nature of Paraśiva, conditioned by those [powers], is the cause of the universe. Due to the predominance of the power of knowledge, he is omniscient; due to the predominance of the power of action, he is the "Beholder" (*īkṣita*). Thus, the different states of Śiva are described by the followers of the Āgamas as "pure" (*śuddha*).
They are carried forward with the mantra *tvānīti*. As it has been said:

Having thus demonstrated the majesty of the Supreme Power (paraśakti), he establishes that everything should be contemplated by the seeker of liberation as being of the very nature of the perfect Supreme Śiva—beginning with the words "This Śivā" and so forth. Consciousness (saṃvit) is Śivā herself, resting solely in pure consciousness (cinmātra) and having entered into the power of Āpa; she is Umā, assuming playful forms (līlāvigraha), and is the pure consciousness that serves as the material cause (upādāna) of the entire insentient realm.

"Everything": all that has been previously mentioned—the entire world consisting of sentient and insentient beings, whose nature is *māyā* and its effects—is superimposed upon the perfectly full essence of Paraśiva, like silver upon a mother-of-pearl shell. Since, like the silver, this "everything" does not exist apart from its substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), only that substratum remains. Thus, the meaning is this: that which is all this [world], that "everything" is not [ultimately real].

Rather, it is the unconditioned Supreme Śiva himself; by directly perceiving Him through the knowledge generated by the great Vedāntic Mahāvākyas, one becomes Śiva oneself, unconditioned at that very moment. Thus, liberation is simultaneous with knowledge. The use of the present tense in "perceiving" (*paśyan*) indicates this simultaneity. Even in the Śruti, it is stated that the attainment of the Supreme Brahman occurs at the very same time as the dawning of knowledge.

He establishes with an illustration that the practical application of injunctions and prohibitions arises solely from the perception of difference, and not for one who is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), beginning with the words "is touched" (*spṛśyate*). Having thus established that Śakti is not distinct from the nature of Paraśiva, he begins to demonstrate that even the appearance of duality in the form of the five Brahmans, such as Sadyojāta and the others, is not ultimately real: "Furthermore... (1).
Śiva alone is directly manifest, characterized by reality, knowledge, and the rest.

"Single" (*eka*) means the exclusion of any difference that is internal to itself or external to it. "Truth, knowledge, and so forth" (*satyajñānādi*): by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), infinity and the nature of bliss are intended. "Devoid of modification" (*vikārarahita*): [this refers to] being free from origination, transformation, and so on.

The meaning is that he is devoid of all modification and is immutably eternal (*kūṭastha-nitya*). For this very reason, he is pure and stainless. Being thus characterized, Paraśiva himself—being the one supreme reality—is established in five ways through the differentiation of his own powers (*sva-śakti*) and states (*avasthā-bheda*), in the form of Īśāna and the others, as previously described. To explain: she who is *Parā*, whose nature is the totality of all powers...

The Śakti previously described, when defined by its specific capacities characterized as creation (sṛṣṭi), maintenance (sthiti), withdrawal (saṃhṛti), concealment (tirobhāva), and grace (anugraha), becomes fivefold, divided according to the nature of these specific powers of emission and so forth. Therefore, the very essence of Paraśiva, which is pure consciousness (cinmātra) alone, conditioned by the power of creation, is Sadyojāta; [conditioned] by the power of maintenance...

Vāmadeva is [the form] characterized by the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the power of withdrawal; Aghora is [the form] characterized by the power of concealment; Tatpuruṣa is [the form] characterized by the power of obscuration.

The Lord is pure consciousness conditioned by hundreds of adjuncts (*upādhi*). Thus, the meaning is that the one Supreme Śiva exists divided fivefold by means of five adjuncts. As it has been said by the followers of the Āgamas:
"He alone is to be known as eternally liberated, yet he possesses five bodies."
"His fivefold activity consists of emanation, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, and likewise the bestowing of grace; this is declared to be the function of Him who is eternally risen. (2)
"Īśāna" and "tatpuruṣa"—thus [are they called], O you of excellent vows.
"O best of Brahmins, [he is] 'Aghoraśca'; O twice-born ones, [he is] 'Vāmadeva'. (3)

"He rules over the entire universe by means of his transcendent attribute."

For the knowledge of the identity with one's own Self (*svātmaikyajñāna*) is indeed the means for attaining the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*), and that arises only from hearing the Vedānta (*vedāntaśravaṇa*). "Hearing" (*śravaṇa*) consists of the ascertainment of the verbal power and intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the great Vedāntic aphorisms (*mahāvākya*), as well as the investigation through reasoning (*nyāyānusaṃdhāna*). Therefore, the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) is to be heard. [This is done] by removing the notions of impossibility (*asaṃbhāvanā*) and misconception (*viparītabhāvanā*) regarding the meaning that has been heard.

Reflection (*manana*) is the investigation of the principles that establish the nature of falsity. Meditation (*upāsana*) is the mental apprehension of that which has been ascertained as such through reasoning, by means of a continuous flow of homogeneous cognitions uninterrupted by heterogeneous ones, for the purpose of direct realization through one-pointedness of mind. In this same manner, reflection and meditation follow after hearing (*śravaṇa*).

The mention of *śravana* (hearing) first here is for the purpose of making it known that the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the identity of the Supreme Śiva and the Self arises only from hearing the great Vedāntic statements (*mahāvākya*) when accompanied by both [reflection and meditation], and not from mere hearing alone. For this very reason, it is said: "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon."

Thus, with reference to the vision of the Self, the Śruti teaches hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth as its means. Among these, hearing alone is enjoined as the primary factor for the sake of the result, like the *āgneya* sacrifice and others; while reflection (*manana*) and so forth follow thereafter, like the *pradhāna* (principal) offerings and others. As Yājñavalkya said: "By means of reflection and meditative concentration, which are subsidiary factors (*aṅga*) that assist the result..."

"By the grace of Śiva"—thus it is said. From the favor of Īśvara comes the favor of the Guru; from that comes the comprehension of the meaning of the Śruti; and from that, devotion to Śambhu. "From Him, indeed, all other beings subsist on a mere fraction of bliss," according to the Śruti. [Objection: It has been established that for that which is of the single essence of indivisible Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*), there exists a state of having two feet by virtue of *māyā*; however, this is untenable. Thus begins the instruction.
"It is commenced once again. || 1 ||
O lords of sages, [this applies] to objects such as jars, water-pots, and granaries.
That which manifests as existence is one; it manifests solely in the form of existence itself.
And some maintain that it is distinguished by its specific form. (2)

A certain genus called "Being" (*sattā*), which possesses a single body that is common to all specific individuals such as pots and cloths by virtue of being the locus for the recurring linguistic usage of "existent"—as in "the pot is existent," "the cloth is existent," and "the wall is existent"—must be admitted. Although it is one in its universal form, it becomes manifold in its particular forms such as pot, cloth, and so forth. For this very reason, the Bhāṭṭas maintain that the relationship between the genus and the individual is identity itself, and not inherence (samavāya). || 2 ||

Because of the absence of specific form, by reason of the non-existence of difference.

He refutes this with the words "that is inconsistent," and so forth. Regarding the term "wise ones" (*manīṣiṇaḥ*), the meaning is "those who know reality. To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of the absence of particulars" (*viśeṣa*). This is because there is an absence of the very nature of particulars—such as jars, cloths, and so on—which serve as the cause for the differentiation of existence (*sattā*). Now, one might object: "But jars, cloths, and the like, which are particular in form, are indeed experienced. To this, he says: "In the absence of difference... (*bhedābhāve*).

It does not [apply]. Because in the tenth chapter, ultimate difference has been refuted everywhere in the phenomenal world (*prapañca*); therefore, for this reason, there is the impossibility of a specific form (*viśeṣa-rūpa*) that inheres in the same object as difference—this is the meaning. He demonstrates this very point with the words "if difference exists.
If there were difference of a jar, a cloth, or the like from anything whatsoever, then even the state of being a *viśeṣa* would be pervaded by difference.

Only then could that [distinction] belong to it; for a single entity does not distinguish itself from itself. Nor is there any distinction for it by way of its own-nature in relation to something else. Therefore, since difference has been refuted, in the absence of difference, the nature of specific forms such as a jar and so forth is not possible in the ultimate sense—this is the meaning. || 3 || 4 ||
If, however, the form of differentiation actually exists in reality within being (sattā), [then...]
If, however, the form of differentiation were distinct from existence, it would be like the principle of emptiness.
O twice-born ones, it would be nothing but emptiness; there would be no form of differentiation whatsoever.

Now, he restates [the opponent's position] in order to refute the differentiated form of existence (*sattā*) by showing its inability to withstand conceptual analysis, beginning with the words "the form of difference" (*bhedākāra*). That which is divided is a "difference" (*bheda*), that is, a particularity (*viśeṣa*); such a thing exists in space within objects like a jar or a cloth.
The form of difference (*bhedākāra*). Is that [form] different from existence (*sattā*) or non-different? It is not the first [option]; thus he says:

"difference," etc. If the form of difference—such as a jar, a cloth, and so forth—were different from that aforementioned existence, then it would be non-existent, like the horn of a hare, because there would be no distinction in its not being of the nature of existence. This might be so—

Even for objects such as a jar or a cloth, their existence [sattva] results from a relation with Being (sattā), yet that relation does not exist in the case of a rabbit’s horn; to this, he replies: "Not at all. Even if one abandons the relation with Being, is this jar and so forth existent or non-existent? If it is non-existent, then because there is no distinction between what is non-existent, that [relation] would attach to a rabbit’s horn as well. In the second case [if it is existent]...

It must be stated that this [existence] is due solely to its being qualified by existence (*sattā*). In that case as well, does existence reside in a substrate already qualified by its own self, or by another existence? In the first case, it is a contradiction of its own nature. In the second case, to avoid the fallacy of infinite regress (*atiprasaṅga*), it must be stated that even that other existence resides in a substrate already qualified by existence. And if that [second existence] is qualified...
If entities were not [inherently] existent, then there would first of all be mutual dependence; if they were [inherently] distinct, there would be the fallacy of circularity (*cakraka*).

If, in order to avoid these faults, one were to accept an infinite series of such existences, then there would be the fault of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) that destroys the very root of the matter.
Because it is seized by such defects as these, the form of difference cannot exist as something distinct from pure existence (sattā), just like the horn of a hare.
This is the meaning. || 5 ||
If that form of differentiation is non-different from existence, then it is indeed that [existence] itself.
If they were both different and non-different, there would be the occurrence of both faults.
Therefore, there exists no object of distinction apart from existence itself. || 7 ||

He says "not the second" with the words "the form of difference. If the particular form (*viśeṣākāra*)—the pot—were non-different from existence (*sattā*), then, because it would be included within its own nature, the result would be the absolute monism of existence (*sattādvaita*); this is the sense in which our desired goal is established. The universal "Being" (sattā) is included within the particular form. The proponent of the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference (bhedābhedavādī) objects, arguing that because non-difference exists, the particular form is not non-existent like the horn of a hare; to him, he replies: "If they were both different and non-different. If Being and the particular form were both different and non-different, then there would be the voidness associated with the position of difference and the monism of Being (sattādvaita) associated with the position of non-difference.

The meaning is that both [of these] will fall upon it. Regarding the word "tasmāt" (therefore): because, according to the manner described, the form of difference is unable to withstand inquiry, therefore the specific object consisting of jars, cloths, and so forth, does not exist at all apart from pure Being (*sattā*). || 6 ||
The cognition of a specific object, however, is established through error; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, that single, eternal existence is itself Brahman, the highest of the high.
If Brahman were different from existence, it would be non-existent, like the horn of a rabbit.

To the question, "How then is there the cognition of existence (*sattva*) regarding that [object]? he says: "Regarding the specific object" (*viśeṣārtha*). Since it is imagined through *māyā* within Brahman, whose nature is existence and which is undifferentiated, the very existence of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is perceived even in the specific object characterized as a pot, a cloth, and so forth—as in "an existent pot," "an existent cloth," or "an existent wall. This is just like [the perception of existence] in a snake, a line of ants, and the like.

In cases where faults are attributed—such as "this snake" or "this [rope] holds this"—the portion that appears is the underlying substrate. By the same logic, according to the principle that "whatever appears interpenetrated by something else is superimposed upon that thing," this entire world, being interpenetrated by Being (*sat*), is shown to be superimposed upon Brahman, whose nature is Being. Thus it is said: "For all this is Being; it is Being, Being. For all this shines because of Consciousness (*cit*)."
And [it is said]: "it appears. Therefore, the meaning is that the perception of the world as real is established solely through delusion. Regarding the word "ataḥ" (therefore):

since there is no such thing as an ultimate specific object in this way, for that reason, that existence (*sattā*) exists at all times and is not differentiated by specific objects; this is the meaning. Now, one might object: existence is indeed the common usage of the term "real" that recurs across many individual instances of the real (*sad-vyakti*).
The specific property (*dharmaviśeṣa*) characterized by "existence" (*sattā*) is established as a universal (*jāti*).

If the individuals (*vyaktayaḥ*), which serve as its substrates (*dharmin*), did not exist, how could it remain without a support? To this, he replies: "That itself is Brahman. This would indeed be so if existence were a universal; however, it is not a universal, because, due to the absence of particular instances (*viśeṣārtha*), it lacks the nature of a universal (*jātitva*).

"Existence alone, my dear, this was in the beginning, one only, without a second"—from this Śruti, that Brahman is indeed Existence (*sat*). Now, an objection may be raised: existence (*sattā*) is indeed an attribute (*dharma*) of the existent (*sat*), for it is stated in the traditional Smṛti: "The suffixes *tva* and *tal* are used to denote the state of that quality by virtue of whose presence a word is applied to a substance. This is not a fault; for the Supreme Brahman, whose very nature is Existence, is itself "Existence" (*sadeva*).
It is called "Being" (*sattā*) because it persists as the underlying substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) throughout the many individual manifestations imagined within itself.

The meaning is that just as the very nature of the moon—its "moon-ness"—persists everywhere through the power of its non-falsity despite the imagined multiplicity of the single moon due to the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of water-waves, so it is here. However, when [it is considered] as the nature of Brahman—

When that ignorance is removed through direct realization, its effect—the phenomenal world (*dṛśyaprapañca*)—is also removed; at that time, that Brahman is called "Being" (*sat*), but not as an objective existence (*sattā*). This is because there is no further persistence of its own nature due to the absence of anything else to be pervaded. Nor does that Brahman persist [as a substrate], since there is nothing else remaining to serve as a limit for its exclusion. As it has been stated by the authors of the *Vārttika*:
"That reality which is neither excluded nor followed along is expressed by the word Brahman. Thus it is said.

But surely, how can the word *sattā*, which denotes the property [of existence], be treated otherwise? Even in the passage, "That alone, my dear, is real" (*sadeva somya*), it must be accepted that *sat* denotes both the substratum and its property as being connected with existence (*sattā*). To this, he says:
"Of existence" (*sattāyāḥ*). If that Brahman, as the substratum, were distinct from existence itself, then the previously mentioned...

By the logic of the form of differentiation, even that Brahman would become as non-existent as a human horn; therefore, the supreme Brahman is essentially existence itself, and the relationship of subject and attribute (dharmin-dharma) is not tenable—this is the meaning. || 8 ||
In that case, O best of Brahmins, those objects such as jars and the like—
But they do not exist in any way apart from pure being (sattā).
Thus, by means of the detailed examination of the noble truth, he concludes that the non-duality of Brahman is established— referring to the phrase "tatraivam" (in that very way).
Since pots, cloths, and so forth are superimposed upon Brahman, whose nature is Being (*sat*), therefore they do not exist apart from it.
The meaning is that they exist. || 9 ||
Even the exceedingly pure Śruti declares: "This is indeed Brahman. (10)
And likewise, there is the experience of the wise; of this there is no doubt.

When it has been established in this manner that the entire world has Brahman as its self, the scripture provides corroboration: "Brahman alone is this"—"This immortal Brahman is before me, behind me, to the south, and to the north; it is below and above; this entire universe is encompassed by Brahman, the most excellent. Whatever shines forth is all that most excellent, most weighty, and most expansive Brahman alone. From that which has become the cause—

[In the *Prajñāvimalakhaṇḍa*—the meaning is that there is nothing whatsoever that is separate [from Brahman]. Regarding the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*): since there is no object whatsoever that is not non-distinct from Brahman, which is of the nature of existence (*sad-rūpa*), because it is superimposed upon its own essential nature, therefore all this visible world, which has become an effect, is entirely...]
The meaning is that [it] does not differ from the nature of Paraśiva, who is its cause. || 10 || 11 ||
Just as it appears by its own nature in the form of a clay pot and so forth.

Just as gold appears in various forms such as bracelets and other ornaments.
Thus Śiva, the illuminator of all, shines as everything in every way. || 13 ||

He establishes this very fact—that the manifold of effects has the nature of the causal Brahman—by means of examples, beginning with the words "Just as in a clay jar," and so forth. Just as clay appears in the form of various effects such as jars and bowls, so too does Paraśiva appear in the form of the entire universe due to the influence of the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of Māyā. From the knowledge of the Brahman that is the cause of all, there arises the knowledge of everything.

Having made that proposition, examples such as clay and so forth were employed for the purpose of establishing it: "Just as, my dear, by means of a single lump of clay, all that is made of clay becomes known—the modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; the reality is simply 'clay'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4), and so on. Bādarāyaṇa also [maintained] that the effect, the world, is not distinct from its cause, Brahman.
He composed the aphorism: "The non-difference from that [Brahman] [is established] on account of such words as 'originating' (ārambhaṇa), etc. (2.1.14). 12 || 13 ||
Just as a piece of mother-of-pearl appears by its very nature in the form of silver, so does Śiva, the illuminator of all, appear as everything. 14.

Now, it might be argued that in the case of clay, metal, and so forth, the effect such as a bowl is not superimposed [upon them], but rather produced by them; and that this effect becomes a different substance from its causal substance, such as clay—thus the logicians disagree. To them, he states another illustration: "As with mother-of-pearl. Just as mother-of-pearl, through the power of Māyā, is superimposed upon the consciousness that is its own substrate...
The meaning is that just as silver appears in the form of silver, so too Paraśiva, by the power of Māyā resting upon Him, appears in the form of the entire universe. || 14 ||
Just as the dreamer appears by his own nature in the form of himself [within the dream].
In that same way, Śiva, who is the illuminator of all things, shines as everything in its entirety. || 15 ||
— Now, one might object: "In cases such as mother-of-pearl appearing as silver, one thing is superimposed upon another; how can such a superimposition be possible upon the non-dual Brahman?
Anticipating this doubt, the author establishes the point by means of another illustration, beginning with the words "the dreamer."

The meaning is as follows: just as the dreamer—the *taijasa* self—assumes the forms of various dream objects through the power of its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), so too the non-dual Lord assumes the nature of the world in its manifold forms through the power of His own *māyā*.
This is because it is observed that the dreamer becomes identical with the dream objects, as stated in the scripture: "Having become a dream through the intellect, he transcends this world..."
"O Death, the forms of intelligence. || 15 ||

Just as darkness and light manifest within space.
All this, both insentient and sentient, thus appears within the Supreme Self.

Now, raising the objection: "How can the world, characterized by the contradictory natures of the sentient and the insentient, be superimposed upon Brahman, which is partless and non-dual?"—the author establishes this by means of another illustration, beginning with the words "Andhakāra" (darkness).

Just as in a single partless space, where distinctions are imagined through the influence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), both darkness and light—though possessing contradictory natures—appear simultaneously; so too, within the nature of Paraśiva, which is imagined through the distinctions of limiting adjuncts, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of the division between the conscious and the unconscious appears as being established. This is the meaning. || 16 ||
Just as the waves and ripples appear first upon the great ocean.
The world, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) and ending with the specific elements (viśeṣa), appears thus within the Self. || 17 ||

He provides another clear illustration of how the entire manifold of effects (kāryaprapañca) results in nothing but its cause, stating: "Like waves," and so forth. Just as a great wave is itself a mere atom of water due to the force of the wind—so that within a single ocean, specific forms such as waves, ripples, and bubbles appear at the very moment they are perceived and then dissolve back into that same [ocean]—in this very way [the world dissolves].

The meaning is that even within the nature of Paraśiva, specific forms consisting of the elements such as space and their derivatives exist by the power of his own Māyā, and they dissolve back into that very same reality. || 17 ||
Śambhu is the elements, Śambhu is the worlds,
and Śambhu is the mountains.
That alone is everything; nothing exists beyond it.
Therefore, that is the one, and this is the ultimate reality.
He is indeed Śambhu who is to be worshipped through sacrifices and likewise attained through all manner of gifts.
He is to be recited with all the distinguished mantras, and he is sought after by the gods, headed by Indra, the lord of the immortals.
She who is constantly distinguished by her austerities [worships] this Maheśa with that which is most dear to him.
The hosts of lords of sages constantly worship, bow down to, and praise him with their speech. || 20 ||

For those who behold the supreme Śiva, the primordial source of all,

Regarding the term *paramaśivam*: for those who directly realize Supreme Śiva—whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*)—within the center of the heart-lotus as their own self (*svātmatayā*), there is the destruction of ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the root of all misfortune; consequently, the succession of manifold births, which is the effect of that [ignorance], [comes to an end].

The meaning is that the accumulated store of merit and demerit, consisting of dharma and adharma and so forth, having ceased, becomes consumed by the fire of true knowledge. And it is heard in scripture: "Just as a tuft of reed-wool thrown into a fire would be completely burnt up, even so all his evils are completely burnt up.
This has also been stated by the Blessed One:
"Just as a kindled fire reduces fuel to ashes, O Arjuna,
so does the fire of knowledge reduce all actions to ashes."

Bādarāyaṇa also established in his Sūtras that through the knowledge of the supreme reality, there occurs the destruction of accumulated karma and the non-clinging of future karma: "Upon the attainment of That, there is the non-clinging and destruction of subsequent and prior sins, because of the scriptural declaration thereof. And this rule applies to karma other than that which has already begun to bear fruit; however, the commenced (prārabdha) karma must be exhausted through experience.

Because the Śruti passage, "For him there is delay only so long as he is not released," teaches that even after the arising of knowledge, a delay persists until the fall of the body, thereby establishing that prārabdha-karma can be terminated only through experience (bhoga).

Furthermore, because it has been specified by that very [text] itself: "But only those whose effects have not yet begun [are destroyed], for that is their limit. Therefore, regarding whatever karma—be it merit, demerit, or the like—is accumulated during the period of experiencing the karma that has already begun, He declares its non-clinging with the words "by actions.
For it is heard in scripture: "Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf..."

They say: Just as a rope, appearing through illusion (*māyā*) in the form of a snake or the like, does not appear in the form of a snake or the like after the knowledge of its true nature has arisen— rather, it is perceived that even previously this was only a rope and was never a snake or the like— even so, the Supreme Śiva, though appearing in the form of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) due to the power of ignorance (*avidyā*) previously, [is not so in reality].
Even after the attainment of knowledge, this [world] is perceived as being nothing other than the supreme Śiva, who alone is real, and not the phenomenal world (prapañca).

Thus, since it is established that the visible phenomenal world is non-existent throughout the three periods of time—having not been, not being, and not being about to be—its falsity (mithyātva) is proven; such is the meaning. || 27 ||
Just as a person, even while perceiving this earth through its nature as water, still knows it to be the ground.

Regarding the phrase "just as": according to the Śruti text, "From these [waters] arose the earth," water is the cause of the earth.

Just as one who knows the earth—which is the effect—to exist in the form of its cause, water, still perceives that earth as such, so too one who knows the Supreme Śiva, who is the cause, to exist in the form of the effect, the phenomenal world (prapañca), nevertheless perceives Him exactly as He is, devoid of all limiting adjuncts (nirupādhika). This is the meaning.
Therefore, the experience of the phenomenal world does not exist at all times;
indeed, it is the experience of the awakening to one's own true nature that exists perpetually.
Thus perceiving, with his experience complete, he is neither bound-and-liberated nor indeed simply bound. (29)

"Not bound, not liberated": thus, in all this phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*), one who directly realizes the perfectly full reality (*paripūrṇa-tattva*) alone is neither bound nor liberated, because there is an absolute absence of any bondage distinct from the nature of Supreme Śiva (*paraśiva*). For this very reason, he is not bound;
for the conventional discourse of bondage and liberation exists only when the perception of duality (*bhedadṛṣṭi*) is real. Thus it has been said:
"There is neither cessation nor arising, neither one bound nor one who strives for attainment; neither one desiring liberation nor one liberated—this is the ultimate truth. || 29 ||

The stainless Supreme Lord himself shines forth by his own nature as his very self.
Therefore, there is no manifestation of conceptual proliferation, nor is there any bondage or liberation for anyone.

Regarding the phrase "as its own essential nature": when the faultless, self-luminous Supreme Śiva manifests as the essential nature of the inner self (*pratyagātman*), then, through the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*), there is an absence of the cause of bondage for the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) which is its effect.
The meaning is the liberation from the bondage of worldly existence. || 30 ||
For this is indeed the supreme culmination of the Veda,
and of the lords of sages, and even of Śaṅkara himself.

Thus, for one in whom the knowledge of reality has arisen, liberation (*mukti*) is simply abiding in the nature of Brahman, which is the single, indivisible essence of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*). He raises a suspicion regarding a limiting condition (*upādhi*) in the aforementioned inference—namely, "of the effect" (*kāryasya*). The meaning is as follows: jars, cloths, and so forth possess impermanence because they are produced (*kṛtakatvāt*), not because they are non-self (*anātmatvāt*). Therefore, how could there be impermanence for things such as space (*ākāśa*)? This is the underlying intention: when "impermanence" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), "being produced" is the limiting condition; for wherever there is "non-self-ness," there is "being produced."

There is no pervasion by the probans (*sādhanavyāpti*). In illusions (*māyā*) and in cases such as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), there is "non-selfhood" (*anātmatva*) despite the absence of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*); therefore, the probans does not pervade [the property] in all instances of the example. Since the pervasion exists in the sense that "wherever there is impermanence (*anityatva*), there is being produced," there is pervasion by the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatva*). Thus, while the probans does not pervade [the locus], it pervades the probandum.
"For 'you' (tvam) is indeed its definition. Therefore, the meaning is that because it lacks self-nature (*anātmaka*), it does not follow that it is impermanent.

He refutes the *upādhi* by showing its lack of pervasion over the probandum (*sādhya*)—stating, "that is not correct.
