Now, at the time of the arising of a cognition such as "this is a jar," the cognition concerning the jar that existed prior to it does not persist; how then can that [cognition]...?

To address the question of its permanence, he says: "The modification of the mind" (*cittavṛtti*). The mind (*citta*) is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which consists of a transformation of *sattva*.
Its modification (*vṛtti*)—which takes the form of objects such as a jar due to the contact between the object and the senses—is itself impermanent.

That very impermanence is perceived even in the consciousness manifested by that modification, just as the redness of a hibiscus flower is perceived in a crystal, but not [the impermanence of the crystal's own nature]. However, it is not [the case for] the Supreme [Self].
The meaning is "in the ultimate sense" (paramārthatas). || 4 ||
But in the case of the object, O virtuous ones, there are both the form of consciousness and the form of the mental modification.
Due to the power of delusion, there occurs the appearance of a single form. || 5 ||

This might be so if, in cognitions such as "this is a jar," two distinct forms were experienced—namely, the form of the substrate (the jar) and the form of the superimposed (the cognition)—just as in the case of a crystal or a flower; however, they are not experienced in that way. Therefore, he says: "In reality" (*pratyakṣe*).
Although, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*), the two forms are indeed distinct, nevertheless, due to the power of ignorance (*avidyā*), [they appear as one].
The meaning is that since the lump appears as having only a single form, there is an error regarding that single form. || 5 ||
The aspect of existence and the aspect of the instrument are also found within the cognition.
The objective aspect is the form of consciousness, while the subjective aspect consists of the mental modification and the instrumental aspect.

He explains these very two aspects with the words "the aspect of being" (bhāvāṃśa). A *pratyaya* is that by which something is cognized (*pratīyate*). The suffix *ac* is applied in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), according to the rule "erac. Thus, since the word *pratyaya* consists of both a base (*prakṛti*) and a suffix (*pratyaya*), its meaning is also twofold, divided as the meaning of the base and the meaning of the suffix. Among those, the aspect of being is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).

That aspect which is of the nature of consciousness (cit) is the "part" (bhāga); however, that which is the meaning of the suffix (pratyaya) is the instrumental portion (karaṇāṃśa), meaning it is non-eternal and of the nature of non-consciousness (acit). || 6 ||
But the aspect of its function alone is lost, due to its insentience, like the substance of a jar.
The aspect of consciousness would not have perished at all, because it was not perceived by anyone.

Let it be so that there is this twofold nature of cognition (*mati*). In that regard, what is the determining reason for the claim that the instrumental aspect (*karaṇāṃśa*) is non-eternal, but not the aspect of consciousness (*pratīti*)? To this he says: "The aspect of the modification" (*vṛttyaṃśa*). The aspect of the modification, which consists of a transformation of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), is non-eternal because it is insentient (*jaḍatva*); but the aspect of consciousness (*cidaṃśa*) is not [non-eternal], because its destruction cannot be brought about by anything.
The meaning is that because it cannot be perceived even as the witness of destruction, consciousness (cit) is understood [to be distinct]. || 7 ||
Even here, the destruction of mere cognition is not observed at all.
Indeed, the destruction of an entity that has been swallowed by its own function becomes manifest.

To the objection that the cognition "this is a jar" does not exist at the time of the cognition of a cloth—since its destruction is indeed experienced—the author replies: "In this case also. It is the destruction of the cognition itself, as qualified by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) bearing the form of the object, that is perceived through the destruction of that qualifying modification; just as, when the staff (the qualifier) is destroyed, the state of being a staff-bearer (the qualified) is destroyed. [The same applies to] the cognizer who is the qualified...
The meaning is that, however, there can be no destruction whatsoever of the mere "I" (timātra), just as there is none of the essential nature of Devadatta. || 8 ||
Therefore, the cognition of destruction is an error regarding the aspect of existence.
Deluded, they [perceive] the form of consciousness manifested within the fluctuations of the mind.
The wise never imagine that anything has been born.
O lords of sages, by the destruction of the mental modification (vṛtti), the form of consciousness situated within that modification [is revealed].

Because, upon such investigation, there is no destruction of the "dependent" (pratītya) aspect of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), for this reason, the cognition of destruction therein arises merely from the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of identity with the activity of destruction; this is the meaning. Now, one might object: "Knowledge is produced in the self, which is the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*), by means of the contact between the self and the mind, which is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*); and that [knowledge] is subject to destruction immediately after its arising."
Suspecting what the root of the claims made by the Vaiśeṣikas and others might be, he says: "In the mental modification" (cittavṛttau).

When a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) arises in the form of an object immediately following contact with that object, those deluded by beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*) imagine that consciousness (*caitanya*), though manifested therein, has itself been born; however, they are not possessors of specialized knowledge (*viśeṣajña*). || 9 || 10 ||
Because it is unmanifest and unknown, they consider it to be as good as destroyed.
Therefore, O believers, there is no impermanence in pure consciousness alone.

Thus, solely due to the force of exhaustion and because of the failure to discern between the aspect of the object (bhāva-aṃśa) and the aspect of the instrument (karaṇa-aṃśa), when the function of the instrumental aspect ceases, there arises the appearance of the destruction of the consciousness delimited by that [instrument] as well; this is the meaning. || 11 ||
He who shines by himself as the witness of all objects, whether known or unknown;
That alone is the self whose nature is pure consciousness directly, and nothing else.

If this is so, and there is no destruction of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) in cognitions such as "this is a jar," then by that very fact the non-duality of the Self (*ātman*) is undermined; to this he says: "The witness of the known and the unknown" (*jñātājñāteti*). "Known" means made an object by knowledge; "unknown" means encompassed by ignorance. He is the witness of both kinds of objects. All—

Since it has been stated that an object is indeed an object of the witness-consciousness (sākṣicaitanya) whether it be known or unknown, that very Self, whose nature is pure consciousness, is the eternal, undifferentiated consciousness that persists through the various specific modifications (vṛtti) such as those having the forms of jars, cloths, and so forth; and that is the nature of the witness itself, not something distinct from it—this is the meaning. || 12 ||

"Upon investigation, neither birth nor destruction exists for him."
But because he is the witness at the time of birth, there is no "birth" (janman) or "origination" (janis) for him.

Now, he begins to demonstrate that even the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) has neither birth nor destruction, starting with the words "its birth" and so forth. At the time of the birth of the witness-consciousness, if it were not present as the illuminator of its own birth, that birth would remain unperceived. Since it is indeed perceived at that time, the existence of that witness must be admitted.
It must be so; thus, the meaning is that for this [person], there is simply no birth, that is, no arising. || 13 ||
Just as there is no destruction of witnesses when a portion of the debt is lost, so too shall it not happen here.
But while it exists, because of its existence, destruction is certainly not possible. ||14||

Thus, even at the time of destruction, because of the rule that it remains as a witness for the sake of illuminating that [object], the meaning is that there is no destruction of this [consciousness] either; however, at the time of cognition, the meaning is that there is no destruction simply because it exists. || 14 ||
But the perception of birth and destruction does not occur without the witness-consciousness (sākṣin).
O best of sages, birth and destruction are not established by their own nature alone. (15)
And because it is an object of perception, it is insentient, like objects such as a jar or a wall.
Furthermore, the birth and destruction of the witness are not established by anything else. || 16 ||
Furthermore, birth and destruction cannot be established by means of any other insentient form.
Furthermore, birth and destruction cannot be established by means of another witness.
And because there is no other witness-form whatsoever, O you of excellent vows. || 17 ||

[Objection: But surely, even in the absence of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) persisting during birth and destruction, manifestation is possible through the consciousness delimited by the respective mental modifications (*vṛtti*) of those states; to this, he says: "birth and destruction. The meaning is that since the witness is precisely the consciousness delimited by those very modifications, birth and destruction are manifested by the witness itself. Without the witness, there would be no illumination.

Do birth and destruction appear through self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) or through something else? Even in that case, do they appear in a non-conscious (*jaḍa*) form or in the form of the witness (*sākṣin*)? Having raised this dilemma, he refutes the first alternative with the words "birth and destruction": [they] are not established without the witness, because, like a jar or similar objects, their nature as non-conscious is determined by their being objects of perception (*dṛśyatva*). Nor is it the second [alternative].

Regarding the first [alternative], he says: "by means of that which is insentient" (*jaḍarūpeṇa*). For it is not logical to say that birth and destruction are manifested by another thing that is insentient; for there is no distinction between them in their common quality of being insentient. Regarding the second [alternative], he says: "by means of that which is of the nature of the witness" (*sākṣirūpeṇa*).
The meaning is that there is no witness other than this very witness. (Verses 15, 16, 17)

Likewise, sages such as Kapila, Kaṇabhuj, Jaimini, and others, in accordance with the capacity of their disciples, [compile] through His very favor those very scriptures created by the Supreme Lord, both in summary and in detail.

There is no contradiction in [the claim that people] act according to these two [scriptures]. Regarding the phrase "by way of a ladder": in various scriptures, the Lord in the form of this or that deity is the cause for attaining the path of the Vedas through a gradual succession (sopānakrama). Regarding the phrase "daily rites and so forth": by the word "and so forth" (ādi), occasional rites (naimittika) are included. Through the performance of daily and occasional rites—prescribed according to one's caste, stage of life, and so on—performed without desire for fruits and with the intention of worshipping the Lord, there occurs the destruction of the sins that obstruct the knowledge of reality. Sūta said:
Now begins the twenty-seventh chapter.
Hereafter, I shall fully describe the state that is higher than the highest.
O twice-born ones, it is through connection with its existence that everything appears as if real.
By whose very light of consciousness the entire world perceives.
Because of its connection with bliss, everything becomes an object of love.

Thus, as a means for the knowledge of the supreme reality (*paratattva*) and as a propitiation of Śiva, he teaches the single nature of Paraśiva: "Higher than the highest" (*parātparataram*). That which is "higher" (*para*) is characterized by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the previously mentioned *Śakti-tattva*;

that which is "higher than that" (*tataḥ paraḥ*) is characterized by the *Śiva-tattva*; and higher even than that is the unconditioned (*nirupādhika*), whose defining characteristics are existence, consciousness, and bliss (*sac-cid-ānanda-lakṣaṇa*), [which is] one's own [true self].

Abiding as the very nature of Supreme Śiva, which is higher than the highest and most excellent— having set aside [the notion of] the categories (tattva), because it is not an object of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)— [I rejoice].
[Page 227] 550 Accompanied by the Tātparyadīpikā—
[In the fourth section, the *Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa*,
having raised the doubt that [the world] is non-existent like the horn of a hare, he refutes it with the words beginning "Because of its connection with existence" (*yatsattāyogataḥ*).]

Just as upon a single rope, many forms such as a serpent or a stream are superimposed due to the power of ignorance (*avidyā*), so too, upon the nature of Paraśiva— which is non-dual and consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*)— the manifold world composed of the elements and their derivatives is superimposed by the force of one's own mental impressions (*vāsanā*). Just as in the case of the superimpositions of a serpent or a stream, [one thinks] "this is a serpent" or "this is a stream."

In this manner, while the superimposed world follows the form of its substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), the nature of that substrate—as being existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*)—is likewise perceived as persisting [throughout]. And thus is the meaning: by virtue of its connection with the reality (*sattā*) that constitutes the very essence of the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*), which serves as the substrate, the entire world imagined within that essence appears as neither existent nor non-existent, due to its being composed of *māyā*.
Even a characteristic (lakṣaṇa), while being a jar, appears as if real through the form of conventional usage such as "it is a cloth" and so forth.

Likewise, by the light of consciousness (citprakāśa) which constitutes the very nature of that substratum (adhiṣṭhāna), Brahman, all the insentient world superimposed upon its own nature becomes conscious and shines as qualified by sentience. Thus, by the very nature of that same substratum—

By virtue of its connection with Nanda, even that which is devoid of bliss becomes of the nature of bliss; thus, the entire world, superimposed [upon it], becomes an object of love and something to be experienced as favorable. The connection [of the verse] is: "I shall proclaim that Supreme Reality, which is of such a nature—being Existence-Consciousness-Bliss.
From this well-known narrative, O bulls among sages, [the elements] have arisen.
Superior to those is the individual soul (jīvātman), which is conscious and the lord.

In order to establish that this reality is higher than the highest, he begins to state that it is the ultimate limit of unsurpassed excellence, starting with the words "pratīta" (perceived) and so forth. The world is the effect of the elements—that is, the material universe—and therefore the elements, such as space (*ākāśa*) and the rest, which are its causes, are superior to it; the meaning is that the acquisition of the nature of the material world occurs through attaining those elements. Furthermore, even compared to the elements...

The conscious individual self (*jīvātman*) is superior because, by virtue of having that [Supreme Self] as its material cause, it has entered into its essential nature and is characterized by the attribute of limited existence;
this is due to the manifestation of consciousness. || 3 ||
Even that [individual soul] is divided from one another by virtue of being both collective and individual.
And likewise, the individual manifestations are differentiated according to their respective natures.
And they obtain bodies as gods, animals, humans, and so forth.
But he who is the collective totality of these, O wise ones, is the most excellent in every respect.

Regarding the phrase "by way of being both collective and individual": therein, because his knowledge is unimpeded due to having a substrate (*upādhi*) of stainless *sattva*, he pervades (*samaśnute*)—that is, extends through—both himself and everything other than himself; thus, Hiraṇyagarbha is the "collective" (*samaṣṭi*). Because his knowledge is limited due to having a substrate of impure *sattva*, and because there is a variety [of states] according to the degrees of that impurity, the individual souls (*jīvas*) who possess such substrates are "divided."

They are called *vyaṣṭayaḥ* because they function by following after their own self alone. Regarding the phrase "in accordance with their own nature":
at the time of departure (*utkrānti*), there arises a specific volition (*saṃkalpa*) directed toward a future birth, produced by matured merit and demerit (*puṇya-pāpa*). This is the state (*bhāva*).

The meaning is "according to their respective order. Among these collective and individual manifestations, Hiraṇyagarbha, being the collective totality (samaṣṭi), is the most excellent because his knowledge is unimpeded. || 4 || 5 ||
Therefore, all the manifestations of Brahmā are indeed distinguished.
And these [powers] are mutually distinct, just as living beings and lords of sages are. ||6||

"Than that, they are more excellent. Therefore, even compared to Hiraṇyagarbha, those manifestations—which are specific incarnations established by the mere will of Brahman when conditioned by the quality of *rajas*—are superior. They may be mutually distinguished from one another; for since will has degrees of intensity (high and low), the manifestations established by that will alone also possess a higher [or lower] status.
The meaning is that increase and decrease are found in the *spara*. || 6 ||
Among them, Brahmā is superior; therefore, Viṣṇu is proclaimed as the foremost.
He too is proclaimed to be superior to those who constitute his own individual manifestations.

"Among them, Brahmā is superior. This means that Brahmā, who is the substratum for such a volition (*saṃkalpa*), is more excellent than his own manifestations (*vibhūtis*). "Therefore, Viṣṇu [is superior]"—Viṣṇu, whose limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is the quality of purity (*sattva-guṇa*), is superior even to Brahmā, whose limiting adjunct is the quality of passion (*rajas-guṇa*). This is because *sattva*, being of the nature of happiness and illumination, is superior to the quality of *rajas*. [Regarding] his individual manifestation (*svavyaṣṭi*)...

"Superior to all beings": even among those specific incarnations of Viṣṇu which are manifested through his mere volition (*saṃkalpa*), Viṣṇu, who constitutes their collective totality (*samaṣṭi*), is superior to them. || 7 ||
Rudra is superior to him, and he too is remembered as superior to his own individual manifestations (vyaṣṭis).
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are the manifestations of the supreme reality.

Therefore, Rudra is superior. For Viṣṇu’s limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is *tamas* characterized by external *sattva*, whereas Rudra’s is *sattva* joined with external *tamas*. This he will establish himself later in the *Sūtagītā*.
And thus, Rudra is superior even to Viṣṇu. Likewise, [the power] of that Rudra consists of mere volition (*saṃkalpa-mātra*).
Even those who are perfected and possess clear vision, for them too, He alone is the most excellent. Regarding the phrase "the manifestations of the supreme reality" (*paratattvavibhūtayaḥ*):

the meaning is that the supreme reality—which will be described as consisting of the single essence of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*), and being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*)—is itself, by virtue of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of its own assumed qualities, abiding in the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and so forth; thus, Brahmā and the others are His manifestations.
The Lord, who is superior to primordial matter (prakṛti) and the individual soul (puruṣa), is the cause of all.

The *Sūtasamhitā* [states]:
"A hundredfold bliss— using the word 'ādi' (beginning) to include all of that, such as human *gandharvas* and so forth— "
Not so. || 10 ||
A hundredfold bliss of Brahmā is said to be one bliss of Viṣṇu. || 11 ||
A hundredfold bliss of that [lower state] is indeed but a single bliss of Rudra.
A hundred times the bliss of Rudra belongs to Śiva, the cause of all.

"That is one hundredfold the bliss of Brahman"— beginning with the bliss of Brahman as described for Brahman when conditioned by the quality of *rajas*, he states that the bliss of Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the causes of the world should be understood as increasing a hundredfold at each successive stage, using the passage beginning with "one hundredfold the bliss of Brahman" and so forth. || 11 || 12 ||
Of Śiva, the Supreme Self, who is characterized as the cause.
The abundance of bliss is declared to belong to that which is of the nature of pure consciousness and truth. || 13 ||
Regarding the phrase "of that whose nature is pure, eternal consciousness": by the word *mātra* (only/pure), the absence of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is intended.

For that which has the nature of pure, eternal consciousness—which is characterized by being the cause—the state of being the Supreme Śiva is illustrated as the "Abundance" (*bhūman*) and "Bliss" (*ānanda*) by the Śruti. Due to the absence of any limiting adjuncts that would cause division, the bliss that constitutes the very nature of Supreme Śiva is unlimited (*anavacchinna*).
The meaning is that it is unsurpassed. And that scriptural passage is: "But the Infinite (bhūman) alone is to be sought after; that which is the Infinite is indeed bliss," and so forth. || 13 ||
In this manner, it is likewise maintained that all possess a progressive increase in knowledge.
Just as a tree is established through the distinctions of its trunk, branches, and so forth. || 14 ||
In the same way, Śiva alone is established through the distinctions of Rudra and the others.
There is increase and decrease in the constituent parts, such as the trunk, branches, and other elements. || 15 ||
Likewise, O Rudra, increase and decrease reside in Viṣṇu and the others.
Just as [the distinctions] between waves, lakes, and so forth are established in the world.
Furthermore, excellence and deficiency likewise reside within Rudra and the others. || 16 ||
Having thus established the unsurpassed nature of the bliss of the essential form of Paraśiva, he extends this principle to the knowledge that constitutes His very nature,
stating that its unsurpassed nature is likewise to be understood by this same logic— this is expressed by the word "evam" (thus).
He then establishes, with an illustration, how the one and only Paraśiva exists in the form of various deities such as Rudra, Viṣṇu, and others.
The *Skandhaśāstra*. || 14 || 15 || 16 ||

the supremacy over the universe of Rudra, the causal Śiva.]
Those people who do not speak thus would undoubtedly be Rākṣasas. || 17 ||
Regarding "being superior to the universe": according to the manner explained, because he is more excellent than everything else, Paraśiva is "superior to the universe" (viśvādhika).
Furthermore, based on the Vedic scripture, "Rudra, the great seer, is superior to the universe," it is Śiva alone who possesses the quality of being superior to the universe. || 17 ||
This division has been proclaimed from the perspective of conventional reality. || 18 ||
From the perspective of valid cognition, the entity is indeed one and eternal; of this there is no doubt.
Out of great delusion, men on earth disregard the authoritative means of knowledge.
"This is one's own, but that is another's"—thus they dispute with one another.
For men who possess great sins, the preeminence of Rudra does not shine forth.
Of those who have attained perfection over many births and who follow the injunctions of the Śruti and Smṛti.
The preeminence of Rudra shines forth by itself, as well as through the means of valid knowledge and through reasoning.
By means of the steps of the ladder, these deities liberate human beings from saṃsāra.
Rudra is the direct liberator from saṃsāra for those submerged in saṃsāra. || 22 ||
Therefore, having completely abandoned every deity other than Śiva.
Śiva alone is always to be meditated upon; he is the manifest liberator from saṃsāra. || 23 ||
Just as the branches truly flourish by watering the root of a tree.
Indeed, by meditating upon Śiva, the gods likewise become truly satisfied.

Now, one might object: "Just as a tree exists in various forms through the distinctions of trunk, branches, and so forth, if the supreme Śiva likewise exists in the form of the world as Rudra, Viṣṇu, and others, then there is a contradiction with non-duality (advaita). To this, he says: "From the perspective of conventional experience. It is upon the changeless nature of the perfect Śiva that the manifold world is superimposed by the power of Māyā; [it does not exist there inherently].

The other transforms itself into the nature of the aggregates, branches, and so forth, like a tree; therefore, the employment of the example is solely for the sake of the similarity in the mere existence of various states—this is the meaning. || 18 || 19 || 20 || 21 || 22 || 23 || 24 ||
Reality is free from conceptual construction; it is knowledge, bliss, and imperishable.
Those who see [this] are liberated; even while living, they have no doubt [of this]. ||25||

"Free from conceptual construction" (*vikalparahita*) means that because there is an absence of distinctions—which are the causes of conceptual construction—in the undifferentiated Brahman, the knowledge that constitutes its very nature is free from conceptual construction; that is to say, it is absolutely non-conceptual (*atyanta-nirvikalpaka*). This remains so at all times, even when sublated...
[page 231]
Chapter 27: Sūta-saṃhitā, [Verse] 555.

Due to its freedom from deficiency, that very reality is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Because its manifestation does not depend on anything else, it is knowledge (*jñāna*). Because it is experienced as being absolutely favorable, it is bliss (*ānanda*). It is imperishable (*avyaya*). "Vyapa" means departure or end; it is devoid of that. The meaning is that it is free from limitations created by space, time, and substance. || 25 ||
For whom the supreme reality, free from conceptual construction, shines forth through reasoning.
He too shall be liberated from cyclic existence, just as one is released from one's own dream-creation.

Regarding the term *tarpha* (reasoning): through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the sublation of [worldly] experience, once the falsity (*mithyātva*) of the fivefold perceptible world is understood, some ultimately real entity (*pāramārthika vastu*) must be admitted as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of that experience. Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasakti*) of an illusion without a substratum and a sublation without a limit; such is the nature of reasoning. Scripture (*śruti*) also demonstrates reasoning...

The sage [continues]: "He becomes non-existent indeed," "If he knows 'Brahman is non-existent,'" and "Who indeed would inhale, who would exhale, if this Ākāśa were not bliss? (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7). || 26 ||
The supreme reality, which is free from conceptual construction, is known solely through valid cognition.
He in whom this shines forth shall be liberated from his own great ocean of saṃsāra. || 27 ||
"By means of valid cognition alone. The Vedāntic statements such as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" and "I am Brahman" constitute the valid cognition. || 27 ||
And indeed, there are neither names nor forms belonging to Śiva, the Supreme Self.
Nevertheless, his name and form were fashioned by means of māyā.

"And yet there are no names. The meaning is that, according to the scripture stating, "That which is indefinable, ungraspable, without lineage, and without color," name and form do not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality. || 28 ||
Śiva, Rudra, Mahādeva, Śaṃkara, Brahmā, and the supreme reality.
Such names as these, however, are specific to another. (29)

"Śiva, Rudra," and so forth: among the names conceptually constructed by *māyā*, names such as Śiva and Rudra are primary because they are established by convention (*rūḍhi*) as referring to the nature of Paraśiva. The four names beginning with "Śiva, Rudra" denote the form of Rudra;
the triad beginning with "Brahman, Sat, Param" is the direct designator (*vācaka*) of Paraśiva. [This is] by means of the form of Paraśiva...
He himself will explain later that there is no distinction [between them], as they have attained non-differentiation like a heated iron ball together with the form of Rudra.
Therefore, because the two forms have become one, those names of both kinds exist in such a state; thus, they are "murarūpāṇi" (having the form of *mura*).
Names such as Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, and others [are applied] to the Supreme Lord.
They exist somehow through figurative application, but not in a primary sense.
[Page 232] 556 Accompanied by the Tātparyadīpikā.

[In the fourth section, the *Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa*—regarding the passage beginning "Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, and others": The author will also state that because the forms of Viṣṇu and the others differ from the form of Paraśiva, they are distinct. Therefore, the words "Viṣṇu" and so forth, which are conventionally established (*rūḍha*) for the forms of Viṣṇu and others, [apply] to that Supreme Reality.

They do not function by way of conventional usage; rather, they function through the etymological derivation of their constituent parts, such as "Viṣṇu" being derived from the sense of "he who pervades" (vi-√viś). || 30 ||
Even for the formless Śiva, by means of his forms and through the bonds [of ritual practice].
She has a body half-formed with Umā, is white in color, possesses three eyes, and has the moon as her crest-ornament. || 31 ||

Having thus shown the names imagined through *māyā*, he now shows the form consisting of a physical body—which is likewise imagined—of Paraśiva for the purpose of meditation, beginning with the words "of the formless," etc. (verse 31).
Blue-necked, she is the delight of supreme bliss and is fond of the tāṇḍava dance.
She is worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Mahādeva, who are the embodiments of the [three] qualities (guṇas).
"By the forms of the qualities" means by those having the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas. || 32 ||
Of Śiva, who is devoid of all form yet possesses all forms.
Nevertheless, this is the supreme form; such is the eternal Vedic revelation. || 33 ||

"Of every form" means that although, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), he is devoid of any kind of form, the entire world imagined through *māyā* is nonetheless his other form. "The eternal scripture" means that even the *Śruti* demonstrates the existence of Śiva, who is ultimately devoid of a physical body. For it is heard in the *Kevalya Upaniṣad*:

"Having meditated upon the Lord, the Supreme Master, accompanied by Umā, the three-eyed, blue-throated, and profoundly tranquil, the sage goes to that source of all beings, the witness of all, who stands beyond darkness. || 33 ||
But this form of Rudra belonging to the Supreme is like a glowing mass of iron.
O best of sages, she was equal to other forms in her physical appearance, yet distinguished by her [auspicious] marks. || 34 ||

It explains the identity of the form of Rudra with the form of Paraśiva through the phrase beginning with "like a mass of heated iron" (*taptāyapiṇḍavat*). For the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of Rudra consists of the quality of pure *sattva*, whereas that of Saṃhāra consists of *tamas*; thus, it exists entirely outside of his true nature (*svarūpa*). Therefore, because the form of Rudra is composed of pure *sattva*, and because *sattva* is characterized by pleasure and luminosity—
Because it is her very nature, she is similar to the form of Paraśiva—whose essence is eternal self-luminosity—by virtue of characteristics such as light and so forth.
Therefore, she is distinct from the forms of Viṣṇu and others; yet, like a heated iron ball, she has attained non-differentiation from the form of Paraśiva. || 38 ||
But the forms of Viṣṇu and all the others are [manifested] through mediation.
Those who have reached the further shore of the Vedānta are not equal to the supreme reality, which is illusory. || 35 ||
[Page 233] Chapter 27.
Sūtasaṃhitā:
"They are not equal to the Supreme Reality," because in the forms of Viṣṇu and others, there is a predominance characterized by *rajas* and *tamas*.
Because it is impossible for the form of Paraśiva— which consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss— to be reflected in its entirety through an intervening medium,

those [reflections] are not equal to the form of Paraśiva. Therefore, since they are perceived only as distinct from that [form], the names such as Viṣṇu and others, which designate such forms, depend upon the well-known parts of the limbs of the very nature of Paraśiva.

The names Śiva, Rudra, and so forth are primary (mukhya) because they produce cognition more rapidly. However, according to the reasoning stated above, since the supreme forms of Śiva and Rudra have become one, these names apply to the form consisting of both through the conventional usage of the whole alone, without depending on the conventional usage of its individual parts; thus, the intention is that they are primary because they generate immediate cognition. || 35 ||
O lords of sages, these are the names of the supreme reality by virtue of their close proximity to it.
O you of excellent vows, among the three forms, those of Rudra are indeed without any intervening [forms].
Thus, having established that names such as Śiva, Rudra, and so forth— which denote the form of Rudra— possess primacy with respect to the Supreme Reality,
[the text now proceeds] to establish the same for names such as Brahma, Sat, Param, and so forth, which express the nature of the unconditioned Supreme Śiva.

He establishes the preeminence of Rudra within the [divine] forms by means of the passage beginning with "of the supreme reality" (*paratattvasya*). Those names of the unconditioned reality (*nirupādhika-tattva*) such as "Brahman," "Being," and "Supreme"—which are the names of Rudra among the three forms (*trimūrti*)—are names that are not separated from the ultimate truth (*satya*).
By means of establishing the nature of the unconditioned, [these names distinguish Rudra] from the conditioned [forms].
The supreme reality (*paratattva*) is "obstructed" (*vyavadhīyate*) by these [names] according to the instrumental derivation (*karaṇavyutpatti*); thus, those names are the causes of obstruction.
Because Rudra’s limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) possesses an unsurpassed excellence of pure being (*sattva*), there exists a complete proximity characterized by the grasping of the reflection (*bimba*).
By such proximity, those names do not obstruct; rather, they constitute an obstruction of this kind.
The conventional usage of those two as distinct is due solely to the power of their existence. || 36 ||
And those names belong to Viṣṇu and the other gods, O you of virtuous vows.
O best of knowers of Brahman, names arise through their connection with reality.

Regarding the phrase "of Viṣṇu and others": these are names of the Supreme Reality (paratattva) belonging to Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Hiraṇyagarbha, and so forth; they establish [the Reality] merely by virtue of its presence within those forms. The meaning is this: Paraśiva alone—whose sole characteristics are existence, consciousness, and bliss, who is non-dual, all-pervading, and supreme—appears as manifold in the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and others due to the influence of various limiting adjuncts (upādhi).

It shines forth. In that regard, since Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Hiraṇyagarbha, Sūtrātman, and others possess unimpeded knowledge within the scope of their respective functions, one must admit that there is an unsurpassed excellence of *sattva* in the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of all of them.

Otherwise, by the consequence of their being limited-knowers like the individual souls (*jīva*) such as ourselves, there would be a collapse of all worldly transactions, such as creation and maintenance.

Because of the [unwanted] consequence (*prasanga*). If it is objected: "Just as with the substrate (*upadheya*), if the adjuncts (*upādhi*) were also uniform in nature, then the conventional distinction between Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and so forth would not arise," we say: not so. For even though there is uniformity in reality (*vastutaḥ*) regarding the excellence of existence (*sattvotkarṣa*) in the adjuncts such as Māyā and the rest—[as seen in the citations from the *Vedāntasūtra-bhāṣya* and others]—[the distinction remains]. Even though they are distinct from the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of Rudra, there exists within them various forms of inferiority caused by the predominance of rajas and tamas.

It exists; therefore, the designation of distinctions such as Brahmā and Viṣṇu, which is prompted by that [superimposition], should not be understood as their actual, intrinsic degradation. For if that were the case, it would follow that they too, like ourselves and others, would be mere individual souls (jīvas). Thus, because there is a presence of artificial degradation within the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the rest, they do not possess proximity to the supreme reality. Such are they.
The meaning is that they are secondary because they are intervening factors. || 37 ||
Nevertheless, those very same [powers] reside in Rudra due to proximity, but by the Supreme [Lord], they are [manifested] otherwise.
They are primary [in this context], whereas in others they are not so because of the intervention of something else. || 38 ||

Now, one might ask: even though there is equality in both cases due to the intervention of an adjunct (*upādhi*), why is there this distinction—that in some instances the supreme reality (*paratattva*) is manifest in its own form, while in others it is not? To this, he says: "Even so" (*tathāpi*).

Although, according to the reasoning stated, there is indeed an intervention from the supreme reality even in the form of Rudra, nevertheless, because the form of Rudra is [identical with] the essential nature of Supreme Śiva (*paraśivasvarūpa*), the former—[the supreme reality]—is...

Because of that proximity which has been described, the names of the Supreme Reality (paratattva) are said to be primary in that regard. However, for others—namely those possessing limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and so forth—such proximity does not exist, due to the presence of an artificial deficiency. Therefore, because of this intervention, the names of the Supreme Reality are not primary for them; this is the meaning. || 38 ||
The thorough knowledge of the supreme reality arises from the grace of His form.
And his grace is obtained only through meditation upon him and worship of him, and not otherwise. (39)
Just as the hunger of men is removed by the consumption of food and other such sustenance, [so too is suffering removed by the knowledge of Brahman].
Likewise, through the grace of the image, that very reality is revealed. || 40 ||
But the supreme reality is always the very nature of all things.
Without the grace of his form, it does not manifest at all. || 41 ||
Therefore, the embodied form indeed bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon all.
Therefore, O best of sages, worship the Mūrti with great devotion.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "An Investigation into the Nature of the Supreme State," in the fourth section, the Yajñavaibhava-khaṇḍa, of the Sūta-saṃhitā within the glorious Skanda Purāṇa. ||27||

Thus, he concludes that the fruit consisting of worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*) is obtained solely through the grace of that form of the Supreme Reality (*paratattva-mūrti*) which was described by the words "having half the body of Umā" (*umārdhavigrahā*) as being distinct from the forms of Viṣṇu and the others; therefore, it should be meditated upon by everyone at all times, [as stated] in the verses beginning with "the thorough knowledge of the Supreme Reality" (*parasatvaparijñāna*). Having thus established the specific form of Paraśiva as conceived for the purpose of meditation, worship, and so forth, he now promises to determine the true nature of the Śivaliṅga as well: "Now, therefore... (1).
Śiva himself is the liṅga; indeed, a liṅga is that which makes [something] known.

In order to dispel the misconception that "Śiva’s liṅga" means a *liṅga* belonging to Śiva, he says: "Śiva himself is the *liṅga*. He establishes this by stating, "A *liṅga* is that which makes known," and so forth. For in the world, smoke and other such things that make known—that is, indicate—another object characterized by its presence are called a *liṅga*. Śiva, too, is his own...

In some respects, [the Self] is the indicator of the entire class of insentient things by virtue of its nature as form (rūpa), but it is not itself indicated as "you" (tvam). Therefore, because it is the indicator, it is itself the logical mark (liṅga). || 2 ||
For that which is insentient is perceived by another, O best of sages, but that which is not insentient is not.
Śiva is certainly not insentient; he is directly characterized solely by self-luminosity.

He establishes this very capacity to make known with the words beginning "For that which is insentient... The insentient world, consisting of jars, cloths, and so forth, is made known by the light of consciousness (citprakāśa) distinct from itself. Consciousness, being of a nature different from the insentient, is not perceived by anything else;
rather, it shines by itself. Therefore, Paraśiva, whose nature is self-luminous consciousness, is never insentient.

Since it is not insentient, it is not an object of inference; rather, because its nature is self-luminous consciousness, it is the means of cognition. Therefore, the meaning is that it is itself the logical mark (liṅga). || 3 ||
If it were not self-luminous, Śiva would not be directly Śiva at all.
Indeed, Śiva is not accepted as being like walls and such things, which are not self-luminous.

This would indeed be so if Śiva were of the nature of self-luminous consciousness (*svaprakāśacidrūpa*); however, since he is always and in every way independent of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whose domain is existent things, it follows as a necessary consequence that he is to be understood solely through the Upaniṣads, and thus he must be non-self-luminous.
Therefore, [the author] says: "If he were not self-luminous" (*asvaprakāśaścediti*). If Śiva were not of the nature of self-luminous consciousness...
Otherwise, its very nature as Śiva would be lost, because objects such as pots and walls, whose manifestation is dependent on something else, are non-Śiva (aśiva).

Because it is observed to be so. If that [second cognition] were perceived by another cognition, then that too would be the same way; thus, its self-luminosity must also be admitted. [If it were argued that] it would be established [by another cognition], then for that third cognition as well, there would necessarily be a requirement for illumination; thus, yet another cognition would have to be asserted, and in that case too, such would be the situation, resulting in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) that destroys its very foundation. And so, if the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatā*) of the nature of Paraśiva is not admitted, then everything consisting of cognition and the cognizable would remain unmanifest and would effectively be a void.

Even the establishment of emptiness, though excellent, is not established by emptiness alone.

If the proponent of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*) should object, "Our desired goal is established," the author replies to him with the words, "The establishment of emptiness. Thus, even in the view that all things are empty (*sarva-śūnyavāda*), since the existence of cognition is necessarily admitted, and because it must be accepted that cognition’s manifestation is dependent on something else, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result; for, in the absence of self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) in cognition, the entire world would fall into blindness. Therefore, it must be accepted that cognition is indeed self-luminous. Furthermore, the perception of diversity—such as "cognition of a jar" and "cognition of a cloth"—is merely caused by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); thus, [cognition] is non-dual (*advaita*).

Therefore, that nature is the knower (*gamaka*). Since, due to its self-luminosity, it is not known by anything else, the meaning is that it is not [objectively] known (*na gamyate*). In this context, whatever insentient object is enumerated as a *liṅga* (sign) of Śiva is not a sign by virtue of its own mere existence; rather, it is so only when it is being known. Therefore, because it serves as the substratum for each respective insentient object, its illuminator is its [Śiva’s] substrate (*upādhi*).

The established fact, the state of reality, is this: Śiva alone, whose nature is consciousness (cidrūpa) and who is delimited by the intellect (dhi), serves as the *liṅga*—the sign—that makes known the essential nature of the Lord, who is all-pervasive and undivided. The meaning is: that support for the feet, such as the image (mūrti) and so forth, which serves as the basis for meditation, worship, and the like upon Śiva, whose own nature is the liṅga—that is the liṅga. The meaning is that because it is an effect (*kārya*), it possesses the quality of being the substratum of all things. Let it be so regarding the perception of existence in the objects of superimposition; however, [what of] the substratum itself, which is devoid of attributes?

We say that the reality of Brahman consists in its being forever free from sublation (*bādhavaidhurya*). Why is that? To this he says: "For [Brahman] is of the nature of consciousness" (*cidrūpaṃ hi*). While the various objects of cognition (*cetyarūpa*), which are subject to change, pass away, it is precisely the nature of consciousness that persists as the witness to their existence and non-existence; therefore, that alone is real. The objective form (*jar̤arūpa*), however, is unreal because it is composed of *māyā*. Thus, because his nature is consciousness, Śiva is the Real.
Now, one might ask: why does reality not also belong to the individual soul (*jīva*)? To this, he says: "Of unreality," etc. (23).
For the unreality of mother-of-pearl appearing as silver and so forth is indeed accepted.

But from where does its unreality derive? To this he says: "of insentient things. The *Tātparyadīpikā* states:
"They say that Śiva is this entire universe; though he is partless (*niṣkala*) and of one undivided essence, he appears as the manifold world."
The term *vismaya* (wonder) refers to the state of being born as one whose nature is that [of Śiva], because of its marvelous character. Regarding the phrase *visarjanīyaniṣṭhānām*:

the suffix *-anīya* is applied according to the rule *“tayoreva kṛtyaktakhalarthāḥ”* (Pāṇini 3.4.70). *Visarjana* means renunciation; those who are *niṣṭha* (established) in that—namely, the seekers of liberation (*mumukṣu*) established in the renunciation of the entire cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*)—are referred to by this term. The genitive case here denotes the agent (*kartari ṣaṣṭhī*). Even through sovereign powers (*aiśvarya*) and so forth, [they remain] Śiva...

The meaning is that just as [Śiva] is to be prayed for, so too is He especially to be sought after by those desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*). Here, the words *visarjanīya*, *vismaya*, *viśeṣa*, and *artha* consist of the letter *va* because they begin with *va*; through them, their referent Śiva is also of the nature of the letter *ca*. Furthermore, since it is well known that the final vowel is also called *visarjanīya*, [Śiva] is [also represented] through the letter *va* which denotes His own name.

Ramaka: By that [reasoning], because of the similarity in being composed of the letter *va*, Śiva is to be contemplated as having the nature of the *visarjanīya* mantra; this is the meaning. || 21 || 22 ||

Regarding the phrase *tramantrārtha*: the meaning of the mantra *ña* is the letter *śa* accompanied by the power (*śakti*) of the letter *na*. To him whose form (*mūrti*) or essential nature (*svarūpa*) is "knowledge" (*jñā*), that is, one who knows (*jānāti*). The supreme Śiva-nature is pure consciousness alone (*jñaptimātra*). Although this qualifier consists of two words, nevertheless, the letter *na* which follows the letter *ja*—the source of pure consciousness—is the final point of the specific cognition (*buddhiviśeṣaṇa*).

Since it indeed persists until the very end, the entire qualifying attribute consisting of the letter *na*—and by extension, Śiva who is its referent—is likewise [of that nature]; thus, the justification for establishing his identity with the letter *na* is established. Now, one might object: here, the letter *jha* is even more primary than the letter *a*, and therefore the cognition of that [letter *jha*] would also persist. Furthermore, the recitation (*japa*) of this [seed-syllable] serves as an instrument for the cessation of the prison of bondage—characterized by ignorance—by means of focusing on its meaning, holding it in the mind, and the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of it.

That by which the world appears as the world-soul is not real, but rather [real] only in its form as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Thus, he is "as he is" (*yathābhūta*); and since he is both that and the object (*artha*), he is "the object as it truly is" (*yathārtha*), using a compound with the middle term elided (*madhyamapadalopa-samāsa*). The word *yathā* is used here in the sense of "that very thing," provided it occurs within a compound.

Regarding the phrase "conforming to the usage of the elders": it is called *pratyak* because it moves toward (*añcati*) that which is opposite (*pratīpam*). Regarding the word "latā": the moon is one of the eight forms (*mūrti*) of Śiva, the Eight-formed One (*Aṣṭamūrti*). Just as each digit (*kalā*) of that [moon] increases daily from the first lunar day (*pratipad*) until the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), and then decreases by one digit daily from the first lunar day back to the new moon (*darśa*), so too does each digit of the *soma*-creeper increase daily up until the full moon.

The growth of the leaf continues until the full moon, while each individual leaf undergoes a gradual diminution. Within, Śiva is also the moon-creeper, whose very nature is *soma* (the lunar essence). Since the growth of all creepers is dependent upon the rays of the moon, the moon is the self (*ātman*) of the creepers. Therefore, Śiva, who is of the nature of the moon, is also the self of the creeper; [salutation] to him. Regarding the word "lābha" (attainment): it refers to that which has not yet been attained.

Attainment (*prāpti*) is acquisition; non-attainment (*aprāpti*) is lack of acquisition. Śiva, however, being eternally one whose desires are fulfilled, lacks anything yet to be attained, and is thus devoid of both. Regarding "having obtained" (*labdha*): because they are veiled by ignorance, individual souls (*jīvas*) do not even obtain their own true nature. Śiva, however, by virtue of his unobscured consciousness-light, is eternally one who has already obtained his own nature. (50–51)

Regarding the word *hakārāya*: although [the Self] is by its very nature partless (*niṣkala*), it attains the state of a living soul (*jīvatva*) through the habitual practice of identifying with the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*). This is according to the Vedic scripture: "Having entered with this living self. For this very reason, it is denoted by the word "I" (*aham*). The fact that even the perfected one (*siddha*) is designated again by his own name as "having the body of the *mātṛkā*" is for the sake of directing the mind toward him in that manner as well. And since these [words] consist of the letter *ma*, just as previously stated, [he is reached] through them.

Śiva, who is the object of that [knowledge], is also of the nature of the letter *ma*. Since the Mātṛkā-mantra is also denoted by that very word beginning with *ma*, he says "the measurer of the mother" (*mātṛmāna*) and so forth, in order to show that it is under the control of the Mātṛkā-mantra, which is also of the nature of the letter *ma*.
The means of knowledge (*mānāni*)—consisting of perception, inference, scripture, comparison, presumption, and non-existence—are the six functions of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

The threefold nature [of the world] consists of these: the object of knowledge (*meyam*), which is the phenomenal world (*vyāvahārikasatya*) and the Mother of the World; the means of knowledge (*mānāni*);

and the knower (*mātṛ*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the apparent reality (*prātītikasatya*), ignorance (*avidyā*), its modifications (*vṛtti*), doubt, error, and the memory directed toward those objects are included. To the witness (*sākṣin*) of all that—that is, to the illuminator who is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*)—[salutations].
For the sake of the ultimate truth; for the great light, as the scripture states: "By His light all this shines. (58)
Salutation to the Great Brahman, the light that is the sole referent of the great mantra, who is the support of the Mātṛkā and whose essential form is the Mātṛkā itself. || 59 ||

"Support of the Mātṛkā": because the Mātṛkā is a manifestation (*vivarta*) of Paraśiva, Śiva is her support. "Root of the Mātṛkā": the root of the Mātṛkā is the Śabdabrahman; [the deity is] of that nature because she has that as her material cause (*upādāna*). "Great Mantra": the great mantras are the Mātṛkā-mantras, such as the *praṇava*, the *hṛllekhā*, the eight-syllable mantra (*aṣṭākṣara*), and so forth.

The forms of those respective deities are to be described individually; however, through them, it is Śiva alone, whose sole essence is consciousness and bliss, who is to be established as the ultimate purport. || 59 ||
It exists in two ways, by way of the forms of the vowels and consonants of the great mantra.
Salutation to the great word, which consists of the form of the syllable *va* and is the object of speech. || 60 ||

"Has become twofold": for it has indeed become twofold—by way of its own nature as sound (*dhvani*) and by way of the *sphoṭa* manifested by that [sound]. For it is said in the *Mahābhāṣya*: "Now, in the word 'cow' (*gauḥ*), what is the word? That which, when uttered, causes the form of the object—consisting of the dewlap, tail, hump, hooves, horns, and so forth—to be perceived; that is the word. Or rather..."

In common usage, "sound" (*dhvani*) refers to three things: [the physical sound, the manifested word, and the universal]. Regarding this, it has been explained that "by being uttered" means "by being manifested.
In that form, the *sphoṭa* is directly denotative; through that [manifestation], it is denotative by way of its own nature as sound, which is the manifester of that [word].
The state of being a word or a non-word was stated previously. (60)
And it is divided into eight parts for oneself by means of the eight groups.
Salutations indeed to Him who has become all sounds without exception and who is the reality of each respective object.

Eightfold": first, it becomes the stainless self (*amala-ātman*), then the partless (*niṣkala*); thereafter, having attained the form of the *mātṛkā* consisting of the speech-natures of *bindu*, *śabda*, *parā*, *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*, it becomes eightfold again through the eight groups of phonemes beginning with *a*, *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, and *śa*.

"To the one who has become differentiated" means to that which has attained the state of being specific words, sentences, and their respective meanings, consisting of the collection of various phonemes (varṇa). || 61 ||
To the witness who is devoid of verbal connection yet is attainable through words.

"Regarding the phrase *śabdānvayāya* (to that which is beyond the application of words): it is free from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), established in a nature where every possible adjunct has been cast away.
For this very reason, because it lacks the generic properties (*jāti*) and so forth that serve as the grounds for the application of any word, it is devoid of expressive words.
It is self-luminous, appearing solely through the manifestation of its own essential nature. Even while being of such a form, when it is the witness of its own immediate effects..."
Then [the self] becomes that which is obtainable through such scriptural statements as, "The witness, the perceiver, absolute. || 62 ||
[It is that which] is not accessible through means of valid cognition such as direct perception, yet is directly manifest.
Salutations to the Great Light, who is known by himself and is the witness of all.

"Pratyakṣa" (directly perceived): [He is] for that which cannot be reached by perception and other means of knowledge whose objects are non-entities, even though [He] Himself exists as the ultimate reality.

The genitive case in "pramāṇānām" is used in the sense of the agent. Nevertheless, He shines forth as being directly manifest through the self-luminosity of His own nature. For the sake of the direct manifestation of everything other than Himself—to the Great One, the Light. || 63 ||
To one who is devoid of their own essential nature and so forth, both in reality and even in appearance.
Salutations indeed to the one who is for the sake of the great purpose, who is manifest, and who is self-luminous.

Regarding the phrase *svasvarūpe*: here, the first occurrence of the word *sva* refers to the self (*ātman*), while the second refers to that which belongs to the self (*ātmīya*) as a real entity (*vastubhūta*). It is not "deprived" (*hīna*) of its own nature, because it would be contradictory for something to exist within itself. Nor is it "deprived" of its own form and so forth as a non-entity (*avastu*), precisely because that [non-entity] lacks substantial reality. [It is devoid of] great limitation (*pariccheda*) caused by space, time, or substance.

To Him who, due to the absence of darkness (*tamas*), is not limited by anything else; to Him for whom the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is Himself alone as the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), being directly and non-mediately manifest. In this hymn, although words such as *mahase* and *svayambhānāya* recur more than once, one should not suspect tautology (*paunaruktya*). For repetition is tautological only when it is purposeless; however, this [repetition] is...

The hymn (*stotra*) is not intended solely for the instruction of its own literal form; otherwise, the instruction of that which has already been understood from a single recitation would be purposeless. For when an act of meditation (*upāsana*) has been performed by Viṣṇu, repetition—whether for the sake of fixing it in the intellect with that very same sequence or as a meditative practice consisting of a textual composition—is an ornament and not a defect, since it constitutes the very body of that [meditation].

Since the worship performed at specific locations serves as the means for attaining all human goals (*puruṣārtha*), Śambhu—having been questioned by Viṣṇu regarding the sites of worship—first described the internal (*ādhyātmika*) locations, beginning with the phrase "that which is called *brahmarandhra*.

The back, the region of the navel, and the region of the heart, O Janārdana.

He states that the joints of the two hands and feet, along with the tips [of the fingers and toes], are the places for the meditation (*upāsana*) on the *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, and *ta* groups: "hands and feet," etc. The mention of "joints" (*saṃdhi*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the entire [limbs]. He states the five places for the *pa* group: "sides," etc. The mention of the "navel" (*nābhi*) is an elliptical expression for the "abdomen" (*kukṣi*) as well. He states the ten places for the meditation on the *ya* group and so forth: "the region of the heart," etc., extending from the feet to the head.

The seven elements, beginning with the skin, as well as the triad of objects characterized by breath (*prāṇa*), life-force (*jīva*), and the vital air (*pāna*), pervade even the heart; thus, the meaning is that the ten locations, beginning with the feet, are to be meditated upon within the heart alone. The mention of the "elements" (*dhātu*) is also an elliptical indication for the triad beginning with breath. || 74 || 75 ||
The Mūlādhāra is the Adhiṣṭhāna, and the Anāhata is called Paraka.

The seat of the seed, the penis, and various kinds of body hair.

(26) Indeed, these are established by convention (*rūḍhi*); that is, these names are established solely through the conventional usage of the whole, independent of the etymological meaning of the individual parts.

[These names] reside in Paraśiva. If they were dependent upon the etymological derivation of their constituent parts (*avayava-vyutpatti*), then immediately upon the utterance of the name, the cognition [of the referent] would be delayed under the pretext of following up on that etymological derivation. However, this fault does not apply to *khaḍga* and similar words. For this very reason it is said: "The conventional meaning of a whole (*samudāya-prasiddhi*) is stronger than the meaning derived from its constituent parts (*avayava-prasiddhi*). If this is so, [then why is it called] Mahādeva?

Names such as Kaparda, Vāmadeva, Virūpākṣa, and so forth, are stated again; otherwise, they would be redundant. This would indeed be the case if one were to rely solely on conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*), as in the case of words like "aśvakarṇa. However, in this context, what is intended is a combination of etymological derivation and convention (*yogarūḍhi*), as in the case of the word "paṅkaja" (lotus). Therefore, since the etymological analysis of the constituent parts is also intended, it serves to demonstrate their distinctness.
By this, the fault previously stated can be avoided. To explain: the word *mahat* is well-known to have both the sense of "worshipful" and the sense of "possessing great magnitude.
Thus, in one case, the meaning is "the worshipful god is Mahādeva," while in the other, it is "the all-pervading god is Mahādeva. Likewise—[in the context of] "abundance" (*bhūman*)...

According to the traditional rule (smaraṇa), "In [the sense of] praise, constant connection, and excellence," there is no tautology: in one case the word *kaparda* signifies praise, while in the other it signifies constant connection. Likewise, *vāmadeva* means "the desirable god" (*vananīyo devaḥ*) in one instance; for it is heard in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa: "The gods said of him, 'He indeed makes us all desirable (*vāmayati*')."

Therefore, in one sense, "Vāmadeva" refers to [the sage] Vāmadeva; in another sense, however, the word *vāmadeva* denotes the Lord who sports with the left side (*vāmena bhāgena dīvyati*), thus signifying the Ardhanārīśvara. Regarding *Virūpākṣa*, in one derivation, it means "he whose eye on the forehead is vast";
in another, however, it means "he whose senses (*akṣāṇi*)—that is, the faculties—are of distinguished form (*viśiṣṭa-rūpa*)," referring to the Lord of the body composed of the senses.

This is the meaning. "Then the body falls apart" means that the soul's connection with agency, enjoyership, and so forth is based on its association with *māyā*;

likewise, for such a soul, the connection with the body—which serves as the locus of experience—is based on karma consisting of merit and demerit, which are the causes of the pleasure and pain to be experienced by itself. The meaning is that through the withdrawal of the self, when the connection with agency, enjoyership, and so forth becomes loosened, the connection with the body—which is caused by merit and demerit—is also dissolved; thus, due to the absence of identification with it, there is its falling away. 643. “‘The Blessed One has said: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Which four? “The person who is like a young jasmine flower; the person who is like a blue lotus flower; the person who is like a white lotus flower; and the person who is like a fragrant sandalwood tree. And how, monks, is one a person like a young jasmine flower? Here, monks, a certain person possesses a small amount of faith, a small amount of virtue, a small amount of learning, a small amount of generosity, and a small amount of wisdom. Just as the jasmine flower is small in size, so too is this person small in faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom. Therefore, monks, he is called a person like a young jasmine flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a blue lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person possesses a greater amount of faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom than that [previous] person. Just as the blue lotus flower is larger in size than the jasmine, so too is this person greater in faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom. Therefore, monks, he is called a person like a blue lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a white lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person possesses a still greater amount of faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom than that [previous] person. Just as the white lotus flower is even larger in size than the blue lotus, so too is this person even greater in faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom. Therefore, monks, he is called a person like a white lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a fragrant sandalwood tree? Here, monks, a certain person possesses an immeasurable amount of faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom. Just as the fragrance of sandalwood spreads in all directions, so too does the fragrance of this person’s faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom spread in all directions. Therefore, monks, he is called a person like a fragrant sandalwood tree.

Yudhiṣṭhira said: "O grandfather, O best of the Bharatas, it was previously heard by me that there was a king named Vidarbha, who was devoted to dharma and possessed of great power. What did that wise king do? And how did he obtain a son? Please tell me this. Bhīṣma said: "O descendant of Bharata, listen to this ancient account of how that king obtained a son through the grace of the great sage Agastya. There was a king named Vidarbha, who was truthful and firm in his vows. He had no son, yet he desired one. O bull among men, he performed many sacrifices for the sake of obtaining a son. However, despite his efforts, he did not obtain a son. Then, O descendant of Bharata, that wise king went to the forest to perform severe austerities. Having gone there, he practiced austerities with great fervor. While he was performing those austerities, a great sage named Agastya, who was compassionate toward all beings, came to that place. Seeing the great sage arrived, the king, full of joy, honored him according to the prescribed rites and then spoke these words: ‘O illustrious one, I am childless and I have come here desiring a son. O best of the twice-born, please grant me a son who will be endowed with virtue and fame. Hearing these words of the king, the great sage Agastya, being pleased, replied to the king: ‘O king, you shall indeed obtain a son who will be famous on earth. But you must first go to your own city and then return here; only then will your desire be fulfilled. Having been thus addressed by the sage, the king returned to his own city. After some time, O descendant of Bharata, that king once again went to the hermitage of Agastya. Upon seeing the king arrive, the sage Agastya, being well-pleased, spoke these words: ‘O king, go to your city and perform a sacrifice for the sake of a son, following my instructions. Then, O lord of the earth, you will obtain a son who will be endowed with great splendor. The king said: ‘O illustrious one, what kind of sacrifice should I perform? And what offerings should be made? Please tell me everything in detail. Agastya said: ‘O king, go to the city of Ayodhyā and have a sacrifice performed there. O lord of the earth, have the priest perform the sacrifice according to the rules, and you yourself should offer oblations into the fire. Having been thus addressed by the sage, the king returned to his own city and had the sacrifice performed. When the sacrifice was completed, the king, accompanied by his wives, went to the hermitage of Agastya. Upon seeing the king arrive, the sage Agastya, being well-pleased, spoke these words: ‘O king, enter the sacrificial fire-pit and offer oblations into the fire while reciting the mantras. By the power of the mantras and the efficacy of the sacrifice, you will obtain a son who will be endowed with great splendor. Hearing these words of the sage, the king entered the fire-pit and offered oblations into the fire. He avoids the charge of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) with the words "of non-existence" (*abhāvasya*). If it were to possess such a property, it would necessarily be an entity (*bhāvatva*) itself, like a jar or other objects, because only that which is indefinable by any property whatsoever is non-existence (*abhāvatva*). Having provisionally accepted this [point], namely the eternality of the non-existence of destruction—
The lack of necessity has not been avoided; that too will be demonstrated as impermanent later on. Now, regarding the unattained self...
[page 329]

verse 653.
"Attainment is an eternal relation"—thus he characterizes the second alternative of the first [position] with the words "If it were eternal.
Liberation, being of the nature of an eternal relation, would also be eternally established and not to be produced by any means whatsoever.
Consequently, since it would be eternally attained, the previously stated point—that it is to be accomplished by knowledge alone—would follow once again; such is the meaning. || 83 ||
If there were oneness of liberation, which consists in the attainment of what was previously unattained; || 86 ||
Therefore, the identity of the two is never established.
Liberation occurs either upon the destruction of the distinction between the two [the self and the Lord] once they were distinct, or while the distinction remains. (87)

He restates the second [position]—that "attainment of what was not previously attained" constitutes identity—in order to refute it, beginning with the words "not attained. He refutes that with the words "that is not so. || 86 || 87 ||
O best of those who know the Vedas, their unity is possible only upon the destruction of their distinction.
If it is argued that there is identity between the two despite their difference, this is not tenable. || 88 ||
In this regard, it must be asked: is there identity between the pot and the Lord upon the destruction of their difference, or is it while the difference still exists?

Regarding the first case, since you accept that difference consists in mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), and since that [non-existence] is beginningless and endless, your position is refuted; thus he says: "upon the destruction of difference. Nor is the second case possible; thus he says: "while the difference exists."
Unity cannot be established in the presence of difference, because of their contradiction.
If it is argued that liberation cannot be attained by means of the self, that is not tenable. (89)
But since liberation is unattainable [by effort], there is indeed no dependence upon a means for it.
When that practice is accomplished, liberation is indeed always attained without fail. || 90 ||

Why is this so? To this he says: "Because of difference" (*bhedasya*). The meaning is that it is impossible for unity—which inheres in a single object characterized by non-difference—to coexist with difference.

Thus, having refuted the position that liberation is something to be attained as distinct from the nature of the Self, he restates and refutes the second position—that it is not attained—by saying: "Not to be attained" (*na prāpyā*). This refers to its nature as being unattainable.
Even if liberation were inferred despite hundreds of means, its non-attainment would remain certain because its very nature is unalterable.
Therefore, since there is no dependence on means, the meaning is that everyone would be liberated effortlessly. || 89 || 60 ||
If it is held that liberation is not eternally established, but rather exists only as something to be accomplished;
That impermanence exists while being something to be proven was stated previously. (91)
