In the *Tātparyadīpikā* (along with its commentary),
within the fourth section on the Majesty of Sacrifice (*Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa*),
having thus raised the alternative inquiry as to whether liberation in the form of union (*sāyujya*) is eternally established or something to be accomplished: [the first position...]

Having established that right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) is the means to liberation by demonstrating its independence from karma through the removal of doubts regarding its possibility, [the author] states, "Not [attained] as eternally established," because a second [type of liberation] is not tenable when those defects persist. The meaning is that it was already stated previously that if liberation were something to be produced (*sādhya*), it would be non-eternal, like a jar or other such objects. || 91 ||
But the eternality of destruction can never be established in any way.
For it is understood that everything which is acidic is subject to destruction. || 92 ||

Now, one might object: "Even if it is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), why could liberation not be eternal, like *pradhvaṃsābhāva* (the negation of destruction)? To this he says: "Of *pradhvaṃsa*...

The meaning is that since the entire objective world (*cetyaprapañca*) distinct from the conscious self (*cidātman*) is sublated by scriptural texts such as "here there is no diversity" (*neha nānāsti kiñcana*), its impermanence must necessarily be accepted. || 92 ||
Since it exists as a real entity and is something to be accomplished, destruction belongs to that which is insentient.
But even if destruction were the probandum, by the reason of its being a non-entity (abhāva), [it would follow that it is not produced]. || 93 ||

One might object: "In the initial apprehension of the relationship [between word and meaning] and so forth, since verbal testimony depends on other means of valid cognition such as perception and inference, its authority is untenable when it contradicts them. Therefore, 'being a positive entity' (bhāvatve sati) while being 'something to be produced' (sādhyatvam) is the proof for non-eternality. Thus, there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of destruction (pradhvaṃsa), because although it is something to be produced, it lacks the quality of being a positive entity. To this, he raises the following doubt: "provided it is a positive entity" (bhāvatve sati).
Destruction, however, is not established; and that [position] is by no means well-founded.
Because even that which is designated as prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) is observed to be impermanent. || 94 ||
Even though antecedent non-existence lacks the status of being a probandum, it remains nonetheless a non-existence.
If impermanence were admitted, it would be the same for destruction as well. (95)

He refutes this by showing its lack of pervasion (avyāpti) with the words "And that is not so. Let it be granted that, because it possesses existence (bhāvatva) and is a probandum (sādhya), impermanence (anityatva) exists in jars and the like; however, regarding the impermanence of prior non-existence (prāgabhāva), another cause must necessarily be stated, as the previously mentioned reason is absent. And that [cause] would have to be non-existence itself (abhāvatva), since any other property (dharmāntara) has already been rejected. The same applies to destruction (pradhvaṃsa).
The meaning is that since this is the same for sound as well, its impermanence must also be admitted. || 94 || 95 ||
O best of sages, this applies to both existent and non-existent things that are to be proven.
And the fact that all incurable things are impermanent is the reason for this. || 96 ||

And if it were thus a positive entity (*bhāvatva*), then the property of being a positive entity would be the cause for the impermanence of things such as jars; whereas [if it were negative], non-existence (*abhāvatva*) would be the cause for the non-impermanence of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). Consequently, there would be the conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*) of having to accept two distinct causes. Therefore, [non-existence] is indeed [negative]. [Note: The manuscript variants provided indicate that the reading in manuscript *ga* is "anvaya" (concomitance), which has been incorporated into the translation.]
[Sūta-saṃhitā, Chapter 38, page 331]
He states that "the very dullness (inertia) inherent in fear must be accepted as the cause of impermanence"—this is expressed by the words "of entities" (*bhāvānām*).

Regarding the phrase "of those not to be proven" (*asādhyānām*): since atoms, space, time, direction, and so forth are accepted as eternal by others, they are included among those things that are not to be proven [of impermanence].
The meaning is that even for them, these [objects] are not desired. || 96 ||
Only insentience has been stated [as the reason], because there is no deviation from it in other cases.
But the eternal Śruti declares the eternality of consciousness. 97.
Therefore, in the manner described, liberation takes the form of *sāyujya* (union).
It is to be attained through knowledge; it is not attained through mere ritual action, nor through their combination. ||98||
"Not the other," meaning not such things as being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth. Why? To this he says: "Because of deviation" (*vyabhicārataḥ*).

The meaning is that although there is impermanence in the case of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the like, [the definition] does not pervade them and thus lacks universal application (*ananugama*). He states the scriptural authority (*śruti*); and that is such passages as, "The eternal among the eternals, the conscious among the conscious. He concludes the point already established.
The limit—therefore, thus. || 97 || 98 ||
All this that is called knowledge is the manifestation of everything in the form of existence.
Action, however, depends upon its factors of action (kāraka) and does not always have cognition as its objective support. //99//
For one who is born [into this state], there is always a contradiction between action and knowledge precisely because of their mutual opposition.
Accumulation would not be tenable; how, then, could there be a supreme state through it? || 100 ||

To the question "What is that knowledge?", he says: "Knowledge, indeed... The meaning is that the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the entire phenomenal world—which consists of both the enjoyer and the enjoyed—as being essentially the non-dual Brahman, which is Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*), is the means for attaining liberation. For it is heard in scripture: "All this is indeed Brahman," and "All this is that Self," and so forth.
He establishes that the combination of knowledge and action, which was promised as the means for attaining the supreme liberation, [in the following]: "The action...

etc. Ritual action, such as the Agnihotra, being dependent upon various factors (kārakas) distinguished by the differences of agent, instrument, object, and so forth, relies solely upon the cognition produced by the scripture concerning its own sphere—the objects such as the substance and the deity—and not upon the agent.

Knowledge consists in the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the reality of the innermost Self (*pratyañca-paramātmatattva*), which occurs through the complete sublation of all distinctions such as cause and effect;

for [the recitation] is in contradiction with that [knowledge]. Indeed, it has been stated by the venerable commentators: "Because of its lack of utility and because of the contradiction with the qualified person (*adhikārin*). Therefore, since there is a state of opposition, and because there is no simultaneous occurrence (*samasamapavartitva*) [of both], [there can be no coexistence with] non-dual knowledge.
The very conjunction of the two [defects] is not possible; what then, by that, could there be any hope for liberation? This is the meaning. || 99 || 100 ||
That liberation which is called "conformity" (sārūpya), and that other which is called "proximity" (sāmīpya);
And that which is called sālokya among them has action alone as its means of accomplishment. || 101 ||
[Page 332] 656 Accompanied by the *Tātparyadīpikā*— in the Fourth Section on the Glory of Sacrifice (*Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa*)— :
The liberations of all embodied beings take the form of both this world and the world beyond.
For they are accomplished through action alone, not through knowledge, because of its opposition [to it]. || 102 ||
Knowledge and action must be exactly as declared in the Vedas; they should not be otherwise proclaimed.
But that which is stated by another, O best of Brahmins, is for the sake of the worldly dealings of the undiscriminating. (103)

"Karma alone" means that ritual action—such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice and the like—which is devoid of the knowledge of the non-dual Brahman as one's own Self, which is accompanied by the knowledge of substances, deities, and so forth, and which persists until the very end; as well as the form of meditation on the Saguna-Brahman, such as Hiraṇyagarbha and others, is the means for attaining results such as similarity of form (*sārūpya*), because it is not yet joined with the supreme [liberation]. This is the meaning. || 101 || 102 || 103 ||
Depending on these, cognition, consciousness, and action are prescribed.
Nevertheless, in conventional practice, they grant conventional validity.
Therefore, the wisest person should not practice atheism in any circumstance.
It is solely due to nihilism that all beings undergo transmigration within saṃsāra. || 105 ||

"With regard to the intellect" (*apekṣya buddhim*) means that, having regard for the gradations of intellect among the qualified aspirants who exist in superior, middling, and inferior states, both the knowledge of the conditioned Brahman (saguṇa-brahma) such as Hiraṇyagarbha and ritual action such as the Agnihotra are taught in combination by such passages as: "He who knows both knowledge and ignorance together" (*vidyāṃ cāvidyāṃ ca yastadvedobhayaṃ saha*). And these...
The meaning is that knowledge and action have their purpose and utility as conventional results during the state of worldly transaction. || 104 ||
O best of sages, I have thus explained the entire method of accomplishment in brief.
Therefore, this wonderful [teaching] must always be kept secret by one who possesses faith. 106.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, Mahādeva, accompanied by Ambā and illuminating all things, [remained].
Having danced in his presence, he vanished right there.
But this entire sādhana has been expounded by me to you solely out of compassion.
O twice-born ones, nothing else should be spoken here; for otherwise, everything would be mere delusion. (108)

The Sūta-saṃhitā. Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "An Investigation into the Means of Liberation," in the fourth section, the Yajña-vaibhava-khaṇḍa, of the commentary on the Śrī Skanda Purāṇa’s Sūta-saṃhitā. || 38 ||
Sūta said:
Now begins the thirty-ninth chapter.
Now, therefore, I shall explain in brief, and not in detail.
But there is no contradiction among all the Vedas without exception, O lords of sages.

Having raised the objection that both duality and non-duality lack authority due to their mutual contradiction—since duality, characterized by distinctions such as agent, instrument, and fruit, is also heard in scripture just like non-duality—he begins to demonstrate their non-contradiction with the words: "Now, therefore" (atha ataḥ). || 1 ||
O sages of firm vows, the collection of the Vedas is indeed twofold.
In brief, there is a certain portion of the Veda that is devoted to the non-duality of reality.
But another portion of the Veda is likewise established upon that which is imagined.
O believers, non-duality alone is always the truth; duality is untruth.

To demonstrate the lack of contradiction between the sections on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*) and knowledge (*jñānakāṇḍa*), he first states the distinction in their respective objects: "In the reality of non-duality" (*satyādvaite*). That portion of the Veda characterized as the Upaniṣads always teaches, through its primary purport, the nature of Supreme Śiva as non-dual and free from all sublation; whereas the other portion of the Veda, consisting of the section on ritual action, [teaches] that which is superimposed upon that very nature.

The intention is that there is no contradiction because the subject matters are different: [the Upanishads] depend upon duality as a fifth category to prescribe sacrifices, oblations, and so forth, with the aim of attaining fruits such as heaven. Why is it not the other way around? To this he says: "It is indeed true," etc.
Moreover, some here describe even duality as being real.
Therefore, duality is superimposed upon that Supreme Self, being conjoined with it.

[The opponent objects: "But surely, since the non-dual world of insentient phenomena (*jaḍaprapañca*) is observed to function without contradiction—and thus differs from superimposed things like silver—why should it not be considered ultimately real (*pāramārthikatva*)? Thus, they state an inference according to the opponent's view:
'Of duality also... [The author] refutes this with: "That... [and so on]. [It is] limited, unreal, and superimposed; because it cannot be established [as real]...
Such is the intended meaning. || 4 ||
Indeed, duality has always been practiced as an object of perception, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
The state of being an object of perception for the entire range of dualistic phenomena is accepted by all embodied beings. (5)

He refutes the objection regarding the non-establishment of the reason (*hetvasiddhi*) with the words "for that which is superimposed" (*adhyastaṃ hi*). Even though non-contradictory worldly practice is observed, one must admit that the manifold of duality (*dvaitaprapañca*), like silver in mother-of-pearl, is superimposed upon the non-dual supreme Self (*paramātman*), which is the locus of perception; and by that [admission], its unreality is established—this is the meaning. He states the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) with the word "perceptibility" (*dṛśyatva*). [The proof for] duality—

The meaning is that because the five [sheaths] cannot appear by themselves due to their inherent insentience (*jaḍatva*), they must appear solely through the nature of the Seer—the self-luminous consciousness whose essence is Supreme Śiva; thus, the reason "being an object of sight" (*dṛśyatva*) exists pervading the entire subject (*pakṣa*), which is a point accepted by all.
Therefore, the portion devoted to non-duality has as its object a duality that is merely imagined.
Non-duality is always true, for in no way whatsoever is there an absence of difference.

He concludes that the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*), which has that [water] as its object, is established as having a conceptualized subject matter, because this very water is presented as a conceptually constructed reality—thus he says, "Therefore. Now, one might ask: why should the non-dual Self (*ātman*) not likewise be considered unreal?
To this he replies: "Because of the absence of difference" (*bhedābhāvāt*). For such a state of being an object of perception necessarily involves difference.

The meaning is that because it is non-dependent, there is no differentiation within the supreme Self; since that [dependence] is absent, there is no possibility of superimposition due to the absence of visibility, and thus non-duality is true because it is forever free from sublation. || 6 ||
And even non-duality, O best of Veda-knowers, is superimposed [upon reality].
Where, indeed, is non-duality superimposed? Not upon non-duality itself, because of its absence there.

To establish this very point, he offers the following alternative: "Non-duality" (*advaitam*). If non-duality were superimposed just like duality, then it would have to have some substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), because an error without a substratum is impossible. Having raised the alternatives—whether that substratum is non-duality itself or duality—he states the first position: "Not non-duality. That—
"By way of its own nature" (bhāvataḥ) means that because there is no other non-duality apart from that very superimposed non-duality. || 7 ||
If those two are merely imagined, the practice of non-duality is impossible.
But in the state of empirical transaction, superimposition is observed even upon that which is real. || 8 ||

He says "not the second" with the words "merely" (*kevalam*). Since no other substratum is possible for the superimposition of non-duality, one would have to say that the superimposition occurs upon the imagined duality alone; yet even that is not tenable, as he states with the word "empirical usage" (*vyavahāra*).

This is because, in the world, the superimposition of silver and the like is observed to occur upon a piece of mother-of-pearl and such things which possess ultimate reality; therefore, following that analogy—
The meaning is that even for the practice of duality, there must be something truly real (*satyabhūta*) designated as its substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and not something merely imagined (*parikalpita*).
Siddha-p; 2. pa. 'jātasya]
Chapter 39 of the Sūta-saṃhitā [page 335]
Furthermore, it cannot be asserted that non-duality is superimposed upon duality.
Because that non-duality is the very nature of practice, O best among the knowers of Brahman. (9)

Let it be that in the world there is the status of being a substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for truth; however, because nothing else is possible within the non-dualistic practice (*advaitābhyāse*), why does the restriction not hold that only the imagined (*kalpita*) is the substrate? To this he says: "And in duality" (*dvate ca*). [This refers to] the duality which is superimposed (*adhyasta*) as one...

The meaning is that because that which is superimposed lacks reality, and because it does not differ from its substratum—the essential nature of the Supreme Self—it is contradictory for one and the same thing to be both the substratum and the superimposed. || 9 ||
Duality as well as non-duality—both are indeed merely imagined.
Because an entity simply does not exist apart from duality and non-duality. || 10 ||

Furthermore, since non-duality (advaita) would likewise be merely imagined if duality (dvaita) were so, one must accept the reality of non-duality, for there can be no [imagined] superimposition without a substratum (adhiṣṭhāna). Thus he says: "And duality... If both duality and non-duality were superimposed, then, because there would be no other distinct entity remaining apart from them, there would follow the consequence of a lack of a substratum; this is the meaning. || 10 ||
O best of Veda-knowers, neither of these two is superimposed upon mere emptiness.
And because that which is indefinable cannot possibly be the locus of superimposition or the substratum. || 11 ||
[Objection: "Let the void itself be the substrate. To this he says: "The void," etc. He states the reason for that:

"of that which is formless," etc. The meaning is that it is impossible for the void—which cannot be described by any form whatsoever—to possess the attributes characterized by being the substrate of superimposition and being the limit of negation. || 11 ||
Therefore, duality has been superimposed upon the non-dual Supreme Self.
Therefore, O wise ones, a certain portion of the Śruti [is to be understood] by the aforementioned method.
He is declared by those who know the meaning of all scriptures to be devoted to the non-duality of reality.
In the same way, O ascetics, some portion of the mass of the Vedas [remains].
But that which culminates in the imagined deity has been described by those who speak the truth. || 13 ||
Thus, having demonstrated that superimposition is impossible upon non-duality, he concludes that duality alone is what is superimposed—with the words "Therefore" (ataḥ).

He concludes the non-contradiction between the ritual and knowledge sections (karmajñānakāṇḍau), which was previously asserted on the basis of their difference in subject matter—with the words "Consequently" (tasmāt).
Furthermore, there appears to be a contradiction between the scriptural passages concerning duality and non-duality.
For, indeed, by the very manner already stated, there is simply an absence of contradiction. || 14 ||
18. 26 Also in the case of a rope.
From the *Tātparyadīpikā*:
"Because non-duality is never accessible through perception and other means of knowledge..."
In that very matter, O believers, the scriptural texts on non-duality are directly meaningful. (15)

Let there be no contradiction between the sections on action (*karmakāṇḍa*) and knowledge (*jñānakāṇḍa*). One might raise the objection that since the section on knowledge itself presents a duality in some places—based on passages such as "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*)—and in other places presents non-duality through statements such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), there would be a contradiction between the scriptural texts on duality and non-duality, resulting in their lack of authority. Anticipating this, he says: "Dvaitādvaita... [referring to the verse beginning with *dvaitādvaitavibhāgahīnam*]. This refers to the appearance of contradiction.

He establishes the threefold nature [of the scriptures] with the words "by what has been said. The meaning is that, according to the stated method, the scriptural texts concerning difference (*bheda*) have as their purport only the imagined duality, whereas the scriptural texts concerning non-difference (*abheda*) have as their purport ultimate non-duality; thus, there is no contradiction between them. Now, one might object: even though both difference and non-difference are equally the purport of scripture, why is non-difference alone the ultimate reality while difference is merely imagined?

From where is this "reality" (tattva) obtained? To this he says: "from perception and so forth. The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) is that which makes known an object not already apprehended. Therefore, the Śruti, being itself a means of valid knowledge, attains its status as such by propounding an object that is not sublated by other means of valid knowledge such as perception. And since non-duality (advaita) is not accessible through perception and the like, it is precisely that [which is established by Śruti].
It is established by scripture through its intended meaning. || 14 || 15 ||
However, difference is always established in the world even without scripture.
Therefore, in that case, scripture—which transcends the means of valid cognition—is not purposeful.
The Veda never requires corroboration by other means of valid cognition.

Regarding the word "in between" (*antareṇa*): since distinctions such as those between a jar and a cloth are apprehended through means of valid cognition such as perception, it is not appropriate for the Śruti to have its purport (*tātparya*) directed toward them. Thus, the meaning is that [the Śruti] would lack authority because it would be merely repetitive (*anuvādaka*). Now, one might ask: how can the Śruti intend to establish non-duality—which is not an object of perception and other means of valid cognition, and which is like the horn of a hare?

To address the objection that [the scripture] might not be capable [of such a function], he says: "transcending all means of knowledge" (*mānātigāminī*). The meaning is that just as it makes known heaven, liberation, and so forth—which are beyond the reach of perception and other means of knowledge—so too is it capable of making known non-duality (*advaita*). Now, one might object: if the subject matter of the scripture is not the domain of other means of knowledge, then, due to the absence of corroborating cognition (*saṃvādajñāna*), the scripture would lack authority (*aprāmāṇya*). To this [he replies]:

He says: "By another means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇāntara*). Since it is accepted that all cognitions possess intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), there is no dependence on a cognition of correspondence with what is heard [in scripture]; this is the meaning. || 16 || 17 ||
And for that Śruti as well, there is no defect either from its own side or from another.
The state of being defective always belongs to the means of valid cognition, such as direct perception and the rest.
Therefore, among these means of valid cognition, scripture is the most powerful. (18)

Now, one might object: "Let it be that there is no dependence on a corroborative cognition; why then does invalidation not result in the cognition being otherwise? To this, he says: "Intrinsic... [page 337] "nigita" (refuted).
Chapter 39: Sūta-saṃhitā, [Verse] 661.

Thus it is said: For that which is produced by a defective means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is indeed sublated; however, in the case of the Veda, there is no defect inherent in itself, because it is capable of conveying its meaning. Nor is there any defect extrinsic to it, because it is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*).

Therefore, since there is no possibility of even the suspicion of sublation due to its being a flawless means of knowledge, the meaning is that the self-evident validity (*prāmāṇya*) of the Veda is unimpeded.

Having thus described the non-dependence of the Śruti, he states that perception and the other means of knowledge possess defects—in the words "perception and so forth"—in order to establish its superior authority. "Possessing the nature of having defects" means being produced in association with defects.
But this scripture is not at all an authority regarding the mere state of being imagined.
In that regard, because there is no purpose in defining ultimate reality, [it is not investigated]. (19)
Non-duality, supreme bliss, the reality of Brahman, and nothing else.
In that regard, O Brahmins, there is indeed a purpose; of this there is no doubt.

Thus, by examining the definition of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) as that which makes known an object not yet cognized, it has been established that the authority of the Śruti resides in non-duality, which is not apprehended through perception and other means. Now, in order to further support its authority therein on the grounds of its possessing a purpose (*prayojana*), he states that there is an absence of purpose if it were intent upon duality, beginning with the words "kalpita" (imagined). Because of the absence of a purpose—

Diti: The meaning is that since the imagined duality is unreal due to its being composed of *māyā*, there is no fruit whatsoever—serving as a cause for the engagement of a discerning person—to be found in a scripture that propounds it. However, he demonstrates the existence of a purpose in propounding non-duality with the words "non-duality": because the reality of non-dual Brahman is of the nature of unsurpassed bliss.
Therefore, by means of its exposition, there exists the most excellent purpose, characterized by the attainment of its true nature;
such is the meaning. || 19 || 20 ||
Where there is a purpose, there scripture is the authority; such is the established rule.
Therefore, because there is no purpose [in doing so], duality is not taught.
Having restated duality, the Śruti establishes non-duality. || 22 ||

[Objection: Is it not the case that the establishment of validity based on purpose is improper, since purpose follows from the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? To this he says: "Where there is a purpose. It is true that in the case of perception and the other [means of knowledge], the purpose follows the means of valid cognition. But scripture, by virtue of its very purpose, impels a person toward its own object; therefore, its validity depends upon that purpose.

[This is] not a lack of definition. Therefore, the meaning is that the established position of those who uphold the authority of scripture (*prāmāṇika*) is that the validity of the Veda (*śruti*) applies only to that matter for which there is a purpose. Now, one might ask: "In that case, why does the scripture beginning with 'Two birds... teach a difference that serves no purpose? To this, he says: "having restated" (*anūdya*). Duality is already established in the world through means of valid cognition such as direct perception regarding the individual soul (*jīva*)—...

Having restated the difference between the Lord and the individual soul, [the text] establishes through such passages as "a person is submerged in the same tree" that the state of being an individual soul (jīva) has its root in ignorance.

The meaning is that [the scripture], preceded by the mention of difference, establishes non-duality alone as its intended purport (*tātparya*). Thus, it should be understood that everywhere the scriptural texts concerning difference are for the purpose of restating (anuvāda) the difference already established in the world, whereas the texts concerning non-difference are for the purpose of establishing, through their intended purport, the ultimate reality of non-duality. || 21 || 22 ||
And likewise of the Smṛtis, the Purāṇas, and the Mahābhārata and other such works.
Likewise, O best of the twice-born, [the authority] of the Śaiva Āgamas and other systems of logic is established.
It is stated that one must always remain established in non-duality alone, never being intent upon duality.

He states, beginning with "of the Smṛtis," that the fact that the Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and so forth also have non-duality as their ultimate purport is to be understood through reasoning in exactly the same way.

Furthermore, the fact that all the Smṛtis and other texts have non-duality as their ultimate purport has already been established previously in the context of explaining the meaning of the six-syllable mantra. || 23 ||
Through the cessation of habitual ignorance and its effects, one attains the non-dual.
Some excellent scholars joyfully cause [others] to awaken through their teachings. || 24 ||

Now, one might object: "Since the application of all words is fourfold—namely, by way of genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), and arbitrary convention (*yadṛcchā*)—how can the Śruti be capable of establishing through its intended meaning the nature of Paraśiva, which is non-dual and devoid of all attributes such as genus and the rest? To this, he says: "Superimposed" (*adhyasta*). [This refers to] Māyā, which is the root of the conceptualization of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*).

Ignorance (*avidyā*), which is synonymous with *māyā* and is of the nature of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*), along with its effects—the elements, elemental products, the body, the senses, and so forth—is superimposed through beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*) upon the supreme, faultless nature of Paraśiva. Its cessation occurs through the knowledge of the true nature of that substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Thus, those [scriptural passages] which establish the cessation of that *māyā* and its effects—
Certain scriptural passages (*śruti*) establish, as their primary purport, that very nature of Supreme Śiva which is of the aforementioned kind—an indivisible, single essence.
Those scriptural passages include such texts as: "That which is invisible, ungraspable," "Soundless, touchless, formless, undecaying," and "Neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long. (24)
Brahman, characterized by truth and other such qualities, is directly [revealed] through the mouth of Dharma alone.
Some excellent scholars joyfully awaken others through their teachings. ||25||

Regarding the phrase "by way of injunction": certain Śrutis, such as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," do not proceed by way of negation like the previous ones; rather, they establish that Brahman is that which is characterized by truth, knowledge, and so forth, solely by way of injunction.
Even in negative Śrutis such as "neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long," that which is grossness and the like—which is the effect of ignorance—[is negated].

Since it is implied that the ultimate reality (*pāramārthika-vastu*), which is manifested through negation, is that Brahman, there is an injunction [of its nature] by implication; therefore, he qualifies it with the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*).
This is the intended meaning: in the world, [Brahman] is first understood as having "truth" (*satyatva*) and so forth as the grounds for its application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*).

Words such as "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and so forth are derived [from their etymological roots]. However, the connection with such attributes is not possible in the Supreme Self, which is partless, of a single essence, and non-dual. Therefore, words such as "truth" (*satya*) take worldly truth and so forth as their basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*).
They define *satya* (the real) with the intention that it is an indivisible entity that is always free from deviation;

they define *jñāna* (knowledge) with the intention that it is the manifestation of the distinction between self and other; and they define *ānanda* (bliss) as being experienced as absolutely favorable. Thus, the words *satya* and so forth directly refer to worldly reality and the like.

The meaning is that the Śruti conveys the impartite reality through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by means of the positive form alone. For it has been said: "It is precisely the worldly categories such as 'Being' (*sat*) and so forth that indicate the impartite.

Thus, the meaning is that the Śruti is capable of establishing non-duality through its intended purport (*tātparya*), both by way of exclusion of the other (*atadvyāvṛtti*) and directly through the positive form. || 25 ||
[He bestows] the state of being essentially Śiva upon the very soul of the practitioner.
Indeed, the Veda, by making [the self] known, sublates the erroneous notion that it is the individual soul (jīva). || 26 ||

Having thus described the manner in which the Śruti establishes the nature of the non-dual Supreme Śiva, he now demonstrates the manner in which the identity between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (Īśvara) is established by means of great statements (*mahāvākya*) such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), stating: "Of the seeker alone... [and so forth]. [He cites: "Having created that, He entered into it," and "Having entered by means of this living self (*jīva*), He manifested names and forms."

According to such scriptural passages as "Speech [is His]," the Supreme Lord alone is indeed directly the individual soul (*jīva*). Therefore, the scripture beginning with "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), which establishes that the innate nature of one who has assumed the state of a *jīva* is that of the non-dual Supreme Śiva, negates the illusory status of being a *jīva*— which, though appearing as if it were the ultimate reality, is actually conditioned by *māyā* dominated by impure *sattva*.

It refutes that [objection]. The meaning is that this sentence conveys its sense by setting aside the contradictory portions—just as in the case of "This is that Devadatta"—[showing] that the consciousness which has the cause of the world as its limiting adjunct (upādhi) and is characterized by truth, knowledge, and so forth, and that consciousness which is the inner self of all and has ignorance and its effects as its limiting adjuncts, are in fact one and the same. || 26 ||
O twice-born ones, this livingness of the conscious being is its inherent nature.
Some say that this is not its inherent nature at all times, but rather due to the consumption of food.
If the state of being a living soul were intrinsic, then it would exist at all times.
For there is no cessation of that which is self-established; it does not perish. || 28 ||

Now, having restated the position favored by the opponent—that the state of being a *jīva* (individual soul) is inherent to the Self—he refutes it with the words beginning "If the state of being a *jīva* belongs to the conscious [Self]," and so forth. If the state of being a *jīva* were inherent to the Self, then it would not cease even in the state of liberation (*mukti*), because an inherent nature cannot be discarded. Consequently, there would be a persistence of pleasure and pain even for those who are liberated.
This is the meaning. || 27 || 28 ||

Just as the impurity of copper is destroyed through contact with medicinal substances, so too is the impurity of the mind destroyed by the practice of yoga. Thus ends the fourth chapter on the majesty of sacrifice (*yajñavaibhava*) in the *Yogavāsiṣṭha*.
In the same way, the cessation of suffering and so forth for the living being might occur through some [means]. || 29 ||

Even though the state of being a *jīva* is inherent, he raises the objection regarding the possibility of liberation with the words "Just as" (*yathā*). Just as the impurity inherent in copper is removed when it comes into contact with acid, so too, through some means such as the propitiation of the Supreme Lord,
when the state of being a *jīva*— which consists of the transmigratory condition of pleasure, pain, and so forth— is removed from the *jīva*, [liberation in] the supreme Śiva occurs.
The meaning is: why should liberation not consist of such a form? || 29 ||
Just as iron, when permeated by mercury, always becomes gold.
By means of a certain practice alone, the individual soul (jīva) may likewise become Śiva.
Thus some disputants speak out of their own delusion. || 30 ||

Since it is observed that even the tarnish on copper, once removed by acid, reappears after some time, one might suspect that the state of being a living being could likewise re-emerge in those who are liberated. Anticipating this objection, he dispels it with another illustration: "pierced by mercury. Just as, through the process of mercurial transmutation (*rasavedha*), the inherent nature of iron as iron is removed and it becomes gold itself.

It exists forever and not merely for a limited duration; likewise, the persistence of this [state] is such that liberation (śivasāyujya) occurs through the absolute cessation of even natural individuality (jīvatva). This is the meaning. || 30 ||
For that which is not contradicted and is established by itself does not perish. || 31 ||
Just as the inherent heat of fire never perishes.
Or rather, just as light [is not destroyed], so too for this [person], suffering and the like do not perish.

He refutes this with the words "that is not so. The meaning is as follows: since there is no destruction of heat, light, and so forth—which constitute its very nature—then the destruction of the inherent quality of being a living being (*jīvatva*) is likewise impossible.
This is due solely to the diversity of power inherent in jewels, mantras, medicinal substances, and so forth.
For that which is obstructed by a non-sacrificer is not considered "destroyed. || 33 ||

[Objection: "But surely we observe the cessation of the heat and light of Mount Meru through the power of gems, mantras, and so forth; likewise, due to the diversity of means, there may be a cessation even of the innate state of being a living soul (*jīvatva*). To this, he says: "The gem...
Just as in this case [of Meru], the moisture and so forth which constitute its very nature merely cease through the power of gems, mantras, and so forth, but are not actually destroyed. || 33 ||
Just as the impurity of copper is not destroyed by anything at all.

In the same way, he states the impossibility of the destruction of this copper, which is established by its own nature, with the words "Just as" (yathā). The meaning is that the ignorant—those people lacking wisdom—thinking they do not understand that [the copper] is merely obstructed, believe it has been destroyed. || 34 ||
And likewise, its state of being a living soul is characterized by pleasure, pain, and so forth.
It would be as if lost and obstructed, yet it is never destroyed by anyone.

He applies the stated point to the subject at hand with the words "jīvatvam" (the state of being a living soul). The meaning is that for the natural state of being a living soul, characterized by pleasure, pain, and so forth, there can only be an obstruction by some means; its destruction is not possible. || 35 ||
Water enveloped by milk is designated as "milk. || 36 ||
Silver, when pervaded by gold, is designated as "gold."
In the same way, by means of its taste and potency, and also through contact with fire, [it acts]. || 37 ||
O Jayas, the state of being gold-colored is not the same as the state of being gold itself at any time.
But when its taste and potency are destroyed, its color perishes as well. || 38 ||

Now, it was indeed stated by way of the analogy of alchemical transmutation (*rasavedha*) that even the natural state may be completely eliminated; to this, he replies with the verse beginning "payaḥ" (milk), etc.: just as water mixed with milk takes on the color of the milk, or as silver mixed with gold takes on the color of the gold, in the very same way, iron through contact with the essence and potency of mercury would become purely golden in color.
The connection is that iron sometimes possesses the nature of gold. || 36 || 37 || 38 ||
The established doctrine on this earth is that what is produced cannot be eternal.
Nevertheless, human beings, being exhausted, consider gold to be mere iron.
Now, one might object: "Since the potency (*rasa*) and efficacy (*vīrya*) are unfailing, they cannot be destroyed; therefore, how could the destruction of color (*varṇa*) caused by them occur?
To this he says: "Of that which is produced" (*kṛtakasya*). The meaning is that because the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—"whatever is produced is impermanent"—is everywhere unrestricted. || 39 ||
Indeed, error is easily incurred by those who lack subtle insight.
In that way, the state of Śiva will be established for the individual soul through another means. || 40 ||

"Likewise, the state of being Śiva [is not real]" means that just as there is the delusion of gold in iron due to seeing only its color while lacking subtle vision, so too the soul's nature as Śiva exists only through delusion and does not occur by way of ultimate reality. || 40 ||
By means of spiritual practice, the individual soul itself can never become Śiva in every respect.

Śiva alone becomes Śiva directly by his own nature; it is not otherwise. ||41||

[In the fourth section on the Glory of Sacrifice (Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa) — To the question "Why?", he says: "By means of the practice" (sādhanena). If, from the perspective of ultimate reality, the individual soul (jīva) were other than Śiva, his state of being Śiva could not be established even by a hundred practices; for mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva), being beginningless and endless, cannot be removed.

The meaning is that [the other case] is untenable. Therefore, he concludes the point already established—that the state of Śiva belongs to Śiva alone, and never at any time does the individual soul (jīva), who is distinct from him, possess the state of Śiva—by saying "tataḥ" (therefore). || 41 ||
Just as water, through contact with fire, is not actually fire in reality.
Even though it is commonly understood by embodied beings that "water is hot," the wise [know otherwise]. (42)
Likewise, O best of scholars, the individual soul (jīva) is sometimes inauspicious by its own nature.
Even if perceived as Śiva, one does not become Śiva by one's own nature. || 43 ||
Now, one might object: "Are not even liberated souls Śivas? However, these [souls] are liberated by His grace;
He alone is to be known as eternally liberated, possessing a body of five mantras."

Based on the authority of such statements as these, one might ask: "Why could even individual souls (*jīvas*), though inherently distinct [from the Supreme Lord], not attain the state of Śiva through the grace of the Supreme Lord? To this, he replies with the words beginning "Just as" (*yathaiva*). Even though the quality of heat, which belongs to fire, is perceived in water due to contact with it, water does not thereby become fire; rather, it is simply designated as "hot water."

Thus it is said: the meaning is that although the individual soul (jīva), which is distinct by its very nature, serves as the substratum for those attributes that constitute the nature of Śiva, it nevertheless does not possess the identity of Śiva. || 42 || 43 ||
But this individual soul (jīva), being inherently inauspicious, could never become auspicious in any way. || 44 ||
By that very means of accomplishment, one shall become equal to Śiva in liberation.
Thus do some disputants, the preeminent among sages, maintain.

Now, [the author] introduces and refutes the view of certain [thinkers] who maintain that liberation is not characterized by the soul’s identity with Śiva, but rather its similarity to Him—stating: "By nature, [the soul] is non-Śiva" (vv. 44–45).
This has been stated merely as a report; in every respect, it is not meaningful.
Are living beings equal [to others] by way of a single part, or rather, by their entire self? (46)

If [it were so] even in part, then all those dwelling in saṃsāra would be Śivas.

Thus begins the thirty-ninth chapter.

The Sūtasamhitā replies: "By a single part. This means that even for transmigrating individual souls (*jīvas*), [the identity with Śiva] exists by way of a single part, such as consciousness (*caitanyatva*). Śiva—
The meaning is that since equality indeed exists, they too would be liberated. || 47 ||
If there is equality in every respect, with his entire self, then he is indeed Śiva in every way.
Because it is devoid of any cause for differentiation and because there is an absence of differentiation in reality. || 48 ||

Nor is the second [alternative] possible; thus he says: "in every respect" (*sarvātmanā*). If it were intended that equality with Śiva exists in every single aspect, then such equality would be untenable. For the relationship of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) occurs only between two things that are distinct yet possess common attributes. With this in mind, he says: "due to difference" (*bhedena*). [This applies to] a soul that is equal in every respect.
Because there is an absence of any distinct form that could produce a difference between the two, and for this very reason there is no difference, the individual soul (jīva) is indeed Śiva himself;
the meaning is that he is not merely equal to Śiva. || 48 ||
Furthermore, if the individual soul were to become equal to Śiva in liberation, [what would be the consequence]?

Furthermore, in this view, it leads to the consequence that even liberation is impermanent—this is indicated by the word "furthermore" (kiṃca). || 49 ||
Therefore, the individual soul (jīva) is in itself directly Śiva, characterized by truth and other such qualities.
Remaining with his own essential nature unfallen, by means of the higher knowledge (paravidyā), || 50 ||
Swallowing one's own ignorance and the cycle of worldly existence born from it by means of one's own self.
By means of its own form as the perfect Śiva, it remains as itself alone.
Having thus refuted the nature of liberation as conceived by others, he concludes the established doctrine with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

Śiva himself, who is characterized by existence, knowledge, and so forth, being directly Śiva, assumes the state of various individual souls (*jīva*) through the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the diverse internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which are transformations of the category of existence (*sattva*); yet, because his own essential nature has not departed, he remains Śiva. And that soul—

The meaning is as follows: one who has attained such a state (*bhāvāpannaḥ*), through the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*) consisting in the realization of one's own self as being the nature of Paraśiva, dissolves by means of the fire of the Self alone both the ignorance in the form of an entity (*bhāvarūpājñāna*) that obscures one's true nature and its effect, which is transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). By that very perfection of one's own self as the nature of Śiva, one remains as oneself alone, and not as anything whatsoever characterized by existence or non-existence.
But silver in mother-of-pearl is [perceived] through the cognition of mother-of-pearl.
Just as in the world, it remains only in the form of mother-of-pearl. || 52 ||
He establishes this very point through an illustration: "As with mother-of-pearl," etc.

Just as when silver superimposed upon mother-of-pearl is removed by the knowledge of the operation of the substrate—mother-of-pearl—it is the mother-of-pearl itself, which constitutes the substrate, that remains.

Now, one might raise the objection of certain thinkers: "Since the world is not perceived in the state of liberation, its non-existence must exist; how then can it be said that only the substratum remains? He addresses this doubt with the words "by the nature of Śiva. In the state of liberation, the world persists solely as the form of the substratum, which is Śiva, and not in the form of an entity distinct from Him. This is what is meant.

This is possible; for the negation of either existence or non-existence is invariably concomitant with the affirmation of the other, since it is necessarily the case that if the world’s existence or non-existence were absent, its absence [of one or the other] would also be certain. Therefore, the intention [of the opponent] is this: if in liberation there is only the non-existence of the world and not its persistence as the nature of Śiva, how can it be said that only the substrate remains? || 53 ||
some maintain this view, but that is an error of those with dull intellects.
But that which has the nature of an existent entity, O twice-born ones, becomes a future reality.
The world is neither existence nor non-existence; it is distinct from both existence and non-existence.
Therefore, that which is sublated by sublation is neither an existent nor indeed a non-existent.
For there remains only the physical basis, O best of the wise.
Śiva is the substratum of the world-illusion by virtue of his true nature.

He refutes this with the words beginning "sa ca" (and that). That which is intended as the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*) of the world to non-existence is not tenable. For it is only things of a positive nature (*bhāvarūpa*), such as jars and cloths, that become counter-correlates of non-existence; the world, however, is not of a positive nature. If it were so, it would follow that it is non-sublatable (*abādhyatva*), since it would necessarily persist at all times like the Self (*ātman*). Nor is it of the nature of non-existence.

What [is it]? It cannot be like a human horn, for that never appears [to consciousness] due to its impossibility. Therefore, since it is otherwise inexplicable that there would be a contradiction with cognition (*pratīti-bādha*), it must be distinct from both existence and non-existence. Thus, the meaning is that because the world lacks the nature of a positive entity (*bhāva-rūpa*), it is not logical for it to be the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of non-existence.

Consequently, what is called the "sublation of the superimposed" (*adhyasta-bādha*) is nothing other than the remaining of the substratum alone (*adhiṣṭhāna-mātra-avaśeṣa*); it is not something else consisting of either existence or non-existence.

He concludes with the words "tasmāt" (therefore): "Something" [is what remains]. Since the silver and other things superimposed upon mother-of-pearl and the like lack the nature of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*), it is impossible for them to be the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) of a negation; therefore, one must necessarily accept that their sublation (*bādha*) consists solely in the persistence of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna-mātra*). Similarly, the sublation of the superimposed world also consists solely in the persistence of the substrate, and not in being the counter-correlate of a negation.

This is the meaning. This might be so if the world-appearance were practiced [as real] somewhere, like silver [in a shell]; however, it is not practiced there because a suitable substratum is impossible. In the excellence of the Vedas, in the excellence of Śiva, and likewise in the excellence of Vidyā;

But in the case of non-contradiction with the Vedas, one should proceed by the very path previously described.

The ignorant act according to their desires; in this matter, sin alone is the cause.
But when there is a decline of the Vedas, as well as of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and so forth, [the same applies].

Mahādeva, Veda, and likewise the horizontal *tripuṇḍra*.
"Those of evil birth, the heretics, say that it is utterly useless. (69)
The majesty of Mahādeva and the splendor of the Vedas as well.
And the greatness of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) cannot be described by me.
Some maintain that the section concerning Brahman is a mere supplement to the section on ritual action, because it involves effort.
The virtuous do not describe them as such; rather, they are deceivers. || 71 ||

Regarding the phrase "the state of being a remainder of karma": when one performs rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, which are the means for attaining results like heaven in the hereafter, one must necessarily understand that there exists some Self distinct from the body, because of the experience of those results. For [it is said]: "The experiencer is the body."

Thus, some maintain that the section on knowledge (*jñānakāṇḍa*) is subordinate to the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*) by means of establishing a self distinct from the body required for ritual action. However, this is not tenable, because the section on knowledge [deals with] the entirety of agency, enjoyership, and so forth, which are utilized in ritual action.

Anticipating the objection that [the Upanishads] are devoted to establishing the true nature of the Self as being devoid of the attributes of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), he says: "From exertion" (*āyāsāt*). This means that the collection of statements establishing the nature of the Self in the manner described would result in exhaustion, because they would have to be treated as objects of meditative worship (*upāsanā*). He refutes this with: "Not so. [He calls them] "deceivers," meaning [they are not deceivers, but rather revealers of truth]. "Brahma—"

"He attains the supreme Brahman; he who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself"; "That which is invisible and ungraspable"; "He pervaded all, pure, bodiless, and without breath"; "Other than dharma, other than adharma, other than this cause and effect"—of such passages, which are untouched even by the scent of injunctions for meditation and whose primary purport is to teach that the Self is not subject to transmigratory existence—[the meaning is] otherwise...
The meaning is that because they conceive of their own intentions [as truth], they are deceptive. || 71 ||
Agency, as well as enjoyership, the state of being enjoined, and the fruit of action.
It grasps the knowledge of Brahman; therefore, it does not have that [knowledge] as its subordinate element. || 72 ||

He provides the reason—that the relationship of principal and subordinate between knowledge and action is untenable—by means of the passage beginning with "If [there were] agency," etc. For knowledge of the Self, which is distinct from the body and characterized by agency, enjoyership, and so forth, requires action; however, the section on knowledge [the Jñānakāṇḍa] [deals with] the Self devoid of all transmigratory attributes such as agency and enjoyership.

It brings about the realization of the non-dual reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) as its primary purport, but not merely the nature of an agent-self distinct from the body. Thus, how could the knowledge of the non-dual Self according to the Upaniṣads— which dissolves all attributes such as agency and enjoyership that appear in the inner self (*pratyagātman*) due to the influence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and depend upon ritual action— be a subsidiary part of ritual action?

The intended meaning is that [the injunction] is obstructed. As for what is called *niyoga*: if the *apūrva* (unseen potency) is the object to be attained, then a person’s status as one to be enjoined (*niyojyatva*) consists in being the cognizer of that [object], while their agency (*kartṛtva*) consists in being its producer.

This has already been explained in detail previously in the twelfth chapter, under the verse: "And likewise, there is the state of being enjoined, as well as the state of being an agent and an enjoyer"; therefore, we shall desist from further elaboration.
Action yields meager gain, whereas knowledge bestows the full fruit.
That being so, O best of sages, how could that [universe] be subordinate to Him? || 73 ||

"Regarding the phrase *allāmamadam*: ritual action (*karman*) yields only a meager fruit, such as heaven, cattle, sons, and the like; however, wisdom (*vijñāna*) yields a perfect fruit characterized by the attainment of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*). For in the world, superiority is observed in the relationship between master and servant and so forth; therefore, knowledge possesses a superior fruit compared to that which has an inferior fruit."
The meaning is that it is not logical to say that [this] is a limb of action. || 73 ||

For it is established that an action without fruit is indeed subordinate to an action that bears fruit.
Knowledge is supreme because it pertains to the fruit; therefore, this [scriptural injunction] is subordinate to it. || 74 ||

Regarding the phrase "as if it were fruitful": for rites such as the *prayāja* offerings, which are themselves fruitless, their status as subsidiaries to the *āgneya* and other sacrifices—which do possess fruits—is observed on the basis of the principle that "that which is fruitless in the proximity of that which is fruitful is a subsidiary to it," due to the requirement of purpose (*kaimarthakya*). However, since knowledge has its own distinct fruit as established by scripture, it lacks any desire for further results; therefore, it does not stand as a subsidiary to anything else. This is the meaning.
For knowledge situated within the section on action is intended as an auxiliary to action.
Knowledge belongs to a different category; therefore, it cannot be subordinate to that [ritual action]. || 75 ||

Now, one might object: just as in the case of the subsidiary injunctions for the *prayāja* offerings, where the fruit mentioned in the supplementary portion—such as "this indeed serves as the armor of the sacrifice"—is considered a mere *arthavāda* (laudatory statement) according to the maxim "the mention of a fruit in a context of subsidiaries is an *arthavāda*," so too, since the fruit of knowledge would likewise be an *arthavāda*, why should it not be a subsidiary (*aṅga*) like the *prayāja*? To this, he says: "Because of the context of ritual action (*karmaprakaraṇa*)."

For, since the *mayājādi* (the *prayāja* offerings, etc. are recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, their relationship as subsidiary (*aṅga*) and principal (*aṅgin*) has been determined; therefore, it is appropriate that the mention of their fruit be considered a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). Knowledge (*jñāna*), however, does not stand within the context of any ritual action such that the mention of its fruit could be assumed to be an *arthavāda*. Therefore, due to this difference in context as well, knowledge is not a subsidiary part of ritual action.
This is the truth. || 75 ||
O wise ones, know that action has its fruit to be accomplished, while the knowledge of Brahman has its fruit already established.
That being so, O best of sages, how could there be such subservience? (76)

"Karma has its fruit to be accomplished," because heaven and so forth are produced by actions such as sacrifice and oblation. "Siddha-phala" (the fruit that is already established) means that the fruit to be attained through knowledge is the very nature of the Self, which is eternally pure, awakened, and liberated. || 76 ||
O best of sages, it has been set forth according to the distinction of those qualified [for its practice].
Therefore, how could the quality of one thing belong to another? || 77 ||

"By way of the distinction between qualified persons (*adhikāri-vibhedena*)" means that the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*) is intended for a qualified person characterized by a desire for fruits such as heaven or sons, whereas the section on knowledge (*jñānakāṇḍa*) proceeds by taking up a specific qualified person endowed with dispassion (*vairāgya*) and so forth. || 77 ||
As long as ignorance regarding karma exists, there is no such realization of Brahman.
That being so, O Brahmins, how can there be a combination of knowledge and action? (78)
He states that the relationship of principal and subordinate between knowledge and action is also untenable because they cannot coexist simultaneously: "Of action and ignorance...

Ignorance, which is the root of the entire manifold of misfortune and which conceals the true nature of the inner self as the ultimate Supreme Śiva, exists only when accompanied by its manifestation (*savilāsa*). It is only through the grace of that [ignorance] while it persists that action attains its own existence.

However, non-dual knowledge (*advaitajñāna*) manifests by subverting that ignorance (*ajñāna*). Thus, because knowledge and action are incompatible in their coexistence, their combination as auxiliary and principal elements (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) is not possible; this is the meaning. || 78 ||
Action is non-luminous by nature, whereas cognition is self-luminous.
But if that were so, O Brahmins, how could there be a combination of knowledge and action? (79)

"Of a non-luminous nature": since it is an effect of ignorance (*ajñāna*), karma is of a non-luminous nature; since its essence is Brahman, which is luminosity, knowledge (*jñāna*) is of a luminous nature. Thus, because their coexistence is impossible—just as between darkness and light—the meaning is: how can there be a combination of these two in the relationship of subordinate and principal? || 79 ||
Therefore, the portion of the Vedas known as the Brahmakāṇḍa is indeed the Vedānta.
In every respect, there is never any remainder whatsoever of the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa).

Thus, since it is untenable for knowledge to be a subsidiary part of ritual action, he concludes that the portion of the Vedānta which teaches that [knowledge] is not a subsidiary part of the section on rituals—“Therefore,” etc. (80).
In exactly the same way, the portion concerning ritual action is entirely subsumed within the section on Brahman.
The knowledge born from the Vedānta texts would not itself be the direct remainder [of the means of knowledge]. //81//

[Objection: "In that case, let the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*) simply be a subsidiary (*śeṣa*) to the section on knowledge (*jñānakāṇḍa*. To this he replies: "In the same way" (*tathaiva*).
Since a subsidiary relationship through a traditional succession will be explained later, he specifies [the distinction] by saying "not directly" (*na sākṣāt*) in order to exclude that possibility.

Do they attain the status of being auxiliary members (*aṅga*) by accomplishing a favorable operation, or rather, are they the instrument (*karaṇa*) for its production, and what is the difference between an auxiliary that assists the result (*phalopakāryaṅga*)?
He explains all of this in sequence, beginning with the words: "Knowledge born from the Vedānta texts," and so forth. (81)

Regarding the phrase "tranquility, self-control, and so forth": the term "and so forth" (ādi) includes qualities such as cessation (uparati) and the rest, as stated in the Vedic scripture beginning with, "He who is tranquil, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.23). || 82 ||
Reflection and contemplation likewise serve as auxiliaries to the fruit of knowledge.
Knowledge does not require assistance for the destruction of ignorance. || 83 ||

"Beneficial to the fruit of knowledge" means that it assists the fruit characterized by the generation of the knowledge whose object is the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, which is the result of *śravaṇa*—consisting of the inquiry into the meaning of the Vedānta texts—which functions as the instrument. For this very reason, it is revealed in scripture:
"Indeed, the Self, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon..."

"It must be heard," it is said. And that Śruti has been explained by the Teacher as follows: "With the vision of the Self as its goal, hearing (śravaṇa)—which is the principal member (aṅgin)—is enjoined by means of reflection (manana) and meditative absorption (nididhyāsana), which are its auxiliary members (aṅgas) that assist toward the fruit. || 83 ||
Just as the sun requires nothing else for the removal of darkness.

He establishes through an illustration that knowledge requires instruments, auxiliaries, and so forth only for its own origination, but does not require anything else for its own effect—thus: "In the cessation of darkness," etc. (84).
But for an action that perishes in a moment, the fruit consists of merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma).

The knowledge born from the Vedānta texts has as its object the oneness of Brahman and the Self.
It burns away all evil committed intentionally, like fire. || 2 ||

"Having as its object the identity of Brahman and the Self" means that it is the immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) produced by Vedāntic statements such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), which has as its object that ultimate unity resulting from the removal of the delusion of difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman caused by ignorance (*ajñāna*). Regarding the phrase "performed intentionally": for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is indeed the remover of only that which is performed unintentionally. [The non-dual Self...]
The meaning is that knowledge, whether performed intentionally or unintentionally by me, removes both types of sin.
He supports the fact that knowledge alone has the power to remove a multitude of various sins through an illustration: "like fire.
This is also recorded by the venerable Vyāsa:
"O Arjuna, a kindled fire reduces even wood piled along its path to ashes."
"Even so, the fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes. || 2 ||
"O best among those who know the Vedas, action indeed binds the agent."
The Knower has no agency whatsoever, for he is the witness of agency.
He establishes that knowledge possesses the promised power of removing all sins, beginning with the words "the agent" (*kartāram*) and so forth.
In the world, it is indeed only for the agent—such as Yajñadatta—that there is bondage, consisting of the connection between one's own performed actions and their fruits;

it is not for the non-agent, such as Devadatta. Thus, one who knows the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self [realizes] the nature of the witness-consciousness alone (*sākṣicinmātrasvarūpa*).

If the Self were also an agent, then it would follow that it must possess the characteristic of being the locus of merit and demerit, which is based on its connection with the attribute of agency. Yet, the Self does not possess agency; rather, by virtue of being their witness, it maintains neutrality like an extraordinary witness. For, standing as a mediator between two contending parties, it merely observes the proceedings characterized by victory and defeat.
It perceives [the agent] directly, yet it is not conjoined with those two. The meaning is that, likewise, there is no conjunction of the witness (sākṣin) with agency.

This is the intended sense: so-called agency is the state of being the substratum of action; and that is not possible for the all-pervading, eternal Self, because, like space, it is devoid of action. If it were the substratum of that [action],...

Furthermore, it would entail the consequence of impermanence according to the principle: "For a property that has arisen brings about a transformation in the substratum. Nor can the body be the agent; for although it is the locus of action, such agency is untenable because it is insentient.
Indeed, only a sentient being becomes an agent by performing actions in succession, possessing the cognition: "This is a means to achieve my desired end."

If agency belonged to the body alone, then because that body—the substratum of actions such as sacrifice—would be reduced to ashes, the fruits of heaven, hell, and so forth, which are to be experienced by the self in another world, would be without a cause for the non-agent who is distinct from the body;
for there is the rule: "The fruit belongs only to the agent. And thus says the supreme aphorism: "The fruit of the scripture [belongs] to the performer..."

"In an instant," it says. Nor should it be argued that agency belongs to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone as something distinct from the body; for even though the vital breath exists during the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), specific cognition is not observed there, and thus the aforementioned defect persists due to its insentience. Nor [does it belong] to the eye... [etc. (as previously cited).

The sense organs alone possess agency, because as instruments (*karaṇa*), they necessarily imply an agent distinct from themselves. For this very reason, even the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) lacks agency. Now, if it is argued that agency does not consist merely in being the substratum of action—which would exclude the inactive Self—but rather consists in being the substratum of the quality of effort (*prayatna*), then [agency belongs] to the conscious [Self].

If it is asked, "Why should the self not be the agent?", it is not so. For if the self were the substratum of qualities characterized by effort—which involve approaching and departing—then, according to the reasoning previously stated, the self would be subject to modification and consequently would be non-eternal.
Therefore, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, and so forth, which others consider to be attributes of the self, [must be understood as internal states].

It must be admitted, even by one who does not wish it, that all perceived phenomena are modifications of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) alone, and not of the immutable Self (*ātman*). For this very reason, the scripture declares the qualitylessness (*nirguṇatva*) of the Self as the witness:
"The witness, the cognizer, solitary and devoid of qualities. And thus, for others as well, [the cycle of] transmigratory existence...

The perception of the association with attributes characterized by agency within the Self is based solely on the superimposition of identity with the body and other factors that serve as the locus of action—just as in the expression "the iron burns"—and is not ultimately real. For this very reason, the scripture declares that the Self, when qualified by the aggregate of the body and so forth, possesses the status of an enjoyer: "The wise say that the Self, joined with the senses and the mind, is the enjoyer."
Thus it is said; and it is also recorded in the Gītās:
"The locus, the agent, and the various instruments,
the diverse and distinct activities, and the divine as the fifth factor in this regard."

"Whatever action a person undertakes through body, speech, or mind—whether it be righteous or its opposite—these five are its causes. Thus, by means of the knowledge that discriminates between the Self and the non-Self, there occurs the cessation of the superimposition of identity with the attributes of the body and so forth; consequently, those attributes—

It is established that there is a cessation of the association with attributes such as being the locus of real action; for the Self, which is the witness, whose nature is pure consciousness, and who is absolute, is a non-agent. For it is recorded [in scripture]: "In this situation, he who [perceives] the isolated Self alone as the agent..."
"He sees, yet because his intellect is unrefined, that dull-witted person does not truly see."

Thus, it is established that because the solitary, non-agent Self has no connection with action, even hundreds of sins committed through the habitual identification with the body and so forth do not touch it; therefore, the power of self-knowledge to remove all evil is proven. || 3 ||
Action is indeed bodily, vocal, and mental; it is not otherwise.
That being so, how could there be karma for one whose nature is that of a witness?

He establishes this very agency with the words beginning "bodily" (*kāyika*) and so forth. Action, existing in three ways through the distinctions of bodily and so on, binds only the one whose nature is action—that is, the one who possesses the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of identification with the body and other such things—and not the one who possesses discriminative knowledge (*viveka-jñāna*).

[The nature of the Self] is characterized by being without attributes (*nalakṣaṇa*) and characterized by the removal of impurity (*malāpakarṣaṇalakṣaṇa*). This is because, even during the state of worldly manifestation (*jagadramāva*), there is in reality an absence of impurity—which is produced by contact with the effects of ignorance—just as there was in the prior and subsequent states; therefore, it is pure by its very nature.

The meaning is that even the refinement characterized by the removal of impurities (*malāpakarṣaṇa*) is useless in that regard; nor is it an object to be produced (*utpādya-karma*). Having thus established the falsity of the phenomenal world of effects, [the author now shows that] even ignorance, which is its cause, does not exist in reality within that [Brahman].

He says it is "stainless" (*nirmala*) to show that [it does not exist]. For a cause must be conceived in accordance with its effect, and since the effect is seen to be illusory (*mithyā*), the ignorance (*ajñāna*) conceived as its cause must likewise be of the same nature; thus, the meaning is that even that [ignorance] does not exist in reality at any time within Him. In this way, due to the absence of a connection with ignorance, there is also no connection with the activity that is its manifestation.

He says it does not exist: "nirasta" (cast off). Regarding "nirlepa" (untainted): the meaning is that because there is no contact with action according to the method already stated, it is free from the taint of merit and demerit produced thereby. For this very reason, the Blessed One said: "Actions do not taint Me;
nor have I any longing for the fruit of action."
Thus [it is said]. Now, one might ask: why is such a reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) not experienced by everyone?

To this he says: "subtle. Because of the abundance of obstacles produced by obstructive sins, those with unrefined minds who perceive only the gross are unable to see the reality of the Self, which is absolutely free from conceptual construction (*atyanta-nirvikalpaka*) due to the absence of any cause for conceptualization.
Such is the meaning. || 22 || 23 || 24 ||
That which has its own distinct characteristics negated by the Vedāntas through the formula "not this, not this."
Seeing the self by means of the self, how could one be slain by karma?

Having stated that [Brahman] is devoid of everything, he elaborates this through scriptural corroboration with the words "not this, not this" (*neti neti*). Having introduced the subject with, "There are indeed two forms of Brahman: the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*)," it continues, "Now, therefore, follows the instruction: 'not this, not this,'" referring to the formed [and the formless].
Since the negation of the entire expansion of non-self consisting of formed things is heard in scripture, the meaning is that nothing exists apart from one's own Self.
Without debt, not short, not thick, not long, consisting of truth, consciousness, and bliss.
Seeing the self by means of the self, how could one be slain by karma?
It is shown that the very absence of all attributes, such as the taint of merit and demerit mentioned above, is established by the authority of the Śruti:

"anaṇvahasvam" (neither atomic nor gross). By the passage beginning with, "O Gārgī, the Brāhmaṇas declare this indeed to be that Imperishable: neither gross, nor atomic, nor short, nor long, nor red," there is the exclusion of what is not that [Brahman], by way of being the limit for the negation of all attributes such as grossness.

The meaning is that it has been established by what was heard from the mouth [of the teacher]. Now, one might object: "If all phenomena (dharmas) are thus negated, does this not ultimately result in mere emptiness (*śūnya*), for there could be nothing whatsoever that is devoid of attributes? To this, he says: "It is the forest of Being-Consciousness" (*sat-cid-vanam*).
That through the penetration of which the entire world is conceived as existing and appearing—that pure Being-Consciousness (*sac-cin-mātra*), the substratum of all, remains.

The meaning is that it does not terminate in emptiness (*śūnya*). Nor is there any suspicion of a difference between existence (*sat*) and consciousness (*cit*), because the two are one and the same; this is the meaning of the word "solid" (*ghana*).

For this very reason, its state of being a single essence (*ekarasa*) is taught through the analogy of a lump of salt: "In this very way, indeed, this great being is infinite, boundless, and nothing but a mass of consciousness. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.12) || 26 ||
