By means of karma produced by the causal factors (kārakas), such as the agent (kartṛ) and others, which arise from ignorance (ajñāna).
How can the lamp of self-knowledge, produced by the sacred revelation (śruti), be extinguished? || 27 ||

Regarding the phrase "born of ignorance" (*ajñānajanyā*): Since all [action] must be the effect of ignorance—given that the knowledge of the factors of action (*kāraka*), such as the agent, instrument, and object, is required to accomplish an act—and since ignorance is removed by the knowledge of the true nature (*yāthātmya*) of Brahman, the substratum, it follows that through the removal of the material cause (*upādāna*), the action which is its effect is also necessarily removed. Thus, how can there be [an effect] from an action that lacks its own essential form (*niḥsvarūpa*)?

For one who contemplates their own self as having Brahman as its essence, there is no fear of bondage; the meaning is that just as a snake, once its nature as a rope has been known, does not produce delusion in a person, so it is here. || 27 ||
It consists of the blinding darkness of ignorance, characterized by karma, dharma, and so forth.
The self, being self-luminous, is not at all capable of touching itself.

Thus, having relied upon the relationship between knowledge and ignorance as that which is to be removed and that which removes, it was stated that there is an absence of bondage for those who possess knowledge. Now, by reflecting on the true nature of that [knowledge], he says—beginning with "ajñāna"—that even contact with ignorance is impossible for the Self. Ignorance is indeed like darkness, an obscuring entity that persists for a long time and is opposed to light; it is not, however, [a positive entity].

The meaning is as follows: such being the case, how could the absence of knowledge—which is established in the form of an effect consisting of action, its means, and its fruit—touch that self which is consciousness, self-luminous, and opposed to it? || 28 ||
Just as the darkness of night does not touch the sun by its own nature, so too [it does not touch] that which has been given.
Likewise, the activity whose nature is darkness [conceals] the great sun that is the light of consciousness. || 29 ||

He establishes this very point by means of an illustration, beginning with the words "ādityam" (the sun). Having refuted the view that the darkness of Śiva is merely the absence of light, its status as a positive entity (*bhāvatva*) has been established:
"Darkness is indeed mobile, blue, and possesses the distinction of being higher and lower."
"Because of its dissimilarity to well-known substances, it deserves to be distinguished from the nine [substances]."
In the same way, since ignorance (ajñāna) is also of a positive nature (bhāvarūpa), this is the intention of one who designates ignorance by the word "darkness" (tamaḥ). || 29 ||
Rahu, whose nature is darkness, is perceived as having resorted to the sun.
Even though there is no connection between those two and that which illuminates them, nevertheless— || 30 ||
Relying upon that ignorance and its effects, [it appears] as self-luminous.
Their connection shines as if they were clothed in that [relation], even though such a relation does not actually exist between them. || 31 ||

One might object: "If ignorance has no contact with the self, which is consciousness that is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa-cidātman*), how can it be perceived during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*)?
Anticipating this doubt, the author establishes the point through an illustration, beginning with the words "tamorūpa" (having the nature of darkness).
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "it is perceived by the light of that [sun] which is its very essence. Even though this is so, nevertheless...
There is no mutual connection between the two; for Rāhu exists at a distance of a hundred thousand suns away, being separated by such a vast interval.

Just as Rāhu is perceived through the light of the sun despite the absence of any actual connection—by virtue of its dependence on that [perceiving] substratum—in the same way, the effect of ignorance, though unattached and indifferent, rests upon the self-luminous conscious Self and shines by means of its light.
The meaning is that, by that much alone, there is in reality no connection between the two. || 30 || 31 ||
Due to ignorance, one falsely imagines a connection with karma for the self because of mental exhaustion.
Therefore, there is no delusion for the wise; consequently, there is no connection with karma. ||32||

Now, one might object: "But has not the connection of the inner self (pratyagātman) with action been established by the Śruti itself in such passages as, 'For he alone makes him perform good deeds'? To this, [the author] says: "Action... The connection of the self with action arises solely from the delusion of identifying with the body and so forth, which is caused by ignorance; it is not real. This is the meaning of the cited Śruti passage.

The intent [of the scripture] is to establish that the Lord does not bestow fruits by depending upon that very [ignorance], which is established as His own delusion. However, for the knower, because ignorance—the root of delusion—is removed through higher knowledge (paravidyā), there is no connection with karma; this is the meaning. ||32||
Therefore, he who indeed forms the notion of "I" with respect to the aggregate of the body and so forth—
O wise ones, for one who is thus perpetually deluded, there is a constant engagement with that very same karma.
But for one who is endowed with wisdom, his association is through action.
What I have spoken is indeed the truth; there is no cause for doubt.

Thus, he concludes the point already established— that the connection with karma belongs only to one who possesses the delusion of identity with the body and so forth, and not to one who is distinct from that and possesses pure knowledge of the Self— with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt). Vyāsa also records in the Smṛti the absence of connection with karma for one who is devoid of the conceit of "I" regarding the body and so forth:
"He whose state of being is free from egoism, whose intellect is not tainted—
even having slain these worlds, he does not kill, nor is he bound."
Thus [ends the section]. 33 || 34 ||

The meaning is that the indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*)— which has as its object the identity of the individual soul and the Supreme Self (*jīvaparatādātmya*), which is taught by the teacher, produced by the Vedāntic statements,
and free from doubt— even when it is preceded by the intellect, burns away the entire web of sins.
The direct realization of the Self is verbal knowledge preceded by a teacher.
He is the sun that shatters the egg of the darkness of ignorance, which is the cause of saṃsāra.

Regarding the phrase "direct knowledge of the Self": since the ignorance consisting of the body, senses, and so forth—which are the effects of that [ignorance]—appears as non-different from the Self, its cessation is impossible except through the direct knowledge of the true nature of the Self. By means of indirect (parokṣa) knowledge, there is only the destruction of the mass of sins, which are the effects of ignorance, just as by means of expiation; however, the root ignorance itself is not destroyed.

The meaning is that the direct knowledge of Brahman as one's own Self destroys, along with its root, the positive entity of ignorance (bhāvarūpājñāna), which is the cause of transmigratory existence and the source of all misfortunes falsely superimposed upon one's own Self. || 36 ||
O lords of sages, [this applies] to those who have committed major sins (mahāpātaka) and other transgressions (pātaka).
For the expiation of well-known secrets is indeed their knowledge.

Having thus described the twofold nature of the realization of Brahman as the Self in terms of being indirect (*parokṣa*) and direct (*aparokṣa*), he states there that indirect knowledge serves as a form of expiation (*prāyaścitta*): "mahāpātaka... (verse 37).
For those who possess direct realization of the Self, no sin exists at all.

"There is no sin. For if there were sin, an expiation would have to be performed to avoid it; however, through the direct realization of the nature of Paraśiva by the inner self—which is pure consciousness (cinmātra) distinct from the body and so forth—ignorance (avidyā), which veils that true nature, is removed. Consequently, since agency and other such qualities, which are its effects, cease to exist, there is simply no possibility of sin at all.

The meaning is that the fruit of immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) is precisely the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). 712 Sūta said:
The Forty-Fourth Chapter, together with the *Tātparyadīpikā*— [In the fourth section,
the *Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa*]— now begins.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the purification of substances in brief.
O best of Brahmins, listen with faith for the sake of purifying the self.

Having taken for granted the inherent purity of the Self, whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*sac-cid-ānanda*), the expiation that removes the multitude of defects— which consist of the manifestations of ignorance (*avidyā*) and its effects superimposed upon that very nature— has been stated. Now, in order to establish that inherent purity of the Self, he proposes the purification of substances (*dravya-śuddhi*).
Now, therefore: || 1 ||
O best of brahmins, substance is established as twofold: self and non-self.
The substance of the Self is itself pure, characterized by truth, knowledge, and so forth.

"Substance is established. Here, the word *dravya* (substance) is a synonym for *vastu* (entity), and not one whose basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is the universal (*jāti*) "substanceness" (*dravyatva*) as postulated by others; for if that were the case, the Self would not be denotable by the word *dravya*, since it lacks a connection with the universal "substanceness. Indeed, existence (*satya*), consciousness (*jñāna*), bliss (*ānanda*), and so forth, constitute the ultimate nature (*svarūpa*) of the Self. Although...

Although it is thus an indivisible, single essence, it is nevertheless conventionally designated as "Being," "Consciousness," and so forth, due to the distinctions of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), because it is forever free from sublation.
As the Teacher has said: "Bliss, the experience of objects, and eternity are attributes;
though non-different from Consciousness, they appear as if distinct. (2)
There is no fault in mere existence, because it is eternally pure by its very nature.
If existence were inherently impure, then everything would always be defiled. (3)

In this regard, he establishes the inherent purity of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) with the words "mere existence" (*sattāmātra*). Because the form of Being (*sad-rūpa*), which is the substratum, persists through the various individual entities imagined within itself, that very Being which constitutes the substratum is, with that intention, called "existence" (*sattā*). Since the inherent purity of that mere existence must be admitted, therefore, in that case...

The meaning is that there is no contact with defects. He states the refutation for the opposite case [the *vipakṣa*] with the words "if existence" (*yadi sattā*). "Inherently" (*svataḥ*) means by its own nature alone, without depending on any other cause. || 3 ||
Indeed, that which is touched by the wicked is always defiled through its connection with the existence of the wicked.
That being the case, nothing whatsoever can be established as pure.

The intention is that everything considered doubtful is defective because it has not been touched by the perceived reality, just like a *māṇḍava* (a wooden vessel) that has been touched [but not verified] by what is seen.
Thus, the meaning is that for purity—which is pervaded by the absence of defects—there is no acquisition of its own nature anywhere [if it is merely suspected]. || 4 ||
Sāṃtakha. | 1. svataḥ | 2. Rā. Gha. 'dānanda' | 3. Cha. 'vibhā' | 4. Ḍa. yeṇādo Ga. Gha.

[page 388]
That which is devoid of existence is insubstantial, whereas pure existence is likewise self-evident.
Even knowledge in the form of cognition is always pure in itself.

Regarding the phrase "but [the world] is empty of existence": if the entire world were to abandon its contact with defective existence because it is itself free from defect, then it would become entirely formless (nirupākhyam). Therefore, the inherent purity of existence must be accepted.
[The word] *sparśaḥ* [is used]. He states the inherent purity even of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*)—[using the term] "knowledge" (*jñāna*).

Since it is possible to derive the meaning of "knowledge" as an instrument (an act of knowing) from the etymology "that by which something is known," he adds the qualifier "of the nature of apprehension" (*jñaptirūpa*) in order to exclude that [instrumental sense]. || 5 ||
For impurity is indeed perceived by everyone even in that which has an insentient form.
If knowledge, which is by nature self-luminous, were to become defective, [it would not be valid]. (6)
Everything would indeed become corrupt through association with the throbbing of the corrupt.
That being the case, nothing at all could ever be established as pure.

"Impurity is of the nature of insentience (*jaḍa*). For in the manifold of non-self (*anātma-prapañca*), impurity is seen to be pervaded by insentience; thus, that [insentience], being excluded from the self-luminous conscious Self (*svaprakāśa-cid-ātman*), also excludes the impurity pervaded by it.
Regarding this as well, he states the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) for the contrary position (*vipakṣa*), as before, with the words "knowledge would be defective," and so forth. || 6 || 7 ||
But an object devoid of manifestation would always be utterly non-existent.
If one were to say that there is a fault in cognition because of a defective cause, || 8 ||
However, there is no fault in cognition arising from its manifestor, nor is there any [fault] inherent in itself.
Otherwise, all knowledge would be inherently defective by its very nature.
Therefore, knowledge, which is of the nature of radiance, is indeed always pure.
"But it is not devoid of manifestation. Since the establishment of an object depends upon the cognition whose domain it is,
and since that cognition is admitted to be defective, the world— which has never been perceived— would become as utterly non-existent as a hare's horn.

[Objection: There is a contradiction [with experience]. Having stated the refutation regarding the contrary position, he anticipates and dispels the suspicion that defects may still exist in cognition by saying "due to defective causes" (*duṣṭakāraṇa*).
One observes defects in erroneous cognitions such as the perception of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, which are produced by causes like the eyes impaired by defects such as cataracts (*kāca*);
on the basis of this analogy, why should there not be a possibility of defects in other cases as well? [Response: This is not to be suspected.

It must be explained as follows: for in that case, it is not the manifestation of consciousness delimited by a mental modification (*vṛtti*) that is produced by a defective cause; rather, it is the very modification of ignorance (*avidyāvṛtti*) residing in the consciousness of the mind (*cittacaitanya*), which—like a mental modification based on the "this-ness" regarding illusory silver supported by Maya and manifesting the consciousness underlying the locus of the "sour thing"—is produced by a defective cause.
Consequently, due to the influence of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), redness appears in the crystal, and likewise, defect appears in the manifestation (*sphuraṇa*).

[In the fourth section on the Glory of Sacrifice (Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa)]:

"Appearance, but not the intrinsic nature"—this is the meaning. "Otherwise" means: if one were to accept that the mere manifestation residing in the cognition of rest is intrinsically defective by its very nature, then, by analogy with that, all cognition would also be intrinsically defective. And so it follows:
The intended meaning is that there is a contradiction with what was stated previously. || 8 || 9 ||
But bliss itself is pure, since it is that which is desired by the person.
Indeed, an impure state is not perceived by persons in any way whatsoever. || 10 ||
For from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, happiness is always sought after.

He establishes the inherent purity of bliss as well, beginning with the words "But bliss... and so forth. Because it is sought after by persons, the inherent purity of bliss must also be accepted; for an impure object is not desired by persons. (10–11)
For pleasure is always produced from the contact between the sense objects and the senses.
If it is argued that "therefore no evil is seen," that is not tenable.
For a fault resides in pleasure only through its manifesting function, and not by its own nature.
The nature of the self is bliss and eternal; it is certainly not subject to birth and destruction.
Having raised the doubt that the bliss [experienced] by all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass is perishable, he explains it as follows:
"By means of objects and senses," etc. Happiness is produced through the contact of the senses with objects presented by virtuous karma;
yet it is not seen in the very next moment. Thus, since happiness possesses the qualities of arising and perishing, [it is impermanent].

The intention of the doubt is that [pleasure] would be defective. Since only a mental modification (*manovṛtti*) directed toward pleasure as its object is produced through the contact of the sense organ with its object, and not the pleasure itself as delimited by that modification, it is only the birth and destruction residing in the manifesting modification (*vyañjakavṛtti*) that appear to belong to the manifested pleasure (*vyaṅgyasukha*). Therefore, the consequence of the defect of perishability does not apply to intrinsic pleasure (*svābhāvikasukha*).

Regarding the phrase "in the purity of food" (*āhāra-śuddhau*): the meaning is that when the food, which serves as the cause, is pure, there also occurs the purity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is its effect in the form of its transformation. "For one whose mind is purified by action, there is the vision of the Truth."

When the supreme knowledge of the Lord exists, the causes of saṃsāra [cease].
But the knots are destroyed; indeed, there is no cause for doubt.

Regarding the phrase "the knots": just as there is a connection between two lumps of clay, the first knot is the delusion of identity caused by ignorance (*ajñāna*) between the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is a transformation of existence (*sat-tva*), and consciousness (*caitanya*). The second is the superimposition of a relationship with the Self, based on the identification of the Self with the substrate (*dharmin*) of the attributes of the internal organ, such as agency and enjoyership.

The other [type of knot] is that which consists of the identification with the gross body and so forth by means of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) pervaded by consciousness; this is the "other. And these are called "knots" because they are the causes of the bondage of transmigratory existence for the Self, which in the ultimate sense is free from attachment. Consequently, when the root ignorance is removed through the direct realization of the nature of the individual self as Paraśiva, the knots—which are its effects—are likewise destroyed.
The meaning is that they cease entirely through the cessation of grasping (*upādāna*). And thus it is chanted in the *Chāndogya*:
"When food is pure, the mind-stuff (*sattva*) becomes pure; when the mind-stuff is pure, there is mindfulness; from the attainment of mindfulness comes the liberation from all knots. || 3 ||

This very point—that pure food is a means to liberation through a gradual process—is established by way of its opposite (vyatireka) in the verse beginning with "abhakṣya": "By impurity, deluded cognition [arises]. Through impure food, one becomes defiled; thus, in this saṃsāra characterized by impurity, suffering, and so forth, there arises a deluded cognition characterized by notions of permanence and purity.

The status of the former as a cause has also been set forth by the Naiyāyikas in their aphorism: "Upon the successive disappearance of suffering, birth, activity, defects, and false knowledge, there follows the disappearance of each preceding one, resulting in liberation. (NS 1.1.2) || 5 || 6 ||

Regarding the term "embodied beings" (*dehin*): the aforementioned discrimination between what is fit to be eaten and what is not fit to be eaten applies only to one who lacks discriminative knowledge (*viveka-jñāna*) and who identifies with the threefold body—gross, subtle, and causal. The Sūtasamhitā (7.25) establishes this very state of being the self of all: "I am food," and so forth. For everything consists of the nature of both the enjoyer and the enjoyed.

The meaning is this: since this entire world is imagined within oneself through ignorance, when it dissolves right there upon the realization of the true nature of one's own essence—including all its causal adjuncts—the contemplation of both the enjoyer and the enjoyed as being nothing but one's own self is indeed the knowledge of Brahman. Thus it is declared in the sacred tradition: "I am food, I am food, I am food; I am the eater of food."

"I am a devourer of food, I am a devourer of food. Having thus demonstrated the impossibility of avoiding what is unfit for consumption, he establishes, on the contrary, that everything is indeed fit for consumption: "The knower of Brahman," etc. (8).

The meaning is that for one who swallows the entire world as being nothing but his own self, the entire world becomes merely food. || 9 ||
The nature of Brahman shines forth for the knower through the realization of that [knowledge].
If that were so, the world would indeed become food for the one possessing knowledge.

Regarding the phrase "of the nature of Brahman": for that person who possesses knowledge of the Self of all, this entire universe appears as the nature of Brahman by virtue of the experience of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*). This being so, the meaning is that because the perceived universe is swallowed by his own Self, it becomes the food (*bhojya*) of that knower. || 10 ||
When it shines as the self of the world, then it becomes the object of enjoyment.
When everything shines as one's own self, then it is undecaying. || 11 ||

He explains this very point with the words "by being the self of the world" (*jagadātmatayā*). When the world, consisting of name and form, which is superimposed upon Brahman whose nature is existence (*sad-rūpa*), appears— having acquired its own existence through the contact with the existence of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) in that state of cognition— then, in that state, there is no separate existence for the superimposed world apart from the existence of the substrate.

Because the knower of such [truth] contemplates the world as being essentially the Self that is pure Being (sanmātra-brahmātman), and because it is impossible to avoid what is inedible since it lacks separate existence, for him the entire world becomes solely food. However, when, in the state of sublation (bādhāvasthā), the entire world is [realized as] one's own Self because the ignorance and its effects have been removed through the knowledge of identity with the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna-sāmānādhikaraṇya).

By that [consciousness], through the inner self (pratyagātman) which has become the ultimate limit of speech and constitutes one's own true nature, [the world] shines forth as nothing but the pure Brahman-self;

the meaning is that it does not shine as having the nature of name and form. At that time, because the entire universe is dissolved into one's own self, which is pure Being (sanmātra), it becomes non-existent [as an object]. || 11 ||

Regarding the phrase "its own essential nature" (*svasvarūpam*): since, according to the manner explained above, the entire world is nothing other than the very self of the knower, it is the Self itself—conceptualized through the forms of objects—that one experiences by oneself; there is no such thing as an "object of consumption" (*bhojya*) separate from the Self that could be distinguished and prescribed as either edible or inedible. Now, [an objection]: [The text continues: "But..."

Having raised the objection that the objects of enjoyment—sound, touch, and so forth—must exist as something distinct from the enjoying Self (*ātman*), he refutes it with the words "If it exists" (*asti cet*). If there is an object of enjoyment, then because it is permeated by existence (*astitva*), like a jar or a cloth, it is in reality Brahman alone, whose nature is existence; for existence is indeed its defining characteristic. As it is said: "If one knows 'Brahman exists'... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1).

This is because of such scriptural passages as, "Those who perceive [it] as 'it exists,'" and so forth. Therefore, the meaning is that only the existence of the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) appears within the superimposed object of enjoyment (bhojya), and thus it has no separate existence of its own. || 15 ||
Existence, characterized by being, is eternally Brahman and nothing else;

One might object: "How can 'existence' (astitva), which is enumerated as the second modification of being in the sequence 'it is born,' 'it exists,' 'it transforms,' etc., be of the nature of Brahman, which is devoid of modification? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Existence" (astiteti). Here, what is intended is not a modification of being, but rather existence (sattā) as its cause; and that is nothing other than Brahman itself, not something different from it.
He states that the "universal" (jāti) postulated by others is empty, saying: "It does not exist. (16)
If it exists as something distinct from existence, then like space, it is indeed empty.

If existence (*sattā*) were itself the universal (*jāti*), then some other manifestor (*vyañjaka*) of it would necessarily have to be admitted. But that is not possible;
for a manifestor distinct from existence must, by necessity, exist at the very first moment prior to the manifestation of existence.
At that time, because there is no connection with existence and because it lacks existence in itself, it would be as void as a hare's horn. Therefore...

The meaning is that because no defining characteristic (*vyañjaka*) can be established, Brahman alone as pure existence (*sanmātra*) is called "Being" (*sat*) due to its pervasion through the various individual manifestations (*vyakti*) superimposed upon itself; it is not the "universal" (*jāti*) postulated by others. This has been explained in detail in the fifteenth chapter with the verse beginning, "That existence which shines is one," and so forth. "There is no *māyā*" means that [Brahman] is not the cause of the insentient phenomenal world (*jaḍaprapañca*).

Māyā, which is distinct from Brahman, does not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*). Since the causal principle is postulated as being of a nature corresponding only to its effect—the phenomenal world (*kāryaprapañca*)—which is itself non-substantial (*avastubhūta*), he says "unexamined" (*avicārita*). For *māyā* is a power that deludes all people, consisting of a form that cannot withstand examination as to whether it is real or unreal; this is because such a thing is observed in the case of magicians and the like. This is the meaning.

To resolve the contradiction regarding the relationship between action and its agent that was stated, he raises an objection with the words "by means of a division of parts" (*aṃśabhedeneti*). [The nature of] substance and consciousness...

The meaning is that since the self (*ātman*) is indeed form (*rūpa*), it possesses visibility through its substantial aspect (*dravyāṃśa*) and the status of being a seer (*draṣṭṛtva*) through its cognitive aspect (*bodhāṃśa*);

thus, because agency (*kartṛtva*) and objecthood (*karmatva*) are established as distinct, there is no contradiction. He refutes this with the words "distinction of parts" (*aṃśabheda*). For, given the admission that the self is a partless substance (*niravayavadravya*), if one were to postulate a distinction of parts, it would follow that it is possessed of parts (*sāvayava*).

The meaning is that, due to its lack of attachment, it would necessarily be non-self (anātman), just like a wall or similar objects. Even granting this for the sake of argument, he refutes it with the words "a division of parts" (aṃśabheda). That part of the self which consists of the substance that is the object of vision is non-self because it is visible, being similar to a wall and so forth; whereas the part which is the substratum of the activity of the root *dṛś* (to see) is of the nature of consciousness (cidātmaka).

That alone is the Self. Therefore, the meaning is that the state of being a seer can never belong to the seer [itself]. Now, one might object: "It is held that the inner self is pure consciousness (cinmātra) alone, distinct from the internal organ and so forth; and since that [consciousness] consists in the very meaning of the verbal root *dṛś* (to see), it cannot logically be its own substratum, and thus the state of being a seer is impossible. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even in the aspect of the seer... [The state of being] an agent...

"Name" refers to the state of being the locus of action (*kriyā*). Due to its connection with the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the internal organ characterized by that [effort], the appearance of agency is said to manifest even in the Self—which is pure consciousness in its essential nature within the aspect of the seer—just as redness appears in a crystal. The meaning is that even that quality of being a seer (*draṣṭṛtva*) within it is adventitious (*aupādhika*), consisting of [the reflection of] the intellect. He states another alternative: "I am seen as manifest.

Even though the conscious Self (*cit-ātman*), which is of the nature of pure seeing, is not the locus of action, its status as a seer is merely figurative (*aupacārika*) because it is the cause of the manifestation of the intellect, and not inherent (*svābhāvika*). || 34 || 35 ||

Now, having raised the objection that there might be an apprehension of the object of cognition due to its connection with consciousness (*cit*), he refutes it with the word "vid" (consciousness).

Even from the relationship between the light of consciousness and its own object—characterized as the relation of subject and object—the manifestation of the phenomenal world (*cetaprapañca*) is not tenable. He states the reason for this: "because of its non-existence" (*tasyābhāvāt*). Of such a [relationship]...

Since the relation itself cannot be established—given that a relation characterized as the subject-object relationship (viṣaya-viṣayibhāva) must be rooted in another underlying relation, and that if such a root is not admitted, the rule that "this very object belongs to this cognition" would be untenable—an underlying relation must necessarily be asserted. And that [relation] is characterized as conjunction (saṃyoga), inherence (samavāya), identity (tādātmya), and so forth. Consequently, such a [relation] between cognition and its object...
The meaning is that since a relation is difficult to establish, the status of object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) is also untenable. And thus,

one must necessarily accept that based on such scriptural passages as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," the consciousness (*cit*), which is of the nature of Brahman, beginningless and endless, and self-luminous,
appears as the world of objects (*cetyaprapañca*) solely through superimposition (*adhyasta*) due to the power of beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*).
Therefore, he states that the appearance of multiplicity in consciousness is merely adventitious (aupādhika)—that is, "therefore" (tataḥ).

Since there is thus, in the ultimate sense, no connection between knowledge and its object, it must be said that the perception of the manifold world of objects occurs solely through its superimposition upon the nature of consciousness. And so, by virtue of its connection with various adventitious conditions such as water, waves, and bubbles, the single moon—

Just as one's own nature (svarūpa) is perceived as diverse, so too the Consciousness that serves as the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) appears divided by virtue of its connection with various superimposed mental adjuncts (upādhi). Therefore, the perception of difference in Consciousness is based solely on the differences between objects of cognition such as jars and cloths; it is not ultimately real (pāramārthika). O Brahmins, it is always something quite indescribable, for it is indeed not visible to anyone at all.

One might object: "In that case, why should even a cognition such as 'this is a jar' not be considered superimposed, given that it is known by a subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) such as 'the jar is known,' just like the five [elements]? That Consciousness which is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the phenomenal world is Consciousness alone, always manifesting itself; it is not, however, [dependent] upon its own obstructed empirical usage.
It depends upon another cognition; therefore, it cannot be perceived by any perceiver, since it is reduced to the status of an object of cognition (*cetya*).

To this, he says: "That" (sā). If it were the case that "that"—the seeing—does not manifest at some time during the state of the perception of an object, then [it would not be eternal].

By what means could even this [statement] "it shines" be established? For no manifestation whatsoever is possible without the light of consciousness (cit). Therefore, the meaning is that even in that case, a manifestation whose object is non-existence must be admitted. ||42||
If it is thought that "vibhāna" means "it does not shine," whereas "bhāta" means "it has shone," [then that is incorrect].
In that case, indeed, that which has not appeared cannot be cognition; for cognition is nothing but appearance itself. (43)

One might object: "In that case, since it is said 'it does not appear,' the absence of manifestation is what is perceived; how then can there be the existence of manifestation at that time, given the contradiction between existence and non-existence? Thus he raises the doubt with the words "it does not appear. When an object such as a jar is known in the form "the jar does not appear," it is known precisely as an object of ignorance—that is, as something not manifested—and not as an object of knowledge in the sense of being manifested. Therefore, at that time, that which is being negated—
The meaning is: how can there be a persistence of that which is not being manifested? He answers with the word "tardi" (then).

It is not the case that it does not manifest; rather, even though it manifests as the object of ignorance, it is indeed manifested and not unmanifested. He states the reason for this: "tajjñānam" (that knowledge).

For knowledge is of two kinds: *vṛttijñāna* (knowledge as a mental modification) and *svarūpajñāna* (essential nature-knowledge). In this context, the term "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is derived from the instrumental sense (*karaṇavyutpatti*), meaning "that by which something is known."

Vṛttijñāna (empirical cognition) is the modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) which, through its transformation into the form of an object, becomes associated with the eyes and other sense organs.
The self-luminous *svarūpajñāna* (essential consciousness), which directly perceives that [internal organ] along with its object, is not itself made an object by the *vṛttijñāna*.

Therefore, even the manifestation of that [consciousness] while it remains unobjectified and unknown is indeed a manifestation. This is because both the known and the unknown are witnessed by the radiance of consciousness (*sphuraṇasākṣika*).
This is the meaning of "svāt" (itself). For this very reason it is said: every object, whether known or unknown, is indeed an object of the witness-consciousness (sākṣicaitanya). || 43 ||
O best of the twice-born, one manifestation does not manifest by means of another manifestation.
Manifestation, however, exists as manifestation in the form of being; it is eternally one, for it is not dual.

In the Sūtasamhitā (1.7.47), he states the distinction between this manifestation of the witness-consciousness and the knowledge consisting of mental modification (*vṛttijñāna*)— beginning with the word "bhānam" (manifestation)— as follows: [the] mental modification...

For knowledge, being insentient (*jaḍa*), shines only through another manifestation in the form of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*). The manifestation in the form of the witness does not shine through yet another manifestation, but rather shines by itself. If the manifestation of knowledge—which makes an object manifest—were dependent on another knowledge, then that too would require another, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*); therefore, knowledge [must be self-luminous].
The meaning is that its being cognizable by another cognition is not possible. For if there were another cognition, the cognizability of that [first] cognition could be established;

however, he says "in the form of a means of knowledge" (*mānarūpeṇa*) to show that such [another cognition] does not exist. Knowledge, which appears as distinct due to the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the various objects of perception such as pots and cloths, is perceived as differentiated;
yet, having abandoned that connection with perceptible objects, it is always one and the same in its nature as pure manifestation (*sphuraṇa*), and not otherwise.

"Differentiated" means that in cognitions such as those of a jar or a cloth, the mere manifestation shines forth identically, because it is recognized [as the same] through recognition (pratyabhijñā).
The Self is ever manifest by its own light, and not from anything else.
That which shines by itself is indeed the object of cognition; for it is the illuminator of this [cognition]. || 45 ||

If, because manifestation is one, there is no other flashing forth (*sphuraṇa*) as its object, then how is it perceived? To this he says: "It is manifested" (*bhātam*). The witnessing consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*), which is of the nature of a flashing forth being perceived, shines by its own light alone, and not from any other external source of illumination. For it is heard in scripture: "There the sun does not shine, nor the moon..."

"Then these lightnings do not shine, much less this fire; everything shines only after Him who shines, and by His light all this is illumined. By the words "that which itself," he shows that it is well known in the world that only that which is self-luminous possesses the quality of being an illuminator—such as a lamp and the like—which is independent of any other light of the same kind.

Indeed, its illuminating nature is observed in the world through a lamp; therefore, knowledge, being self-luminous without dependence on another cognition, must illuminate the object to be grasped. For if that [knowledge] were cognizable by another cognition, an infinite regress would result. As for those who hold that consciousness, like the eye and other senses, remains latent while producing a result in the form of "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*) regarding the object—
They describe [the object] as "producing" [knowledge]; even by them, the state of being known (*jñātatā*), which consists in the manifestation of the object, must be admitted to be self-luminous.
This being so, let that very [state of being known] be produced by the instruments such as the eye; what is the use of an internal, redundant knowledge (*jñāna*)? || 45 ||
Therefore, he is the self-luminous witness of all that is witnessed.
The self is not bound by actions through qualities that reside in the witness. || 46 ||

Having thus established that the Self consists solely of non-dual, self-luminous consciousness, he concludes—by the word "therefore"—the previously asserted absence of connection with the actions residing in the objects of perception, since the Self, as the witness of all, does not enter into those objects of perception. || 46 ||
It cannot be said that the post is connected with what is seen. || 47 ||

Accompanied by the *Tātparyadīpikā*—[in the fourth section, the *Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa*]:
Since even the relationship is an object of perception, the relationship pertains to an object that is itself perceivable.
Indeed, the conjunction of perceptible things such as a rope and so forth is observed. || 48 ||

Furthermore, suspecting that such a seer might again have a connection with karma, [the author] refutes this with the word "seer" (*dṛk*): for the designation "seer" applies to such a Self only in dependence upon a connection with the seen (*dṛśya*). Likewise, that karma is also indeed the seen.
It cannot be asserted that a relationship with the nature of the seer (*dṛg-rūpa*) necessarily exists [with the seen].

For a relationship is a property (*dharma*) constituted by two related entities; if that [relationship] were of the nature of the seer, it would not be distinct from the seer as a related entity, and thus its status as a relationship would be lost. Even if it were of the nature of the seen (*dṛśya-rūpa*), because it would be included within the category of the related entity characterized as the seen, it would simply be a related entity, and not a relationship.

The meaning is that it consists of the nature of a relationship. And he demonstrates that the absence of a relationship between the object of perception (*dṛśya*) and the seer (*dṛk*) is well-established by saying, "of that which has become an object of perception" (*dṛśyabhūtasya*). Just as there is no ultimate relationship between an object of perception such as a rope and the seer, because it was previously established that its cognition occurs solely through superimposition (*adhyasta*). || 47 || 48 ||
For the supreme Śruti also declares: "Indeed, this is unattached."
Therefore, the Self is indeed of the nature of consciousness; it is not bound by actions. || 49 ||
He corroborates the stated point with scripture, saying: "asaṅga" (unattached). That scripture is:

"The Puruṣa is unattached," and "Being unattached, it is not attached," and so forth. Therefore—meaning, because there is no real relationship between the two, namely, the seer and the object of sight. || 49 ||
For the Śruti indeed declares the direct Brahman-hood of the Self whose nature is consciousness.
And the supreme Śruti declares the absence of any connection with action for Brahman.

Having thus stated that the inner self (pratyagātman) lacks connection with action because its nature is pure consciousness as a witness, [the author] now shows—by means of the phrase "of Brahman"—that its lack of connection with action is also well-known from scripture, in order to establish that [the self] is non-different from Brahman. For it is heard in scripture: "He does not become greater by good action, nor indeed smaller by evil action."
"By meritorious action one increases, not by what is less. || 50 ||
That being so, O wise ones, how can he be bound by actions?
Therefore, by its own delusion, the Self is manifested as if it were a transmigrating being. || 51 ||

"Thus, this [is he]" means that the Supreme Self (paramātman), which was established through hearing as being free from contact with merit and demerit, is precisely this Self (ātman) abiding in the form of the witness; this is what is taught by sentences such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) through the realization of their identity. If it is thus the case that the Self has no connection with karma, then how can it be a transmigrating being?

From the *Sūtasamhitā*:
"Because there is no cognition of 'you' [as distinct from the Self], it says: 'Therefore,' etc. By 'one's own delusion' (*svamohena*): by the delusion of one's own [true] self (*ātman*)."
The meaning is: by reason of not fully realizing that [the Self] has the nature of non-dual, self-luminous pure consciousness alone. || 51 ||
The distinctions of caste, stage of life, and age arise from the delusion regarding the self.
Having presided over all the Vedas, he would be the one to enjoin them, and not by his own authority.

Regarding the phrase "castes and stages of life" (*varṇāśrama*): the appearance of all specific distinctions such as being a Brahmin or being a householder within the Self is based solely on the habitual identification (*tādātmyābhyāsa*) with the gross body and so forth. Regarding the word "superimposing" (*adhyasya*): it means by the superimposition of Brahminhood and the like. Regarding the phrase "of all the Vedas": [it refers to passages such as] "A Brahmin should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava," and "A King [should sacrifice] with the Rājasūya."
The meaning is: [this applies] to such passages as "with which one should sacrifice," and so forth. || 52 ||
Due to ignorance, this person possesses a cognition that is otherwise than [the truth], such as the notion of being human and so forth.
But even the supreme self is bound helplessly by karmas. || 53 ||

"Knowledge other than [true] knowledge arises from ignorance. For ignorance (*avidyā*) is indeed twofold: the power of projection (*vikṣepa-śakti*) and the power of concealment (*āvaraṇa-śakti*). Among these, by the power of concealment, the specific nature of the Self—its identity with Brahman—is concealed, just as the blue back, triangularity, and so forth [conceal the true nature of a conch]. By the power of projection, false things such as "humanity" [are projected], just like silver [is projected upon a mother-of-pearl shell].

The meaning is "the establishment of the formless. Regarding the term "helpless" (*avaśa*): it means that for one who possesses the conceit of identity with gods and so forth, there is indeed dependence on the merit and demerit produced by them, and not independence. || 53 ||
Though bound by his own māyā in the course of worldly transactions through actions,
this one is in reality the Supreme Self and is indeed not bound by them.

If even the Supreme Self, having assumed the state of an individual soul (*jīva*), is subject to the helplessness of karma according to the manner described above, then what is gained by the knowledge of the Self as the Supreme Self?

To this he says: "By actions" (*karmabhiḥ*). The meaning is that for the Supreme Self—who, during the state of phenomenal existence (*vyavahāra*), directly perceives the connection of his own self with karma as being composed of *māyā*—there is not even the slightest trace of real bondage.
The state of being the witness of all for one's own self, and the distinctness of that self from the body and so forth.
And having understood the state of Brahman from the Śruti, one is indeed not bound by ritual actions.
How, then, can one who has attained the state of a living being (*jīva*) due to ignorance dispel the subjection to karma? To this he says:

"Of one's own self" (*svātmanaḥ*). Having ascertained—by means of the previously stated reasonings—that the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is distinct from the body and so forth and consists solely of witnessing consciousness, and having known its nature as Brahman through the instruction of a teacher based on the sacred texts such as "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*)— [The remainder of the sentence follows: ...having realized that [the self] is of the nature of Brahman...
This is the meaning. Even though indirect knowledge of Brahman as the Self lacks the capacity to remove the immediate delusion of saṃsāra, [the performance of] karma—

The fact that [this knowledge] brings about the cessation of bondage was previously established in the passage beginning with: "The indirect realization of Brahman is verbal and preceded by a teacher" (verse 55).
The Self, which is the witness of all and is devoid of caste and stage of life.
Perceiving [the self] as being of the nature of Brahman, one is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence. || 56 ||

"Beholding" (paśyan): the meaning is that he who, through reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), realizes the aforementioned identity of Brahman and the Self by dispelling both doubt and contrary notions, becomes liberated at the very moment of that realization from the bondage of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), which is the effect of ignorance—the cause—having been removed. || 56 ||
Therefore, due to the lack of full knowledge of one's own self, one resorts to the notion of "I" in the body.
The wise man performs everything prescribed in all the scriptures; of this there is no doubt. || 57 ||

Thus, because there is an absence of connection with ritual action once the knowledge of Brahman as the Self has arisen, he concludes that all rites such as the Agnihotra prescribed in the Karma-kāṇḍa pertain only to one who possesses the superimposition of identity with the body and so forth, by saying "therefore" (ataḥ). || 57 ||
Such is this supreme knowledge of Śaṅkara, which destroys worldly existence.
For it arises indeed from the very grace of living beings, and from their own power alone. || 58 ||

Regarding the phrase "for [it is] from Śakti alone": the particle *eva* (alone) is intended to exclude connection with anything else; the meaning is that [the supreme knowledge arises] from the supreme Śakti, whose nature is consciousness, and not from any other deity. Furthermore, the particle *eva* in the phrase "only from grace" (*prasādādeva*) is intended to exclude non-connection; the meaning is that the arising of supreme knowledge occurs only when there is the grace of Śakti, and not when it is absent. Moreover, the attainment of Brahmanhood through the grace of Śakti is described in the Taittirīya...
In the Kāropaniṣad it is said: "Into that very space there came a woman, Umā Haimavatī, who was exceedingly beautiful;
he said to her, 'What is this yakṣa?'; she replied, 'It is Brahman. (58)
The supreme power, which is of the nature of consciousness and designated as "Parā," is manifested as speech.
I worship her incessantly with devotion, she whose body is half that of Śrīkaṇṭha. || 59 ||

Therefore, he begins the hymn which is the cause for His grace, starting with the words "Speech" (*vāk*) and so forth. That supreme power, whose nature is consciousness, manifests itself first in the form of the Supreme (*parā*) while undergoing the process of *vivarta* (illusory transformation) into the form of sound. Arising from the bursting forth of the *bindu*, it is the sound that is woven through everything. It is the cause of the desire to express meaning among living beings, produced by the wind generated by the effort [of speech].

The vibrationless state (*niṣpanda*) manifested in the *mūlādhāra* as the cause of all bonds is called *parā-vāk*. As the Teacher has said: "That state which first arises from the *mūlādhāra* is of the nature of *parā*. He characterizes it as "Śrīkaṇṭha": in the *Śrīkaṇṭha*-nyāsa, Śrīkaṇṭha is the embodiment of the letter *la*; for the letter *a* is the essence of all speech.

*Sūtasamhitā*, 7.51: "The letter *a* is indeed all speech; this [speech], being manifested by the *sparśa* and *ūṣman* [consonants], becomes manifold and assumes various forms."

This is because of such scriptural passages as "it exists," and so forth. Or rather, the supreme power (*parā śakti*) whose nature is speech (*vāgrūpā*), when manifesting in the form of *vaikharī* (articulate speech), consists of all fruits;
the meaning is that she is the power of Śrīkaṇṭha due to her identity with the totality of all speech. || 59 ||
And that power which is the ideation of desire has the perfectly full Śiva as its interior.
I worship her with devotion alone, she who bestows my desired fruits. || 60 ||

Regarding the term *icchā-saṃjñā* (the designation "Will"): that very same Supreme Power (*parā śakti*), when defined by the specific characteristic of the entire universe as the object of her desire, is called the power of Will (*icchā-śakti*). She is qualified as "complete" (*paripūrṇā*): she is so described because her womb (*udara*) is accompanied by that which is complete—namely, the infinite Śiva, whose nature consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*sat-cit-ānanda*). [The text continues with] *japā-ku*...

The meaning is that [the letter] is pervaded by the self-luminous consciousness of Paraśiva, which, through the coloration of memory (*smarāga*), is like a crystal. For thus, in the *Śrīkaṇṭhādinyāsa* of the letter *A*, the teachers have stated that its form is Śakti: "Pūrṇodarī, Virajā, and thirdly Śālmalī. Since this is the power of will (*icchāśakti*), the meaning is that she is capable of bestowing the desired fruit upon her worshiper.
That power which is supreme, manifest, and the seed of everything.
I worship her incessantly with devotion, together with Nakulīśa and Śiva. || 61 ||

Regarding the phrase "become the seed": the connection is that she is the Supreme Consciousness-Power (*paramā cicchakti*), who has swallowed up the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) and serves as the direct seed for the entire universe about to arise again. Regarding the phrase "endowed with Nakulīśa Śiva":
in the *Śrīkaṇṭhādi-nyāsa*, Nakulīśa is the name of the letter *Ha*, which exists in the form of the body of Nakulīśa.

Accompanied by Śiva in the form of the letter *ha*, she is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), capable of generating the universe, consisting of the seed-syllable, and whose form is consciousness; she is denoted by the letter *ka* as *Śakti*, because the Teachers have stated: "Now, the name shall pervade the universe. Therefore, the meaning is that she is connected with Nakulīśa Śiva in the form of the letter *ha* through the relationship of the signifier and the signified. || 61 ||
Though her form is upward-facing, she is also downward-facing; likewise, though situated below, she dwells in the center.
I bow to her who, though abiding within as the intermediate form, bestows boons.

"Having an upward form" (*ūrdhvarūpā*): she is so called because her form consists of the dissolution that exists after the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) has ceased, occurring above—that is, subsequent to—the proliferation of effects. Likewise, although she has an upward form, she also has a downward form (*adhorūpā*), for her form consists of the causal essence capable of producing that [world], existing below—that is, at the time of the origination of—the phenomenal world of effects.

She is described as such. Thus, by virtue of being the cause, she who exists below even the phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*)—though situated beneath it—is that very same "intermediate" (*madhyagā*) power; for it has been shown that the consciousness-power (*cicchakti*), which exists pervading even the intermediate time between the prior non-existence and the destruction of the phenomenal expansion, is itself pervasive throughout the three periods of time. Regarding the word "within" (*antastha*): although she is of a middle nature through her pervasion of time...
Existing within the manifold of effects as their internal material cause; or rather, [existing within] the stationary and moving [beings].
[Page 426, verse 7]
Accompanied by the *Tātparyadīpikā*—
[in the fourth section, the *Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa*]—
She remains having entered within the world created by herself as its very self-nature. For it is heard in scripture:
"Having created that, He entered into that very thing. (62)
By means of arrangements refined through phonemes, in the form of a university.
I reverently praise her who shines forth within speech. 63.

In this context, having perceived that what is of the nature of the upper [state] possesses the nature of the lower, and that what is of the nature of the lower possesses the nature of the middle, and that the Intermediate Speech (*madhyamā*) abides within,
he demonstrates the absence of such contradiction by means of the phrase "by arrangements" (*vinyāsaiḥ*). By means of arrangements—
specific structures such as prose and verse— composed of the phonemes beginning with *a* and ending with *ha*, she is the locus of all branches of knowledge.
The meaning is: "that [power] which is shining forth in the word in that manner. || 63 ||
She exists as one, as two, and likewise as sixteenfold.
And I salute her who is divided into thirty-two forms and who bestows the supreme self. 64.

"And as one" means that it first exists in a single mode, as the nature of *vaikharī* speech manifested by the palate and lips; then it remains divided into two modes through the distinction between vowels and consonants; and furthermore, it exists in sixteen ways—
She exists divided into the sixteen forms beginning with *ka* and ending with the visarga (*ḥ*). Furthermore, she is differentiated into thirty-two divisions:

twenty-five beginning with *ka*, eight beginning with *ya*, and so forth; since *ra* and *la* are non-different, the letter *lū* is not to be counted separately. The letter *kṣa* is also not distinct due to being a conjunct consonant (*saṃyuktākṣara*). The letter *ha* as well, because it denotes the primal nature (*mūlaprakṛti*), is the root of the entire universe.
Abiding as *latva*, she does not deserve to be counted in her individual (*vyaṣṭi*) form. For this very reason it has been said: "followed by Nakulīśa and Śiva.

Thus, seven [letters] beginning with *pa* remain. And so the meaning is this: she who abides divided into the thirty-two consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *sa*, thus existing in the form of the *mātṛkā*, is the Supreme.
The meaning is that she is Śakti. || 64 ||
By means of the letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa', which are utterly stainless.
We praise her who shines forth through all words and bestows bliss.
Regarding "beginning with *a*": these are the phonemes from *a* to *kṣa*, which constitute the parts of the power (*śakti*) that is divided according to the aforementioned distinctions;

they are exceedingly pure because they consist of nectar (*amṛta*). Having been purified upon the petals of the six lotuses beginning with the Foundation (*ādhāra*), they have flowed forth as drops of nectar from the lunar orb situated in the twelve [petals] in the form of the phonemes from *a* to *kṣa*.
They have been transformed. As the Teachers have said:
"Emerging from the *mūlādhāra* like a flash of lightning, possessing a terrifying luster and a subtle form, it ascends to the crown of the head as the most minute essence, the root of all lights."

The Sūtasamhitā says:
"That [meditation], which is skilled in traversing the path along with Puṣṇan, and which is bound to Savitṛ,
when meditated upon, immediately causes the nectar of the Sun to flow forth from the well-prepared Soma."
"The stream of drops that falls upon the head becomes nectar;
when it takes the form of letters, by means of those [letters], one should wash the face and limbs."

The meaning is: that power which shines as the *mātṛkā*, consisting of sounds existing in the form of phonemes (*varṇa*) of such a stainless nature, established as the essence of phonemes, words, and sentences, and as their various structural arrangements (*saṃsthāna-bheda*). || 65 ||
She who shines like a dancer in the forms of Lakṣmī, Vāk, and others.
I bow to that lady of beautiful countenance, who is liberated from both beginning and end.

"Like a dancer" means: just as a dancer, being herself only one, appears as many through various forms assumed for the sake of others, so too the single supreme power (*parā śakti*) appears as the manifold powers such as Lakṣmī and Vāk, whose distinctions are merely imagined—this is the meaning.
"Free from beginning and end" means: free from both that which is the beginning, namely birth, and that which is the end, namely destruction.
The meaning is that it exists at all times. || 66 ||
From Brahmā down to the stationary beings, all have emerged from her alone.
Salutations again and again to her in whom they all dissolve eternally. || 67 ||

Regarding the phrase "beginning with Brahmā": the meaning is that the origin, subsistence, and dissolution of the entire manifold of enjoyers (*bhoktṛ-prapañca*), which extends from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, are imagined within her own nature. For it is heard in scripture: "From which indeed these beings are born; by which, once born, they live; into which they enter when they depart."
Peace! || 67 ||
From whom the universe, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) and ending with the specific elements (viśeṣa), has emerged.
I bow to that Ambikā, in whom alone all things go to their dissolution. || 68 ||

He states that it is not only the substratum for the manifold of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ-prapañca*), but also the substratum for the conceptualization of the manifold of the enjoyed (*bhogya-prapañca*)— namely,

"the Great One and so forth" (*mahadādi*). Because the Root Nature (*mūla-prakṛti*) is absolutely free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpaka*) and has attained non-differentiation from the aspect of consciousness (*cicchakti*) like milk and water, and because the Great Principle (*mahat-tattva*) is the first effect, it is taken as the beginning.

It is given. The meaning is that this entire world—beginning with the Great Principle (mahat), the ego (ahaṅkāra), and so forth, and ending with specific objects such as jars and cloths, which consists of the form of experience—has arisen from this Supreme Power and remains sustained by having arisen from it. || 68 ||
She who assumes the form of the Guru, who is to be cherished, and who bestows the knowledge of domestic life.
We praise her who delights in those devoted to the secret [teachings] and who is established within the cave. || 69 ||
